front_matter.purpose:
# Purpose

This Policy & Procedure Manual sets out how **[AGENCY NAME]** operates its **[Adult Home / Enriched Housing Program]** in New York State. Depending on the licenses and certifications **[AGENCY NAME]** holds or is applying for, the program may include an Assisted Living Residence (ALR), Enhanced Assisted Living Residence (EALR), Special Needs Assisted Living Residence (SNALR), and/or the Medicaid Assisted Living Program (ALP).

The manual has four purposes:

1. **Put the rules into daily practice.** It turns the requirements of 18 NYCRR Parts 485, 487, 488 and 494, 10 NYCRR Part 1001, and the related Public Health Law and Social Services Law provisions into written policies and procedures that staff can follow.
2. **Protect residents.** It sets standards for admission and retention, resident rights, grievances, medication management, supervision, incident reporting, emergency preparedness and quality assurance. These standards protect residents' health, safety, dignity and choice.
3. **Support the state's review.** It is written to be submitted to the New York State Department of Health (DOH) Regional Office as the Schedule 6, Program Information (Part II) policy content of the Adult Care Facility Common Application (form DOH-5098), and to be used when the program is surveyed or recertified.
4. **Give staff and the governing body one reference.** It is a single source of agency policy for administrators, case managers, direct-care staff and the governing body.

This manual does not replace the laws and regulations it cites. If anything here conflicts with a statute, regulation or DOH directive, the law controls. Staff should report the conflict to the Administrator so the manual can be corrected.

# How to Use This Manual

## Who should use it
The governing body, the Administrator (and Program Coordinator, if enriched housing), the Designated Individual (if ALP), case managers, nursing staff, direct-care, housekeeping, food service and maintenance staff, and volunteers should all know the sections that apply to their work.

## How it is organized
- The main sections follow the **numbering of the 32 items on DOH-5098** (Schedule 6, Program Information, Part II). A reviewer can go straight from a form item to the policy that answers it.
- Items 13 (EALR), 14 (SNALR) and 15 (ALP) apply **only** to agencies holding or seeking those license types. If **[AGENCY NAME]** does not hold or seek that license type, mark the section "Not Applicable" and say so in the application.
- Items 17, 20 and 26 of DOH-5098 state their own sub-requirements. Those sections keep the form's wording.
- **Appendix A** is the cross-reference to the official checklist. It lists each item of DOH-5098 and identifies the policy (section and page) that satisfies it. Use it to prepare the application and to check completeness before submission and at each update.
- Items on DOH-5098 that call for administrative paperwork rather than policy content are not written as policies. They are assembled separately and noted in Appendix A. They are: application-type check-boxes (item 1), administrator/coordinator qualification documents (item 2), the Mental Health Agreement (item 9), the list of forms (item 12), support letters, the nursing-facility transfer agreement and the DSS contract (items 15d–15f), the waiver and equivalency list (item 16), the workers' compensation certificate (item 18), the dietary consultant agreement, resume, licenses and kitchen/dining room diagram (items 26(b)–(d) and (f)), and the resident fund account statement (item 31).

## Customizing the manual
1. Replace every **[AGENCY NAME]** placeholder and every other bracketed field (program type, address, county, bed count, license types, names and titles) with the agency's actual information.
2. Delete or mark "Not Applicable" any section for a license type the agency does not hold or seek.
3. Where a policy states a number (hours, ratios, square footage, time frames), confirm it against the current regulation and the facility's size, license type and operating certificate before adopting it.
4. Where a policy refers to a DOH-mandated form, use the DOH form. A substitute needs DOH equivalency approval and must be listed on DOH-5098 under items 12 and 16.

## Submitting the application
- Applications are submitted through **NYSECON**.
- Schedules 1–5 are reviewed by DOH Central Office (Part I). Schedule 6 (DOH-5098) is reviewed by the **DOH Regional Office for the county where the facility is or will be** (Part II). Part I and Part II may be reviewed at the same time, and final approval needs both.
- Send the completed Schedule 6 with a cover letter to the Regional Office, and copy the cover letter to the assigned Central Office project manager in Albany. Schedule 6 may be submitted at any time, but no later than **90 days after the Part I approval notice**.
- For each item, give the attachment number of the responsive policy, or check **"No Change"** where the form offers that box. For ALR and ALP applicants, the form's instructions say to submit only changed or new materials.
- Model documents, such as the model residency agreements, are posted on the DOH Common Application web page.

## Adoption, currency and training
- **Adoption.** This manual is not in force until the **governing body of [AGENCY NAME]** formally adopts it. Record the adoption date and the governing body's action on the approval page: **[DATE ADOPTED / RESOLUTION NO.]**.
- **Keeping it current.** Review the manual at least annually. Review it also whenever a law, regulation or DOH guidance changes, an operating certificate or license type changes, or a survey, incident or quality review shows a need. Record each revision with its date and the governing body's approval. Make sure no outdated copies remain in use. Statutory and regulatory figures that change on a schedule, such as minimum wage and home care aide rates, must be checked at each review.
- **Staff training.** All staff must be trained on the manual. This covers new-hire orientation and the in-service training required by regulation. Staff must also be retrained when policies change. Keep signed acknowledgments and training records in each staff member's personnel file.
- **Access.** Keep a current copy where staff can reach it on every shift, and make the relevant parts available to the regulators on request.

# Regulatory Framework

The program is licensed and regulated in New York State by the Department of Health. The rules below are cited by their exact cite text. The manual's policies draw on them, but the full current text controls, so verify it when customizing and updating the manual.

## Governing rules

### Operating certificates (Title 18 NYCRR Part 485)
- **18 NYCRR §485.5**, Operating certificates: certificate term up to 4 years and non-transferable; the facility may not use a designation not on the certificate (§485.5(f)); 120-day written notice and a DOH-approved plan before closure (§485.5(k)).
- **18 NYCRR §485.6**, Application for operating certificate: Part I and Part II approval. Part II must include the disaster plan, admission and residency agreements, personnel policies and service plans, and final inspection requirements.
- **18 NYCRR §485.7**, Renewal of operating certificates: apply for renewal 45 to 90 days before expiration.

### Adult homes (Title 18 NYCRR Part 487)
- **18 NYCRR §487.4**, Admission standards: admit and retain only people whose needs the home may lawfully meet; the list of people who may not be accepted or retained; medical evaluation (DSS-3122) and administrator interview; documents given to applicants; efforts at alternative placement.
- **18 NYCRR §487.5**, Resident protections: resident rights statement, resident organizations, written grievance system, admission agreement content, and termination procedures.
- **18 NYCRR §487.7**, Resident services: minimum services, supervision and incident duties, personal care, and medication management.
- **18 NYCRR §487.9**, Personnel: orientation and in-service training, staffing schedules, personnel records, health and TB assessments, first-aid coverage, Justice Center staff exclusion list checks, administrator qualifications, and staffing levels.
- **18 NYCRR §487.10**, Records and reports: resident and facility records, quality assurance plan and committee, financial and statistical reports, mandated forms, postings, and retention.
- **18 NYCRR §487.11**, Environmental standards: sprinklers, bedroom and bathroom standards, and call system.
- **18 NYCRR §487.12**, Disaster and emergency planning: DOH-approved plan, fire and evacuation drills, drill records, notifications to DOH, and HPN contacts.
- **18 NYCRR §487.14**, Reporting of reportable incidents: Justice Center reporting and investigation duties, in addition to other Part 487 reporting.

### Enriched housing (Title 18 NYCRR Part 488)
- **18 NYCRR §488.9**, Enriched housing program personnel: program coordinator hours, case manager time, and combined personal care, housekeeping and food staffing.

### Medicaid Assisted Living Program (Title 18 NYCRR Part 494)
- **18 NYCRR §494.5**, ALP resident services and services in the capitated rate.
- **18 NYCRR §494.6**, ALP personnel: designated individual, qualified case manager and minimum staffing.

### Assisted Living Residences (Title 10 NYCRR Part 1001)
- **10 NYCRR §1001.5**, Applications for ALR licensure and EALR/SNALR certification.
- **10 NYCRR §1001.10**, Resident services (ALR), including EALR and SNALR service rules and medication policies.
- **10 NYCRR §1001.11**, Personnel (ALR): case manager hours, resident aide training, nursing coverage for EALR/SNALR, and related staff health records.
- **10 NYCRR §1001.13**, ALR structural and environmental standards.

### Statutes
- **Public Health Law §4651**, Assisted living definitions (Art. 46-B).
- **Public Health Law §4655**, Enhanced assisted living certification and aging in place.
- **Public Health Law §4656**, General requirements; fees; quality reporting and price posting. Operating an ALR without approval is a class A misdemeanor (§4656(5)).
- **Social Services Law §461-b**, Establishment of adult care facilities; eligible operators; ownership changes. Operating without approval is a class A misdemeanor (§461-b(2)(d)).
- **Social Services Law §461-a**, Inspections/surveys of adult care facilities.
- **Social Services Law §460-d**, Posting of complaint line and resident rights materials. The DOH adult care facility complaint line is 1-866-893-6772.
- **Social Services Law §461-l**, Assisted living program (Medicaid).
- **Public Health Law §3614(6)**, ALP capitated rate methodology.
- **Public Health Law §4403-f**, Managed long term care (ALP exclusion).

### Employment law
- **Labor Law §196-b**, Paid sick leave.
- **Labor Law §652**, Minimum wage, including home care aide minimums for LHCSA aides.

The **[AGENCY NAME]** Regional Office is the DOH Regional Office for the county where the facility is located: **[REGIONAL OFFICE / COUNTY]**. The DOH adult care facility complaint line (1-866-893-6772) must be posted as required by Social Services Law §460-d.

## Official policy checklist and application documents
DOH reviews this manual against the following official documents:

1. **Adult Care Facility Common Application, Schedule 6, Program Information (Part II), Regional Office, form DOH-5098** (version DOH-5098 (1/26), 5 pages), issued by the NYS Department of Health. It is the official Part II program-review checklist for new adult homes and enriched housing programs, changes of operator, and new ALR, EALR, SNALR and ALP applications. https://www.health.ny.gov/forms/doh-5098.pdf
2. **Adult Care Facility and Assisted Living Common Application** (Schedules 1–5 are reviewed by Central Office for Part I; Schedule 6 is DOH-5098), issued by the NYS DOH Bureau of Licensure and Certification. Applications are submitted through NYSECON. Model documents, such as the model residency agreements, are posted on this page. https://www.health.ny.gov/facilities/adult_care/application/

**Appendix A** maps each item of DOH-5098 to the policy in this manual that satisfies it, using the form's own item numbers. Where an item calls for administrative paperwork rather than policy content, Appendix A says so and points to the separate submission. Use Appendix A to check that every official item is covered before the application is submitted, and again after each revision of the manual.

## Obligations that apply to this manual
- **Customize it.** Replace all **[AGENCY NAME]** placeholders and bracketed fields with the agency's actual information, and confirm the figures against the current rules.
- **Adopt it.** The governing body must formally adopt the manual.
- **Keep it current.** Revise it when the rules, the operating certificate or the agency's practices change.
- **Train staff.** All staff must be trained on it at hire and when it changes, with the training documented.

citations.title: Admission standards
citations.requirement: Admit and retain only people whose needs the home may lawfully meet. Lists 13 people who may not be accepted or retained, including those needing continual medical or nursing care, chronically bedfast, chronic unmanaged incontinence, or danger to self or others. Requires a medical evaluation (DSS-3122) within 30 days before admission and at least every 12 months, and a written administrator interview. Applicants receive the admission agreement, rights statement, facility rules and Ombudsman/legal-services sheet at or before the interview, and may review the latest DOH inspection report. Requires persistent efforts at alternative placement when a resident can no longer be retained.

citations.title: Resident protections
citations.requirement: (a) Resident rights statement: posted, given at admission, reviewed annually, with 19 minimum rights. (b) Resident organizations. (c) Written grievance system with posting of the procedure. (d) Admission agreement content, including SSI/HR personal-allowance offer and refunds. (f) Termination: 30 days' written notice on a DOH form, list of free legal and advocacy services, copy to the regional office within 5 days, and a court proceeding if the resident objects.

citations.title: Resident services
citations.requirement: (a) Minimum services: room, board, housekeeping, supervision, personal care, case management, activities. (d) Supervision duties, evacuations, missing-resident steps, emergency and illness response, death, suicide attempt and felony reporting, and the Incident Report triggers. (e) Personal care, including a ban on physical restraints and monthly weights. (f) Medication management: self-administration, staff assistance limits, secure storage, no injectables by staff (except licensed staff), no dose changes without physician authorization.

citations.title: Personnel
citations.requirement: Orientation and in-service training with documentation (a)(3)-(5). Staffing schedules kept 12 months (a)(6). Personnel records (a)(7). Annual physician/PA/RN statement plus TB assessment (a)(8). Staff must speak, read and write English (a)(13). First-aid-trained person on duty at all times (a)(15). Notify the regional office within 3 business days of key vacancies (a)(16). Justice Center staff exclusion list check (a)(7), (a)(17). Administrator approval, hours and qualifications (c). Resident volunteers and employees (b). Supervision census table, personal care 3.75 hrs, housekeeping 1.0 hr and food service 2.0 hrs per resident per week ((f)-(j), per the fact-checked research).

citations.title: Records and reports
citations.requirement: Resident and facility records (c)-(d). Quality assurance plan updated at least every two years, with a quality improvement committee meeting at least every six months (d)(5)(ix). Annual financial statement DSS-2963, quarterly statistical report, quarterly resident roster (e). Mandated forms (f). Postings (g). Retention (h): 3 years after death or discharge for individual records, 7 years for program, business and renewal records.

citations.title: Environmental standards
citations.requirement: Per the fact-checked research: sprinklers throughout buildings of 25+ beds, bedroom minimums of 100 sq ft single and 160 sq ft double, 1 toilet per 6 and 1 bath per 10 residents, and a call system.

citations.title: Disaster and emergency planning
citations.requirement: DOH-approved written disaster and emergency plan. Monthly staff fire drills at varied times, with full and partial evacuation. Quarterly drills with residents, and one total evacuation every 12 months. Annual observation of a resident drill by fire authorities, a certified service agency or DOH. Drill records. Notify DOH by the next business day of a work stoppage, fire, loss of a fire system, no hot water or loss of essential services. HPN account with 24/7 contacts, kept current monthly.

citations.title: Reporting of reportable incidents
citations.requirement: Facilities subject to the Justice Center, and their mandated reporters, report a reportable incident to the Justice Center immediately on reasonable cause. The facility must start an investigation. These duties are in addition to the other reporting duties in Part 487.

citations.title: Enriched housing program personnel
citations.requirement: For enriched housing programs: program coordinator hours, case manager 0.5 hr per resident per week, and 6 hrs per resident per week of combined personal care, housekeeping and food staff (per the fact-checked research).

citations.title: ALP resident services and services in the capitated rate
citations.requirement: Defines ALP resident services and the services covered by the Medicaid capitated rate (per the fact-checked research).

citations.title: ALP personnel
citations.requirement: Designated individual, qualified case manager, and minimum staffing at the §487.9(f)(6) levels (per the fact-checked research).

citations.title: Applications for ALR licensure and EALR/SNALR certification
citations.requirement: Must also hold an adult home or enriched housing certificate. 60-day response rule. ALR approval lapses if the residence is not licensed and operating within 1 year. Licensure fee rules (per the fact-checked research).

citations.title: Resident services (ALR)
citations.requirement: Minimum ALR services: housing, 24-hour on-site monitoring, daily food service, case management, ISP, and personal care and/or home care. Residents may use outside providers and choose their own health care providers. Case management duties include evaluation before admission and at least every 12 months using the DOH personal data and resident evaluation form. Health services come from an Article 36 home care agency unless EALR/SNALR-approved. Hospice permitted without EALR when conditions are met. Medication policies must meet 18 NYCRR 487.7(f)/488.7(d). Medication assistance record and PRN rules. EALR and SNALR service rules, including the 24-hour skilled nursing retention exception.

citations.title: Personnel (ALR)
citations.requirement: Case manager on site at least 20 hrs/week under 25 beds, scaled up to 40 hrs/week at 45+ beds. Resident aides: 40 hrs initial training, 12 hrs annual in-service, and an annual performance assessment with direct observation. Orientation topics and written job descriptions. Bloodborne pathogen exposure program and post-exposure procedure. EALR/SNALR: RN 8 hrs/day 5 days/week, LPN 8 hrs/day the other 2 days, RN on call 24/7, with a waiver option at 40 or fewer beds. Immunization and TB records for EALR/SNALR direct-care staff. Advanced home health aide rules.

citations.title: ALR structural and environmental standards
citations.requirement: Additional structural standards for ALRs. SNALR beds must be in a fixed area (per the fact-checked research).

citations.title: Assisted living definitions (Art. 46-B)
citations.requirement: ALR means 5 or more residents with 24-hour on-site monitoring. ALP is excluded from the definition.

citations.title: Enhanced assisted living certification and aging in place
citations.requirement: EALR certification and aging-in-place rules, including the physician's report.

citations.title: General requirements; fees; quality reporting and price posting
citations.requirement: ALR biennial fee. ALRs must post starting monthly rate, rent range, approved agreement and fee summary on the website and in the facility, and report annual quality measures to DOH. Operating an ALR without approval is a class A misdemeanor (§4656(5)).

citations.title: Establishment of adult care facilities; eligible operators; ownership changes
citations.requirement: Eligible operator structures. DOH approval of LLC articles before filing. Transfer of 10% or more of interests needs prior DOH approval, and smaller transfers need 90 days' notice (§461-b(9)). Operating without approval is a class A misdemeanor (§461-b(2)(d)).

citations.title: Assisted living program (Medicaid)
citations.requirement: ALP eligibility. Requires a LHCSA or CHHA under identical ownership and PHHPC approval. Case-by-case public need review for new beds from April 1, 2025.

citations.title: ALP capitated rate methodology
citations.requirement: ALP capitated rates equal 50% of low-intensity nursing home prices by wage-equalization region.

citations.title: Operating certificates
citations.requirement: Certificate term up to 4 years, non-transferable. Facility may not use a designation not on the certificate (§485.5(f)). 120-day written notice and DOH-approved plan before closure (§485.5(k)).

citations.title: Application for operating certificate
citations.requirement: Part I and Part II approval. Part II must include the disaster plan, admission and residency agreements, personnel policies and service plans. Final inspection requirements.

citations.title: Renewal of operating certificates
citations.requirement: Apply for renewal 45 to 90 days before expiration.

citations.title: Inspections/surveys of adult care facilities
citations.requirement: Cited in the fact-checked research as the basis for recertification surveys every 12 or 18 months. Correct cited violations within 30 days (research checklist).

citations.title: Posting of complaint line and resident rights materials
citations.requirement: Cited in the fact-checked research for posting the DOH ACF complaint line (1-866-893-6772) and resident rights materials. Do Not Refer List consequences.

citations.title: Paid sick leave
citations.requirement: 40 hours of paid sick leave for 5-99 employees, 56 hours for 100+ (per the fact-checked research).

citations.title: Minimum wage
citations.requirement: From 1/1/2026: $17.00/hr in NYC, Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester; $16.00/hr elsewhere. General rates stay the same on 1/1/2027. Home care aide minimum for LHCSA aides is $19.65/$18.65 in 2026 and $20.00/$19.00 on 1/1/2027 (per the fact-checked research).

citations.title: Managed long term care (ALP exclusion)
citations.requirement: People enrolled in the assisted living program are not eligible for MLTC (per the fact-checked research).

policies.title: Organization, Governing Body, Licensure Stack and Regulatory Compliance
policies.applies_to: Owners, governing body, administrator and all management staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To state how [AGENCY NAME] is organized and governed, which approvals it must hold to operate as an Adult Home / Enriched Housing Program with an Assisted Living Residence (ALR) and any EALR, SNALR or ALP add-on, and how it keeps those approvals current.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will operate only under the approvals issued to it by the NYS Department of Health (DOH). An ALR serves 5 or more residents with 24-hour on-site monitoring (PHL §4651), and it must also hold an adult home or enriched housing operating certificate (10 NYCRR §1001.5). The Enhanced ALR (EALR) and Special Needs ALR (SNALR) are add-on certifications. The Assisted Living Program (ALP) is a separate approval and is not part of the ALR definition (PHL §4651). The facility will not accept residents, advertise or use a designation that is not on its operating certificate (18 NYCRR §485.5(f)). Operating an adult care facility or an ALR without approval is a class A misdemeanor (SSL §461-b(2)(d); PHL §4656(5)). The owner or operator is an eligible operator structure under SSL §461-b. The governing body is responsible for compliance with 18 NYCRR Parts 485-488, 494 and 10 NYCRR Part 1001 and for the policies in this manual. The Part II application contents (disaster plan, admission and residency agreements, personnel policies and service plans) are kept in this manual as required by 18 NYCRR §485.6.

definitions.definition: The DOH certificate authorizing an adult home or enriched housing program. It lasts up to 4 years and cannot be transferred (18 NYCRR §485.5).
Assisted Living Residence: an entity serving 5 or more adult residents with 24-hour on-site monitoring, licensed under PHL Article 46-B.
Enhanced ALR and Special Needs ALR, add-on certifications to the ALR license.
Assisted Living Program: a separately approved Medicaid program, not within the ALR definition.
The DOH regional office (Capital District, Central NY, Western NY or Metropolitan Area) that reviews Part II, surveys the facility and receives notices.

procedures: The governing body adopts this manual by written resolution before filing Part II. It reviews and re-adopts the manual at least annually, and the minutes record this.

Before any construction or filing, the owner confirms with the DOH Bureau of Adult Care Facility Licensure and Certification ((518) 408-1624, acfcon@health.ny.gov) that the ownership structure qualifies as an eligible operator under SSL §461-b.

If the owner is an LLC, the administrator or owner's counsel submits the proposed articles of organization, including the purpose language, to DOH for approval before filing with the NYS Department of State.

The administrator files the Part I and Part II ACF Common Application. Part II includes the disaster plan, admission and residency agreements, personnel policies and service plans (18 NYCRR §485.6). The administrator answers DOH questions promptly. DOH has 60 days to respond to ALR applications (10 NYCRR §1001.5), and the administrator logs each DOH request and response date.

The administrator applies for the ALR license, and for EALR or SNALR certification if offered, only together with the adult home or enriched housing certificate. The ALR license fee is paid with the application: $500 plus $50 per resident above 400% FPL (maximum $5,000), plus $2,000 for EALR or SNALR, or $3,000 for both (PHL §4656; 10 NYCRR §1001.5).

The administrator calendars the 1-year deadline after ALR approval. If the residence is not licensed and operating within 1 year, the approval lapses (10 NYCRR §1001.5), and the owner reports readiness status to the governing body at 90, 180 and 270 days.

The administrator keeps the posted operating certificate and ALR license current. Staff and marketing materials may use only the designations on the certificate (ALR, EALR, SNALR, ALP), and the administrator approves all brochures, web pages and signs before release.

The administrator calendars the certificate expiration date and files the renewal application 45 to 90 days before expiration (18 NYCRR §485.7). The first reminder goes to the governing body 120 days before expiration.
The administrator calendars the biennial ALR fee and pays it by its due date. The business office keeps the payment record.

Before any transfer of ownership interests, the owner notifies the administrator. A transfer of 10% or more requires prior DOH approval. A smaller transfer requires written notice to DOH at least 90 days before it takes effect (SSL §461-b(9)). No transfer closes until the DOH approval or the notice period is documented. The operating certificate is non-transferable, so a change of operator requires a new application.
The administrator reports changes in the administrator, the ownership structure or the services offered to the Regional Office as required by DOH. Key staff vacancies are reported under QUAL-01.

If the facility plans to close, the owner gives 120 days' written notice to the Regional Office and follows a DOH-approved closure plan (18 NYCRR §485.5(k)). Resident transfers during closure follow AD-06.

The administrator posts the ALR starting monthly rate, rent range, approved admission agreement and fee summary in the facility and on the website. The administrator also submits the annual quality measures to DOH (PHL §4656; see AD-05 and GOV-02).
The administrator keeps a compliance calendar (certificate, license, fees, quality reports, in-service, drills, renewal dates). The governing body reviews it at each quarterly meeting.
The governing body meets at least quarterly, and minutes record the review of incident trends, survey results, grievances and QA findings (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Adopts policies, maintains eligible operator status, approves ownership changes through DOH, funds compliance, and reviews the compliance calendar quarterly.
Files applications, renewals and fees, posts certificates and prices, keeps the compliance calendar, and acts as the contact for DOH.
Pays fees on time and keeps payment proof and the ownership records.
Follow this manual and tell the administrator about regulatory changes or deficiencies.

documentation: Operating certificate, ALR license and EALR/SNALR/ALP approval letters
Part I and Part II applications and DOH correspondence log
Governing body resolutions and quarterly minutes
Compliance calendar and fee payment records
Ownership transfer approvals or 90-day notices
LLC articles and DOH approval letter, if applicable
Closure notice and plan, if applicable

policies.title: Administrator, Case Manager and Activities Director Qualifications, Hours and Vacancy Notice
policies.applies_to: Administrator, program coordinator, case manager, activities director and the governing body
policies.purpose: To make sure the facility is managed by DOH-approved, qualified people who work the required hours, and that DOH is told promptly when a key position becomes vacant.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will not designate anyone as administrator without prior written DOH approval (18 NYCRR §487.9(c)). The administrator will meet the qualifications in §487.9(c) and be on duty at least 20 hours per week in a facility of 24 beds or fewer, and at least 40 hours per week in a facility of 25 or more beds. The administrator will complete 60 hours of continuing education every 2 years. Under 50 beds, a qualified administrator may also serve as case manager and activities director. At 50 or more beds, separate qualified staff are required. The ALR case manager will be on site at least 20 hours per week in a residence under 25 beds, scaling up to at least 40 hours per week at 45 or more beds (10 NYCRR §1001.11(c)(1)). Enriched housing programs will have a program coordinator and a case manager providing 0.5 hour per resident per week (18 NYCRR §488.9). If the ALP is approved, the facility will have a designated individual and a qualified case manager (18 NYCRR §494.6). The facility will notify the Regional Office within 3 business days of a vacancy in the administrator, case manager, activities director, dietary consultant or health consultant position (§487.9(a)(16)).

definitions.definition: The person with DOH written approval who is responsible for day-to-day operation (18 NYCRR §487.9(c)).
The person who directs an enriched housing program (18 NYCRR §488.9).
The qualified person who evaluates residents before admission and at least every 12 months, develops the ISP and coordinates services (10 NYCRR §1001.10).
Administrator, case manager, activities director, dietary consultant or health consultant.
Monday through Friday, excluding state holidays.

procedures: The governing body selects a candidate for administrator only after the administrator's qualifications, as listed in §487.9(c), have been verified against the application, references and credentials. The verification is written and signed.
The owner submits the administrator application to DOH and does not let the person act as administrator until DOH's written approval is received. The approval letter is filed in the personnel record.
The administrator's weekly schedule shows at least 20 hours (24 beds or fewer) or 40 hours (25 or more beds) on duty. Hours worked are shown on the time record.
The administrator tracks continuing education and completes 60 hours every 2 years. Certificates are kept in the personnel file and reviewed by the governing body at each annual evaluation.

At fewer than 50 beds, the governing body may name the administrator as case manager and activities director only after confirming that the administrator meets those qualifications. This is recorded in writing. At 50 or more beds, separate qualified staff are hired.

The case manager schedule is set from the current ALR bed count: at least 20 hours per week on site under 25 beds, scaling up to at least 40 hours per week at 45 or more beds (10 NYCRR §1001.11(c)(1)). The administrator recalculates the required hours whenever licensed capacity changes.

For enriched housing, the administrator calculates case manager time at 0.5 hour per resident per week from the weekly census (18 NYCRR §488.9) and adjusts the schedule when the census changes. The program coordinator is named in the application and the staffing schedule.
If the facility operates an ALP, the governing body names the designated individual and the qualified case manager (18 NYCRR §494.6) and keeps their credentials on file.
The activities director's qualifications and hours are documented in the job description and the schedule (see JD-01 and ACT-01).

When a key position becomes vacant, the administrator notifies the Regional Office within 3 business days (18 NYCRR §487.9(a)(16)) by phone or e-mail and confirms in writing. The notification names the position, the date of the vacancy and the interim plan.

If the vacancy is the administrator position, the governing body immediately names a DOH-approved interim person. Until then, the employee in charge (see STF-01) handles shift operations and the owner contacts the Regional Office.
The administrator posts and starts recruitment for the vacancy within 5 business days and keeps a log of recruitment steps.
When a replacement is hired, the administrator notifies the Regional Office, sends the required DOH approval request for an administrator, and files the new qualifications.
Each January the administrator audits all key positions for approvals, hours, CE and credentials, and reports the result to the governing body.

responsibilities.duty: Selects the administrator, requests DOH approval, and confirms qualifications and dual roles.
Meets hours and CE requirements, schedules the case manager and activities director, and makes vacancy notices.
Works the required on-site hours and carries out the duties in AD-02 and AD-03.
Directs the activities program under ACT-01.
Keeps the time records and the position and approval file.

documentation: DOH written approval of administrator
Qualification verification for administrator, case manager, activities director
Weekly administrator and case manager time records
Continuing education certificates (60 hours / 2 years)
Vacancy notices to Regional Office with date and time sent
Recruitment log and replacement approvals
Annual key position audit

policies.title: General Staff Orientation (All Employees)
policies.applies_to: All employees of [AGENCY NAME], regardless of department or hours, before they work with residents
policies.purpose: To make sure every employee is oriented before working independently and that orientation is documented.
policies.policy: This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Schedule 6, item 3a — Staff Orientation and Aide Training: general staff orientation to be used for all employees. A copy of the orientation outline below is submitted with Part II. Every employee receives documented orientation (18 NYCRR §487.9(a)(3)-(5)) before working alone. The orientation covers: the resident rights statement (RS-02); emergency, fire and evacuation procedures (EM-01, EM-02); incident, abuse and neglect reporting duties (SAF-01, SAF-02); infection control and the bloodborne pathogen exposure prevention and post-exposure procedure (SAF-04; 29 CFR 1910.1030; 10 NYCRR §1001.11); confidentiality (RS-07); the grievance process (RS-03); professional boundaries (PER-01); and the employee's written job description (JD-01), as required by 10 NYCRR §1001.11. Where the facility is subject to the Justice Center, the orientation includes mandated reporting and the code of conduct. All staff must speak, read and write English (§487.9(a)(13)).

definitions.definition: The introductory training given to every employee on hire, before independent work.
The facility's written plan to prevent exposure and to manage exposure incidents under 29 CFR 1910.1030.
The NYS Justice Center for the Protection of People with Special Needs, where its jurisdiction applies to the facility.

procedures: During interviewing, the hiring manager confirms that the applicant speaks, reads and writes English (§487.9(a)(13)) and records this in the hiring file.
On the first day, the administrator or designee gives the employee the orientation checklist and sets the orientation schedule. The employee does not work alone until the checklist is complete.
The employee receives and signs for the resident rights statement and is taught each right and how to protect it (RS-02).

The trainer walks the employee through the facility on a floor plan: exits, fire alarm pulls, extinguishers, assembly points, the disaster plan and evacuation procedures, and each employee's role (EM-01, EM-02).

The trainer covers reporting duties: who to tell, how to complete an Incident Report, the time frames for abuse, neglect and exploitation reports, and the statement that no one will be retaliated against for reporting (SAF-01, SAF-02).
Where applicable, the trainer covers Justice Center mandated reporting and the code of conduct and obtains the employee's signed acknowledgment.

The trainer teaches infection prevention (handwashing, standard precautions, PPE) and the bloodborne pathogen exposure prevention and post-exposure procedure: immediate wound care, reporting to the supervisor, medical evaluation and documentation (SAF-04).
The trainer reviews confidentiality and HIPAA (RS-07), the grievance policy (RS-03), non-discrimination and language access (NDI-01), professional boundaries (PER-01) and personnel policies (PER-01).
The employee receives the written job description, reviews it with the supervisor and signs it (JD-01).
Department heads give position-specific orientation. The employee is supervised by an experienced staff member until the department head signs off on the competencies.
Employees with resident-care duties also complete the training in ORI-02 within the time frames there.
The trainer gives a short written or oral check of the content, and any gaps are retrained the same day.
The administrator signs the completed orientation record within 7 days of hire and files it in the personnel record (PER-04).
Each January the administrator reviews the orientation outline for changes in law and revises it. The revised outline is dated and the changes are recorded.

responsibilities.duty: Owns the orientation program, delivers or assigns it, and signs completion.
Give job-specific orientation and verify competency.
Completes every element, signs acknowledgments and asks questions.
Supervise the employee until orientation is complete.

documentation: Orientation outline submitted with Part II (Schedule 6, item 3a)
Signed orientation checklist with dates and trainer names
Signed resident rights statement acknowledgment
Signed job description
Justice Center acknowledgment, if applicable
English proficiency note in hiring file
Annual orientation outline review

policies.title: Aide and Medication-Staff Initial Training and 12-Month In-Service Schedule
policies.applies_to: Resident aides, personal care staff, home health aides, medication-assistance staff and their trainers
policies.purpose: To ensure that staff who give personal care, home health care or medication help are trained and competent, and that in-service education is planned for the year.
policies.policy: This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Schedule 6, item 3b — Staff Orientation and Aide Training: initial training for each job title that provides personal care, home health care and/or medication services; and Schedule 6, item 20 — In-Service Training: 12-month in-service schedule. The training outline for each such job title and the 12-month in-service calendar are submitted with Part II. ALR resident aides complete 40 hours of initial training on the DOH curriculum (or an approved equivalent), 12 hours of in-service each year, and an annual performance assessment with direct observation (10 NYCRR §1001.11(c)(2)). The adult home in-service plan for personal care staff is submitted for DOH approval, and new personal care staff complete their training within 3 months (18 NYCRR §487.9(g)(4)-(5)). Staff who assist with medications are limited to the tasks allowed by 18 NYCRR §487.7(f), and may not give injectables unless licensed. EALR/SNALR home health aide training follows the requirements cross-referenced in 10 NYCRR §1001.11. Attendance and competency records are kept in personnel files (§487.9(a)(3)-(5)).

definitions.definition: Non-licensed staff who give personal care in an ALR (10 NYCRR §1001.11).
Ongoing education during employment, separate from initial training.
A supervisor or RN watching the aide perform tasks with residents as part of the annual performance assessment.
The limited help permitted by 18 NYCRR §487.7(f) for residents who self-administer, as defined in MED-02.

procedures: The administrator keeps a training outline for each job title that gives personal care, home health care or medication help: resident aide, personal care aide, medication-assistance staff and (EALR/SNALR) home health aide, with the hours and the competencies tested. These outlines are included in Part II.

On hire, the administrator checks any prior training certificates. A new resident aide completes 40 hours of initial training on the DOH curriculum (or approved equivalent), taught by a qualified instructor. The aide gives no independent personal care until the training is complete or the aide has been paired with a trained aide and signed off.

The instructor teaches each skill with demonstration and a return demonstration, and records competency on a skills checklist. The checklist covers bathing, toileting, transfers, skin care, falls prevention, weights, infection control and resident rights.

For adult home personal care staff, the administrator submits the in-service plan to DOH for approval and ensures each new staff member completes the required training within 3 months of hire (§487.9(g)(4)-(5)).

Staff who assist with medications complete the medication-assistance training required by MED-02 and are authorized in writing by the administrator before assisting. They assist only within §487.7(f): self-administration help, no dose changes without physician authorization, and no injectables unless licensed.
For EALR/SNALR home health aides, the administrator confirms training meets the home health aide requirements cross-referenced in 10 NYCRR §1001.11 and that the RN supervises per EALR-01.

The administrator prepares a 12-month in-service calendar each January. The calendar lists topics, dates, trainers and hours. Required topics include resident rights, abuse and neglect prevention, infection control, emergency and fire procedures, falls and skin integrity, dementia care (SNALR), medication assistance and boundaries.
Each resident aide is scheduled for at least 12 in-service hours during the year. The administrator tracks hours in a log by employee and adds sessions if an employee is behind at mid-year.
Attendance sheets for each session are signed by the trainer and attendees. Staff who miss a session make it up within 30 days.

Each aide's annual performance assessment is done by the case manager, RN or administrator with direct observation of resident care. The assessment is written, reviewed with the aide and signed by both.
If the assessment shows a deficiency, the supervisor retrains the aide, observes again within 30 days and documents the result. Staff who cannot show competency are removed from the task.
Records of initial training, skills checklists, in-service hours and assessments are filed in each personnel record and are available for DOH review (PER-04).
The administrator reviews the in-service plan each quarter and revises it after incidents, survey findings or QA results (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains outlines and the in-service calendar, authorizes medication staff and ensures training is complete.
Teaches or approves clinical content, checks competency and supervises EALR/SNALR aides.
Assists with annual performance assessments and training on the ISP.
Attend training, show competency and work within the limits of their training.

documentation: Training outlines for each job title (Schedule 6, item 3b)
12-month in-service schedule (Schedule 6, item 20)
Skills checklists and competency sign-offs
Sign-in sheets and in-service hours log
Annual performance assessments with direct observation
Medication-assistance authorization letters
DOH approval of the in-service plan, if applicable

policies.title: Staffing Levels, 24-Hour Supervision, First Aid Coverage and Employee in Charge
policies.applies_to: Administrator, department heads, scheduling staff and all direct-care, housekeeping and food service employees
policies.purpose: To make sure that enough trained staff are on site on every shift of every day, that a first-aid-trained employee and an employee in charge are always identified, and that schedules are kept.
policies.policy: This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Schedule 6, item 4 — Planned Staffing Schedule. The planned staffing schedule submitted with Part II shows adequate staffing for each shift on each day of the week, the persons trained in first aid (one scheduled on every shift), the employee in charge of each shift when the administrator or program coordinator is absent, and all employees in all departments. The facility will have the following staff on site 24 hours a day: 1 for a census of 1-40; 2 for 41-80; 3 for 81-150; 4 for 151-200; plus 1 for each additional 60 residents (18 NYCRR §487.9(f)(6)). Minimum weekly hours per resident are: personal care 3.75 (covering day and evening), housekeeping 1.0, and food service 2.0, with food service never under 35 hours per week. For an enriched housing program, personal care, housekeeping and food service staff together provide at least 6 hours per resident per week (18 NYCRR §488.9). ALP staffing is at the §487.9(f)(6) levels (18 NYCRR §494.6). At least one first-aid-trained person is on site on every shift (§487.9(a)(15)). Staffing schedules are kept 12 months (§487.9(a)(6)). If EALR or SNALR is approved, an RN works 8 hours per day 5 days per week and an LPN works 8 hours per day the other 2 days, with an RN on call 24 hours a day, 7 days a week (10 NYCRR §1001.11); a waiver option exists at 40 or fewer beds. Case manager hours are in QUAL-01.

definitions.definition: The number of residents in the facility at midnight, used for staffing calculation.
The employee designated in writing to run the facility on a shift when the administrator or program coordinator is absent.
Hours worked by personal care staff, aides, and in EALR/SNALR the nursing staff.
Holding a current first aid certification from a recognized provider.

procedures: Each week the administrator takes the census and compares it with the supervision table: 1 staff for 1-40, 2 for 41-80, 3 for 81-150, 4 for 151-200, plus 1 for each additional 60 residents. The required number is the minimum on site at all times, including nights, weekends and holidays.

The administrator figures required weekly hours by multiplying the census by 3.75 for personal care, 1.0 for housekeeping and 2.0 for food service. In an enriched housing program, the administrator checks that the combined total is at least 6 hours per resident per week. Food service is scheduled for at least 35 hours per week.

The scheduler builds a written weekly schedule showing every department, every shift, every day and each employee's name, title and hours. Personal care staff are scheduled across both day and evening shifts.

The scheduler marks on each shift at least one employee with a current first aid certificate. If that person calls out, the scheduler replaces them with another first-aid-trained employee before the shift begins.

The administrator names an employee in charge for every shift in which the administrator or program coordinator is absent. The name is shown on the schedule, and the employee in charge knows the emergency contacts and has access to the disaster plan.
Employees designated in charge are trained in emergency procedures, incident reporting and resident rights. The administrator confirms this before the designation.

Staff may not leave a shift until relieved. If relief does not arrive, the employee notifies the administrator or on-call manager, who finds coverage. The facility will not fall below the minimum staffing at any time.
The scheduler keeps a call-out and replacement list and an on-call manager list with phone numbers [PHONE]. Agency or float staff may be used only if oriented under ORI-01.
The shift supervisor completes a daily staffing record at the start of each shift showing actual staff present, the employee in charge and the first-aid-trained person.

If the actual staffing falls below the table or the hours minimum, the supervisor records it, takes immediate action to restore coverage and notifies the administrator the same day. The administrator documents the corrective action.

If EALR or SNALR is approved, the administrator schedules an RN 8 hours per day for 5 days, an LPN 8 hours per day on the other 2 days, and an RN on call every day and night. The on-call roster is posted. Any waiver at 40 or fewer beds is requested from DOH in writing and kept on file. See EALR-01.
When the census rises above a staffing tier, the administrator adds staff before admissions bring the census into the next tier, and records the change in the schedule.
The administrator reviews schedules against the census weekly and signs the review. The monthly staffing summary goes to the governing body.
Staffing schedules are kept for at least 12 months (§487.9(a)(6)) and are available for DOH surveyors (PER-04).

The administrator reviews staffing patterns for resident needs at least quarterly using falls, incidents, call-bell response and resident feedback, and adds staff above the minimum where the data show a need.

responsibilities.duty: Sets staffing from census, names the employee in charge, approves schedules and responds to shortfalls.
Builds schedules, assigns first-aid-trained staff and arranges replacements.
Runs the shift in the absence of management and reports staffing problems.
Works the required EALR/SNALR hours and acts as the RN on call.
Report as scheduled and stay until relieved.

documentation: Planned staffing schedule for Part II (Schedule 6, item 4)
Weekly staffing schedules (kept 12 months)
Daily staffing record with employee in charge and first-aid person
First aid certificates
Weekly hours calculation worksheet
Shortfall and corrective-action log
RN/LPN schedule and on-call roster (EALR/SNALR)

policies.title: Resident Services Program: Philosophy, Goals and Scope
policies.applies_to: All staff, residents and families of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To describe the philosophy, goals and scope of the resident services program and to name the services the facility provides to each resident.
policies.policy: This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Schedule 6, item 5 — Resident Services: philosophy, goals and scope of the resident service program, including the cultural, spiritual, diversional, physical, political, social and intellectual activities provided by the facility and the community. Philosophy: [AGENCY NAME] provides a home-like setting that respects each resident's dignity, privacy, choice and independence, and supports residents to age in place with the services they need. Goals: (1) keep residents as independent as possible; (2) meet each resident's needs through an individualized service plan; (3) protect safety and health; (4) support social connection and participation in the community; and (5) honor each resident's rights and choices. Scope: the facility provides, at minimum, room, board, housekeeping, supervision, personal care, case management and activities (18 NYCRR §487.7(a)). As an ALR, the residence also provides housing, 24-hour on-site monitoring, daily food service, case management, an individualized service plan (ISP), and personal care and/or home care (10 NYCRR §1001.10). Residents may use outside providers and choose their own health care providers (§1001.10). Personal care includes monthly weights, and physical restraints are not used (§487.7(e)).

definitions.definition: Watching over residents' safety and well-being, including the duties set out in 18 NYCRR §487.7(d).
Help with activities of daily living such as bathing, dressing, grooming, toileting, mobility and eating.
Evaluation, service planning, coordination and follow-up for each resident, including evaluation before admission and at least every 12 months (10 NYCRR §1001.10).
Individualized Service Plan describing the resident's needs, goals and the services that will meet them.

procedures: The administrator gives each prospective resident the written services description before admission (AD-02, AD-05), including the philosophy, goals and scope of services, and explains which services are included and which cost extra.

The case manager evaluates each resident before admission and at least every 12 months using the DOH personal data and resident evaluation form (10 NYCRR §1001.10). Evaluation findings are used to build the ISP (AD-03).
Room and board: staff provide a room and three meals daily with snacks, and menus follow FS-01. Daily food service is provided every day of the year.
Housekeeping and laundry are provided on the schedules in HK-01 and kept up to the standards in that policy.

Supervision: staff are on site 24 hours a day at the levels in STF-01. Staff do rounds, respond to calls and carry out the duties on illness, emergencies, missing residents and incident reporting (18 NYCRR §487.7(d); SAF-02).

Personal care: aides give help as the ISP states, respecting preferences and privacy. Residents are weighed monthly and weights are recorded. Significant changes are reported to the case manager and the resident's physician (RS-04, RS-05). Physical restraints are not used (SAF-03).

Case management: the case manager coordinates services, meets residents regularly, links residents with outside providers and community resources and reviews the ISP at least every 12 months and after any significant change (AD-03).

Health services: residents choose their own physician and outside providers. Health services come from an Article 36 home care agency, or from the facility's EALR/SNALR-approved services if approved (10 NYCRR §1001.10; EALR-01). Hospice is allowed when conditions are met (RS-06).

Activities: the activities director plans a monthly calendar that includes cultural, spiritual, diversional, physical, political, social and intellectual activities. Examples include music and arts programs, religious services and visits by clergy, games and crafts, exercise and walking groups, voter registration and candidate forums, discussion groups, book clubs, community outings and visits by schools and volunteers. Community resources such as libraries, senior centers, houses of worship and civic groups are used. See ACT-01.

The activities director asks residents about interests at least once a year and after admission, and uses the resident council to shape the calendar (ORG-01). Activities are offered at accessible times and places, and residents are never required to take part.
Residents are told of their rights on admission and each year (RS-02), including their right to complain without retaliation (RS-03).
Medication services are given as set out in MED-01 and MED-02: residents self-administer where able, staff assist only within §487.7(f), and no dose changes are made without physician authorization.

The administrator reviews the services program every year with resident feedback, grievance data and QA results (GOV-02), and updates this policy when services change. The governing body approves the changes.
Staff are trained on this policy at orientation (ORI-01) and receive updates at in-service.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures all required services are provided and reviews the program each year.
Evaluates residents, writes and reviews ISPs and coordinates outside providers.
Plans and runs the activities program and records participation.
Deliver services as set out in the ISP and policies.
Take part in planning their services and tell staff of needs and concerns.

documentation: Written statement of philosophy, goals and scope of services (Schedule 6, item 5)
Services description given at admission
Pre-admission and annual evaluations (DOH personal data and resident evaluation form)
ISPs and reviews
Monthly weight records
Monthly activities calendar and participation records
Annual services program review

policies.title: Resident Rights, Responsibilities and Ombudsman/Legal Services Access
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers and contracted providers; all residents, applicants and resident representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident and applicant knows their rights, can exercise them without fear of retaliation, and has easy access to the Long Term Care Ombudsman, free legal and advocacy services and the Department of Health (DOH) adult care facility complaint line.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written Resident Rights Statement containing at least the 19 minimum rights required by 18 NYCRR §487.5(a). The statement is posted in a public area, given to each resident at admission and reviewed with residents at least annually. Applicants receive the rights statement, the admission agreement, the facility rules and the Ombudsman/legal-services information sheet at or before the admission interview (18 NYCRR §487.4). The DOH adult care facility complaint line (1-866-893-6772) and the resident rights materials are posted as required by Social Services Law §460-d. Residents may meet and communicate privately with the Ombudsman and other advocates at any time. The facility does not discriminate against residents or applicants on the basis of race, color, national origin or disability, consistent with 42 USC 2000d and 42 USC 12101, and no resident is retaliated against for exercising a right. This policy meets the resident rights, posting and applicant-disclosure requirements of 18 NYCRR §487.5(a) and §487.4.

definitions.definition: The written statement of resident rights, with at least the 19 minimum rights required by 18 NYCRR §487.5(a), in the form prescribed by DOH.
The Long Term Care Ombudsman Program representatives who advocate for residents of adult care facilities and may visit and speak privately with residents.
A person the resident has designated, or who is legally authorized, to act for the resident, such as an agent under a health care proxy or power of attorney.
Any adverse action, threat, discouragement or change in treatment because a resident or representative raised a concern or used a right.

procedures: The Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) keeps the current DOH-prescribed Resident Rights Statement on file and replaces it whenever DOH issues a revised form.

Staff post the Resident Rights Statement, the DOH complaint line (1-866-893-6772) and the Ombudsman/legal-services contact sheet in [LOCATION OF PUBLIC POSTING, e.g., main lobby] at resident eye level and in large print. The Administrator checks the posting weekly and logs the check.

The Case Manager gives each applicant a packet at or before the admission interview. It contains the Resident Rights Statement, the admission agreement, the facility rules and the Ombudsman/legal-services sheet (18 NYCRR §487.4). The Case Manager records the date and time the packet was given on the interview form.
The Case Manager tells applicants they may review the facility's most recent DOH inspection report and shows them where it is kept.

At or before admission, the Case Manager reads or explains the rights in plain language, using an interpreter or accessible format when needed (see NDI-01). The Case Manager answers questions and checks that the resident understands.

The resident, or the resident representative, signs an acknowledgment of the Resident Rights Statement at admission. If the resident declines or cannot sign, the Case Manager writes the reason and the date on the form and tries again within 7 days.

The Case Manager reviews the Resident Rights Statement with each resident at least once every 12 months, normally with the annual reassessment. The resident signs a new acknowledgment, which is filed in the resident record.
The Administrator also reviews the rights with all residents at a resident meeting at least once a year. Attendance and the date are recorded.
Staff must let the Ombudsman and other advocates enter the facility to visit residents. Visits take place in a private space, and staff do not ask the purpose of a private visit or listen in.
Residents may use a telephone, mail or other means to contact the Ombudsman, legal services and DOH privately. Staff do not open, read or screen these communications.
Staff who receive a complaint about a rights violation record it and refer it under RS-03. Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation is handled under SAF-01 at once.

Staff do not retaliate against, discourage or treat differently any resident who uses a right. An allegation of retaliation is investigated by the Administrator within 2 business days and the outcome is documented. Substantiated retaliation leads to discipline under PER-01.
Orientation for every employee and volunteer includes the Resident Rights Statement, how to report a violation, and the rule against retaliation (see ORI-01).
The Administrator reviews the rights acknowledgment file each quarter and corrects any missing or overdue acknowledgments within 14 days. Findings go to the QA committee (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Keeps current rights materials, makes sure postings are complete and current, and investigates retaliation allegations.
Provides the applicant packet, explains the rights, collects signed acknowledgments at admission and annually, and records them.
Respect resident rights, support private contact with advocates, and report complaints and suspected violations.
Are encouraged to follow the facility rules, respect the rights and safety of others, and bring concerns forward through the grievance procedure.

documentation: Signed Resident Rights Statement acknowledgment at admission and each year (resident record)
Applicant packet checklist with the date given (admission interview file)
Weekly posting check log
Annual resident rights meeting sign-in sheet
Log of Ombudsman and advocate visits
Retaliation investigation notes, where applicable

policies.title: Grievances and Complaints
policies.applies_to: All residents, resident representatives, employees and volunteers
policies.purpose: To give residents a clear, posted, written way to raise grievances and complaints, and to make sure each one is received, investigated, answered and used to improve care.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] operates a written grievance system as required by 18 NYCRR §487.5(c). The procedure is posted in a public area with the DOH adult care facility complaint line (1-866-893-6772), as required by Social Services Law §460-d. Residents, their representatives, family members and others may file a grievance orally or in writing, anonymously if they wish, and without fear of retaliation. Every grievance is logged, investigated, answered and reviewed by the Administrator. Residents may also bring grievances to the resident organization (see ORG-01) and may contact DOH, the Ombudsman or legal services at any time, whether or not they have used the internal procedure.

definitions.definition: Any complaint, concern or dissatisfaction raised by or for a resident about care, services, staff, other residents, the environment, rules or rights.
The facility record of each grievance, with date received, a summary, the response, the resolution and the Administrator's review.
The resident-run group described in ORG-01 that may raise concerns on behalf of residents.

procedures: The Administrator posts the written grievance procedure, the complaint line (1-866-893-6772) and the Ombudsman contact information together in [LOCATION OF PUBLIC POSTING], and gives each resident a copy at admission (AD-02).

Any staff member who hears a grievance accepts it respectfully, makes sure the resident is safe, and gives it to the Administrator or designee the same day. Staff may not discourage, screen out or delay a grievance.

Grievances may be made verbally, in writing, by a drop box at [LOCATION OF GRIEVANCE BOX], by telephone to [PHONE], or through a representative or the resident organization. Staff help any resident who needs assistance to write a grievance.

The person receiving the grievance completes a Grievance Form recording the date and time, the resident, the complaint in the resident's own words, and the resident's desired outcome. The form is entered in the grievance log the same business day.

If a grievance alleges abuse, neglect, exploitation, or a medication error or injury, staff immediately follow SAF-01 or SAF-02 in addition to this policy. These matters are not handled only as grievances.
The Administrator acknowledges the grievance to the resident within 2 business days. This is the facility's own standard.

The Administrator, or a manager not involved in the complaint, investigates by interviewing the resident, the staff involved and witnesses, and by reviewing records. The investigator notes the findings on the Grievance Form.

The Administrator gives the resident a written response within 10 business days (agency standard). The response states the findings, any action taken and the right to take the matter further. If the investigation takes longer, the Administrator gives the resident a written status update within that period and a final response as soon as possible afterward.

If the resident is not satisfied, the Administrator offers a meeting with the resident, their representative and, if the resident wishes, an Ombudsman or the resident organization. The Administrator reminds the resident of the right to call DOH at 1-866-893-6772.
The log records the resolution date, how the resident responded and the Administrator's signature as reviewer.

The Administrator protects the resident from retaliation. After closing the grievance, the Case Manager or Administrator checks in with the resident within 14 days to see whether the concern is resolved and whether any retaliation has occurred. This check-in is documented.

Grievances brought through the resident organization are logged and answered in the same way. The Administrator replies in writing to the organization's officers and discusses the matter at the next resident meeting.

The Administrator summarizes grievance counts, categories, response times and repeat issues for the QA committee for review at each meeting (see GOV-02). The QA committee meets at least every six months. Trends lead to written corrective actions.
Grievance records are kept in the facility records under REC-01. Staff may not remove or alter log entries.

responsibilities.duty: Owns the grievance system, investigates or assigns investigation, signs responses, reviews the log and reports trends to the QA committee.
Helps residents file grievances, follows up with residents, and links grievance findings to the ISP when appropriate.
Accept grievances without discouragement and forward them to the Administrator on the same day.
May bring resident concerns to the Administrator and receive responses.

Grievance Forms
Grievance log (date, response, resolution, Administrator review)
Written responses to residents
Follow-up check-in notes
QA committee minutes with grievance trend reports

policies.title: Change of Condition, Physician Notification and Hospital Transfer
policies.applies_to: All direct-care staff, case management staff, the Administrator, and any nursing or home care providers serving residents
policies.purpose: To make sure staff recognize and respond to a change in a resident's condition, get medical help promptly, notify the physician and representative, arrange safe hospital transfer, and decide whether the facility can continue to retain the resident.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] responds to every illness, injury or change of condition under the emergency and illness duties of 18 NYCRR §487.7(d). Staff get appropriate medical help immediately, notify the resident's physician and representative, document each event, and complete an Incident Report whenever a §487.7(d) trigger applies. After any significant change, the Case Manager re-evaluates the resident and updates the Individualized Service Plan (AD-03). Retention is limited by the exclusions in 18 NYCRR §487.4, including a need for continual medical or nursing care. A facility approved for EALR or SNALR may retain a resident who needs 24-hour skilled nursing only within the exception in 10 NYCRR §1001.10. If a resident can no longer be retained, the Administrator makes persistent efforts to find an alternative placement as required by §487.4 and follows AD-06.

definitions.definition: A noticeable decline or change in a resident's physical, mental or functional status, such as new confusion, a fall, loss of appetite, new incontinence, skin breakdown, a significant weight change, or a change in behavior or mood.
A situation that threatens life or health and requires immediate medical care, such as chest pain, difficulty breathing, stroke symptoms, unresponsiveness or serious injury.
The DOH incident report form completed when a trigger listed in 18 NYCRR §487.7(d) occurs.
The person designated by the resident or legally authorized to act for them.

procedures: Any staff member who sees a change of condition stays with the resident, checks safety and immediately tells the Employee in Charge (see STF-01).

For an emergency, the Employee in Charge or the first staff member on the scene calls 911 at once. Staff with current first-aid training give first aid within the scope of their training until help arrives (see STF-01).
Staff do not give treatments, medications or doses beyond what the resident's physician has authorized and what staff are permitted to do under MED-02.

For a non-emergency change, the Employee in Charge contacts the resident's physician or the physician's covering service on the same shift and describes the change. Staff write down the physician's instructions, including any medication change, only if the physician provides it as an authorization (MED-02).

The Employee in Charge notifies the resident's representative or emergency contact on the same shift for any emergency, transfer, significant change or incident. If no one can be reached, the attempts are documented with times and the staff member keeps trying.
The Employee in Charge notifies the Administrator promptly, and the Administrator decides whether additional reporting applies (see SAF-02 and REC-02).

Before the resident leaves for the hospital, staff send a packet with the face sheet, current medication list and last doses given, diagnoses and allergies, physician and representative contacts, advance directive or MOLST if one exists (AD-04) and a copy of the current ISP. A staff member goes with the resident or follows up by phone if the representative cannot go.
The Employee in Charge writes a dated, timed entry in the resident record covering what was observed, actions taken, who was notified and when, and the outcome.

When a §487.7(d) trigger applies, the Employee in Charge and the Administrator complete the Incident Report by the deadline in SAF-02 and file it as required. Falls with injury and unplanned hospital transfers are reviewed by the Administrator for reportability.

Within 24 hours of the change, or sooner, the Case Manager reviews the resident and decides whether to arrange an updated physician evaluation, a home care or nursing referral, or other services. Re-evaluation and the ISP update follow AD-03.
Staff monitor the resident for the following 72 hours. They note changes in meals, mobility, mood and sleep, and report concerns to the Employee in Charge each shift.

While the resident is hospitalized, the Case Manager keeps in contact with the hospital discharge planner and obtains discharge instructions and orders. Before readmission, the Case Manager and the Administrator confirm that the facility can meet the resident's needs.

On return from hospital, the Case Manager reviews the discharge summary with the physician orders, reconciles medications under MED-01, updates the ISP and arranges any needed home care or nursing services.

The Administrator decides whether the resident can be retained by comparing the resident's needs to the §487.4 exclusions, which include a need for continual medical or nursing care, being chronically bedfast, unmanaged incontinence, and danger to self or others. In an EALR or SNALR, the Administrator also considers the 24-hour skilled nursing exception in 10 NYCRR §1001.10.

If the resident cannot be retained, the Administrator and Case Manager start persistent efforts at alternative placement right away. They contact the resident, representative, physician and potential placements, and document each effort. They then follow AD-06 for notice, rights and legal services information.
The QA committee reviews change-of-condition events, transfers and delays in notification (see GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Directs the response, calls 911 and the physician, notifies the representative and Administrator, and documents the event.
Recognize and report changes, give first aid within their training, and monitor the resident.
Re-evaluates the resident, updates the ISP, coordinates hospital communication and arranges services.
Decides on retention, ensures Incident Reports are filed and arranges alternative placement when necessary.
