Physician and representative notification record
Hospital transfer packet checklist
Incident Report, where triggered
Updated ISP and re-evaluation notes
Alternative placement effort log
QA review of change-of-condition events

policies.title: Personal Care, Falls Prevention and Skin Integrity
policies.applies_to: Personal care aides, direct-care staff, the Case Manager, the Employee in Charge and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure residents receive the personal care they need with dignity, and to reduce falls and skin breakdown through assessment, supervision, monthly weights and prompt referral.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides personal care to residents as described in their ISPs in accordance with 18 NYCRR §487.7(e). Physical restraints are banned and are never used. Each resident is weighed monthly. The facility provides at least 3.75 hours of personal care staff time per resident per week, scheduled on the day and evening shifts, as required by 18 NYCRR §487.9(g). Falls with injury and other incidents that meet the triggers in 18 NYCRR §487.7(d) are reported on the Incident Report, and falls are reviewed by the QA committee. Skin checks and fall-risk review are part of the Case Manager's evaluation at least every 12 months and whenever a resident's condition changes. Pressure injuries are referred to a physician or to a home care or nursing provider, and the referral is documented.

definitions.definition: Assistance with activities of daily living such as bathing, dressing, grooming, toileting, mobility, eating and use of prescribed assistive devices, provided as described in the ISP.
Any device, material or method that restricts a resident's movement or access to their body and that the resident cannot remove easily. Physical restraints are prohibited (see SAF-03).
An unintended event in which a resident comes to rest on the floor, ground or a lower level.
Localized damage to skin or underlying tissue, usually over a bony prominence, from pressure or friction.

procedures: The Case Manager lists each resident's personal care needs and preferences in the ISP (AD-03), including level of help with bathing, dressing, toileting, mobility and eating, assistive devices and any fall or skin risk.

The Administrator builds the staffing schedule so personal care staff hours meet at least 3.75 hours per resident per week, with personal care staff assigned on the day and evening shifts. The Administrator checks the totals against the census each month (see STF-01 and PER-04).
Aides provide care in accordance with the ISP. They respect privacy, encourage independence, explain what they are doing, and record care given on the daily care sheet each shift.

Aides do not use physical restraints, including bed rails used to restrict movement, locked chairs, tied sheets or restraining garments. Any request or suspected use of a restraint is reported to the Administrator the same day (SAF-03).

A designated staff member weighs each resident on the same scale, at about the same time of day, once each month and records the weight in the resident record. The Case Manager reviews the weights each month and tells the physician or representative about a significant loss or gain, using the change of condition steps in RS-04.

The Case Manager screens for fall risk at admission, at least every 12 months, and after any fall or change of condition. The screen covers fall history, gait and balance, vision, medications that may affect balance (reviewed with the physician or pharmacist), continence and the environment.

Staff reduce fall risk by keeping walkways clear and well lit, making sure residents have well-fitting shoes, glasses and mobility devices within reach, answering calls promptly and offering toileting on a schedule when the ISP calls for it. Maintenance staff fix hazards reported by staff (HK-01).

After any fall, staff check the resident for injury before moving them, get medical help if needed (RS-04), notify the physician and representative, and document the circumstances in the resident record.
The Administrator decides whether the fall meets a §487.7(d) trigger, such as a fall with injury, and completes the Incident Report by the deadline in SAF-02.
Within 3 business days after a fall, the Case Manager reviews the cause and updates the ISP with new interventions. Staff monitor the resident closely for the next 72 hours.

Aides check skin during bathing and dressing, paying particular attention to heels, hips, tailbone, elbows and areas under braces. They report redness, blisters, open areas or pain to the Employee in Charge the same shift.

The Case Manager records a skin check at admission, at least every 12 months, and on any change of condition. Residents with limited mobility have their position changed and their skin checked in accordance with the ISP.

When a possible pressure injury is found, the Case Manager contacts the resident's physician, or a home care agency or nursing provider (EALR-01 where applicable), that same day. The referral date, the person contacted and the orders given are documented. Staff follow the provider's instructions and do not treat open wounds beyond their authorized duties.
If the resident's needs for wound care or other care exceed what the facility may provide, the Administrator applies the retention process in RS-04 and AD-01.
The Administrator brings counts of falls, falls with injury, weight changes and pressure injuries, with a review of repeated events, to the QA committee for each meeting (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Provide care per the ISP, record it each shift, report skin and mobility changes, and never use restraints.
Assesses fall and skin risk, reviews monthly weights, updates the ISP after falls and refers pressure injuries.
Responds to falls and skin concerns, notifies the physician and representative and ensures documentation.
Maintains required personal care staffing hours, files Incident Reports and reports trends to the QA committee.

documentation: ISP personal care section
Daily care sheets
Monthly weight record
Fall-risk screening and skin check records
Fall documentation and Incident Reports
Physician or home care/nursing referral records for pressure injuries
Staffing schedules showing personal care hours (kept 12 months)
QA committee falls and skin review

policies.title: Hospice, Home Health Coordination and Death of a Resident
policies.applies_to: The Administrator, Case Manager, Employee in Charge, all direct-care staff, and contracted hospice and home care providers
policies.purpose: To coordinate hospice and home health services with outside providers, support residents and families at the end of life, and handle a resident's death with dignity and in accordance with state reporting requirements.
policies.policy: Residents may receive health services from outside providers of their choice. Under 10 NYCRR §1001.10, health services are provided by an Article 36 licensed home care agency unless the facility is approved for EALR or SNALR. Hospice is permitted without EALR when the conditions in §1001.10 are met. Facilities approved as EALR operate under the certification and aging-in-place rules of Public Health Law §4655, including the physician's report. [AGENCY NAME] coordinates in writing with hospice and home care agencies about the ISP, medications and emergency contacts. Deaths, suicide attempts and felonies are reported as required by 18 NYCRR §487.7(d). After a death, the facility secures the resident's belongings and funds under FUN-01 and follows the notification steps in §487.7(d).

definitions.definition: A home care services agency licensed or certified under Article 36 of the Public Health Law, which provides health services to residents of an assisted living residence that is not EALR/SNALR-approved.
A coordinated program of palliative and supportive care for terminally ill persons and their families, delivered by an authorized hospice provider.

Enhanced Assisted Living Residence and Special Needs Assisted Living Residence certifications, which allow the facility to retain and serve residents who would otherwise be ineligible, under PHL §4655 and 10 NYCRR §1001.10.
The person designated by the resident or legally authorized to make decisions for them.

procedures: The Case Manager asks each resident at admission, and at each reassessment, whether they use or want an outside home care or hospice provider, and records the resident's choice (10 NYCRR §1001.10).

Before an outside provider begins services, the Administrator confirms the provider's license or certification (an Article 36 home care agency, or a hospice) and obtains a signed written agreement or coordination statement that covers the roles of each party, communication, emergency contacts and notification of changes. If the facility is EALR/SNALR-approved and provides services directly, the Administrator follows EALR-01.

The Administrator and Case Manager confirm that the conditions in 10 NYCRR §1001.10 for hospice in a facility that does not hold EALR approval are met before the resident is accepted for or continues hospice in the facility. The finding is documented. If the conditions are not met, the Administrator tells the resident and representative and reviews options, including AD-06.

The Case Manager meets with the hospice or home care nurse to share the current ISP. They agree on who provides each task, update the ISP to include the hospice plan of care and record the agreed roles (AD-03).

The facility keeps current medication orders and administration or assistance records for the resident, and the Case Manager reconciles them with the hospice or home care medication list. Staff follow MED-01 and MED-02, and staff do not change doses without physician authorization.

The Case Manager lists the contacts for the hospice or home care agency, the physician, the representative and the resident's advance directive or MOLST (AD-04) on a sheet kept where the Employee in Charge can find it at all times, including nights and weekends.

Staff follow the hospice plan for comfort care. For a change of condition, staff first call the hospice or provider's 24-hour line if the plan says so, and follow RS-04 for other required notifications. Staff do not call 911 for a resident with a no-resuscitate order in place without first checking the order and the hospice plan.

The Administrator and Case Manager review at each ISP review whether the resident can still be retained. If the resident's needs reach a level excluded under 18 NYCRR §487.4 and no exception applies, the Administrator follows RS-04 and AD-06.

The Case Manager supports the resident's and family's wishes for spiritual care, visitors and privacy at the end of life, and tells staff about any cultural or religious practices to respect (NDI-01, SOC-01).

When a resident dies, the Employee in Charge makes sure that death is confirmed by a person authorized to do so. This may be a hospice nurse, physician or emergency personnel. Staff call 911 if the resident has no hospice and no other order directs otherwise.

The Employee in Charge notifies the resident's physician, the representative or next of kin, hospice if applicable, and the Administrator immediately, and documents the time of each call. Other notifications required by 18 NYCRR §487.7(d), including to DOH, are made by the Administrator by the deadline in SAF-02 and REC-02.

If the death is unexpected, unattended or suspicious, the Employee in Charge preserves the room as found, contacts the appropriate authorities as required by law and informs the Administrator. Suspected abuse or neglect is handled under SAF-01.

The Administrator completes an Incident Report where a §487.7(d) trigger applies and files it as required. Reporting of suicide attempts or felonies follows the same steps and is documented in the resident record.

Staff treat the resident's body with dignity and release it only to the funeral director or authority designated by the representative or required by law. The release time and the receiving party are documented.

The Administrator secures the resident's room, belongings, personal funds and any medications. Two staff members inventory the items, list them and sign the inventory. Funds and property are handled under FUN-01. Medications are disposed of under MED-01.
The Administrator notifies the representative how and when to claim belongings and funds and gives them the final accounting. Refunds of fees follow AD-05.

The Administrator offers staff and residents the chance to talk about the loss and, where appropriate, offers a memorial. The QA committee reviews end-of-life care and deaths at each meeting (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Confirms hospice and home care arrangements meet 10 NYCRR §1001.10, makes required state notifications, secures belongings and funds and completes Incident Reports.
Coordinates the ISP with hospice and home care providers, maintains the contact sheet and supports the resident and family.
Responds to a decline or death, makes notifications and preserves the scene where required.
Provide services under their own licenses, share care plans and communicate changes to the facility.

documentation: Resident's provider choice record
Provider license or certification verification and coordination agreement
Hospice eligibility findings under 10 NYCRR §1001.10
ISP updated with hospice or home care plan
Emergency contact sheet
Death notification log and Incident Report
Belongings and funds inventory signed by two staff
Final accounting and release of belongings

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers, contractors, residents and applicants; all resident, personnel and facility records
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy and confidentiality of resident, applicant, employee and volunteer information, including HIV-related information, and to meet HIPAA requirements where they apply to the facility.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps resident records secure and releases information only as permitted by law or with the written consent of the resident or representative. Confidentiality of HIV-related information on residents, employees, volunteers and applicants follows 18 NYCRR §485.11(g)(9)-(15), cross-referenced in 18 NYCRR §487.10(d)(3)-(4). Resident records are kept as required by 18 NYCRR §487.10 and REC-01. The Administrator designates a Privacy Officer, and all staff are trained on privacy at orientation. Where [AGENCY NAME] is a HIPAA covered entity under 45 CFR 160 and 164, it gives residents a notice of privacy practices and follows the HIPAA Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules. Because ALP and EALR/SNALR services may make the operator a covered entity, the Administrator confirms the facility's status with counsel before opening and whenever services change.

definitions.definition: Individually identifiable health information about a resident, in any form, held or transmitted by the facility.
Any information indicating that a person has had an HIV-related test, has HIV infection, illness or AIDS, or is at risk of HIV infection, which is subject to special confidentiality rules.
A health plan, health care clearinghouse or health care provider that transmits health information electronically in connection with standard transactions, as defined in 45 CFR 160.103.
The staff member designated by the Administrator to oversee privacy policies, training, complaints and breach response.
A written, signed permission from the resident or representative that allows the facility to use or disclose PHI for a stated purpose.

procedures: The Administrator designates a Privacy Officer, [PRIVACY OFFICER NAME], and records the designation in writing. Residents and staff are told how to reach the Privacy Officer at [PHONE].

Before opening, and whenever services change (for example adding EALR/SNALR or ALP services), the Administrator and counsel decide whether [AGENCY NAME] is a HIPAA covered entity. The written determination is kept on file.

If the facility is a covered entity, the Privacy Officer prepares a notice of privacy practices, gives it to each resident or representative at or before admission, records acknowledgment of receipt, and posts the notice in [LOCATION OF PUBLIC POSTING].

Every employee, volunteer and contractor receives privacy and confidentiality training at orientation, including HIV confidentiality, and signs a confidentiality statement before working with residents (ORI-01). Refresher training is given at least once a year and documented.

Staff access resident information only when needed to do their job. Staff must not discuss residents in public areas, with other residents or with visitors, and must not post resident information or images on social media.

Paper resident records are kept in locked cabinets or a locked room that is attended or locked when unattended. Medication and care records used on the floor are kept out of sight of visitors and other residents.

Electronic records are protected with individual user IDs, passwords, automatic log-off and access limited by job role. The Privacy Officer reviews access lists at least once a year and removes access when an employee leaves or changes role.

Staff may release resident information without written consent only in the cases allowed by law, such as treatment, emergency care, reporting required by DOH or the Justice Center, or a valid legal order. All other releases require a signed authorization stating what is released, to whom and for what purpose. The Privacy Officer reviews every request that is not routine treatment.

Residents or their representatives may ask to see or get a copy of the resident record. Staff refer such requests to the Privacy Officer, who responds in accordance with applicable law and the timeframes in 45 CFR 164 if the facility is a covered entity.

HIV-related information is disclosed only as allowed by 18 NYCRR §485.11(g)(9)-(15) and New York law. It is kept in a separate restricted section of the record, and only staff who need it to provide care can see it. The Privacy Officer decides on any disclosure and documents it. Applicants, employees and volunteers have the same protection.
Staff must protect resident privacy during care. They knock before entering rooms, close doors and curtains during personal care and hold care conversations away from others.
Confidential records are not removed from the facility except under written direction of the Administrator, for example to send with a resident to a hospital, and then only the minimum necessary.

Resident, personnel and facility records are retained under REC-01 and the periods in 18 NYCRR §487.10(h), 3 years after death or discharge for individual resident records and 7 years for program, business and renewal records. Records are destroyed by shredding or secure electronic deletion after that period, and the destruction is logged.

Any employee who learns of a possible privacy breach, such as a lost record, a misdirected fax or email, or unauthorized access, reports it to the Privacy Officer the same day. The Privacy Officer investigates, limits harm and documents the findings.

If the facility is a covered entity and a breach of unsecured PHI occurs, the Privacy Officer notifies affected residents, and notifies the federal Department of Health and Human Services and others when required, without unreasonable delay and within the time limits in 45 CFR 164 Subpart D. Counsel is consulted on whether other state notifications apply.

Employees who violate this policy are disciplined under PER-01, up to and including termination. Residents may file a privacy complaint with the Privacy Officer under RS-03, and no one is retaliated against for filing one.
The Privacy Officer reports privacy incidents, training completion and any complaints to the QA committee at each meeting (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Designates the Privacy Officer, determines covered-entity status with counsel and makes sure records are secure.
Maintains privacy practices and notices, trains staff, reviews disclosure requests, investigates breaches and reports to the QA committee.
Protect confidential information, access only what is needed, sign the confidentiality statement and report suspected breaches immediately.
Explains privacy practices to residents and obtains authorizations for non-routine disclosures.

Covered-entity determination
Notice of privacy practices and signed acknowledgments, if applicable
Signed staff and volunteer confidentiality statements
Privacy training records
Authorizations and disclosure log
Access list reviews
Breach investigation and notification records
Record destruction log

policies.title: Optional Resident Services (Respite, Social Day Care, Non-ACF Space Use), Special Services and Transportation
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Administrator, the case manager, residents, respite guests, social day care participants and outside service providers
policies.purpose: To state which optional services [AGENCY NAME] offers beyond the required resident services, to set the conditions for offering them, and to describe special services and transportation, so that optional programs never reduce the safety, space or supervision of permanent residents.
policies.policy:
This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Schedule 6, item 6 (Optional Resident Services) and Schedule 6, item 25 (A Description of Special Services, if any).

Item 6 election. The Administrator records the facility's choices in Schedule 6 as follows: (a) Respite program: [WILL / WILL NOT] be offered. (b) Social day care program: [WILL / WILL NOT] be offered. If offered, [AGENCY NAME] will submit the Schedule 7D application and will not start the program until the Department of Health (DOH) approves it. For a change of operator, Schedule 7D must be submitted to continue any previous operator's respite or social day care program. (c) Use of part of the adult home for purposes other than operating an adult care facility, such as a medical office for outside providers: [WILL / WILL NOT] occur. If it will, [AGENCY NAME] will submit a waiver request for 18 NYCRR §487.11(l)(1) (C8) with the application. The space will not be used for that purpose until DOH approves the waiver in writing.

Optional programs and non-ACF space use will not displace required resident space or reduce the staffing and supervision of residents. Part II of the application includes the program's policies and service plans (18 NYCRR §485.6, C29), so any optional service listed here is described in Part II and is not started or changed without DOH review. Respite guests follow the admission and medical evaluation rules in AD-02. Resident bedrooms, toilets, baths and the call system must continue to meet the environmental standards in 18 NYCRR §487.11 (C8) while any optional program or non-ACF use operates.

Item 25 special services. [AGENCY NAME] describes every special service it offers or arranges, who provides it, and who pays. Services are listed in Procedure 12 and in the attachment [SPECIAL SERVICES LIST]. Residents keep the right to use outside providers of their choice.

Transportation. [AGENCY NAME] helps residents get to medical appointments, activities and community outings as described in the Procedures below, and discloses in the admission agreement which transportation is included and which is a separate charge.

definitions.definition: A short-term, temporary stay of a person who is not a permanent resident, used to give a caregiver relief or to meet a short-term need.
A daytime program of social and supportive activities for participants who go home each evening. It requires a Schedule 7D application and DOH approval.

Use of part of the adult home building for a purpose other than operating an adult care facility, such as an outside provider's medical office. It requires a waiver request for 18 NYCRR §487.11(l)(1).
A service beyond the required resident services, such as podiatry, therapies or other outside vendor services, provided on site or arranged by the facility.
The DOH application schedule used to request approval of a social day care program.

procedures: Before filing Schedule 6, the Administrator decides with the governing body whether to offer respite, social day care and non-ACF space use, and records each decision in the Schedule 6 election above.
If social day care is chosen, the Administrator completes and submits the Schedule 7D application with the application package. The program does not begin until DOH approves it in writing.

If a portion of the building will house an outside provider's office or another non-ACF use, the Administrator prepares the waiver request for 18 NYCRR §487.11(l)(1), including a floor plan showing the space, the user, the hours and the separation from resident areas, and submits it with the application.
Before any non-ACF use begins, the Administrator confirms in writing that DOH has granted the waiver. The approval is filed in the facility administrative file [LOCATION].

The Administrator verifies that the space used for non-ACF purposes is not needed to meet the bedroom minimums (100 sq ft single, 160 sq ft double), the toilet ratio (1 per 6 residents), the bath ratio (1 per 10 residents) or the call system requirement in §487.11, and keeps the verification on file.

Respite referrals go to the case manager. The case manager applies AD-01 retention standards and AD-02 pre-admission evaluation, including the medical evaluation (DSS-3122) and the written Administrator interview, before the respite stay starts.

For each respite stay, the case manager records the start and end dates, the reason for the stay, medications, diet, emergency contacts and the physician. The case manager gives the guest the rights statement, the house rules and the fee and charge disclosure at or before arrival.

The Administrator confirms before each respite stay that a bed is available and that staffing under STF-01 is adequate for the added guest. A respite stay is declined if it would reduce supervision of residents.

For social day care participants, the program coordinator keeps a participant file with the enrollment form, emergency contacts, attendance, and any incident. Participants are not residents and do not receive overnight services.
The Administrator ensures that social day care activities and participants do not interfere with resident dining, personal care, medication passes or evacuation routes, and reviews this monthly.
All optional programs follow the facility's abuse reporting (SAF-01), incident reporting (SAF-02), infection control (SAF-04), fire safety (EM-02) and background check (PER-02) policies.

Special services (item 25): the Administrator maintains a [SPECIAL SERVICES LIST] naming each service (for example podiatry, physical or occupational therapy, speech therapy, vision, hearing, dental, barber/beautician, or other outside vendors), the provider, the schedule, the location, and who pays.

Before any outside vendor provides services on site, the Administrator obtains the vendor's license or credentials where applicable, proof of insurance, and a signed confidentiality statement, and confirms the vendor's staff meet the facility's health screening requirements in PER-03.
Residents choose whether to use a facility-arranged vendor or their own provider. Staff do not require use of a particular vendor and tell residents in writing that choice is theirs.

Transportation to medical appointments: the case manager schedules appointments with the resident, arranges the ride (family, facility vehicle, Medicaid transportation where the resident is eligible, or a private service), and arranges an escort when the ISP or the resident's condition requires one.

Transportation to activities and outings: the Activities Director posts the schedule and sign-up, confirms each rider's ability to participate, and assigns a staff member or volunteer to accompany groups [RATIO].

Costs: the admission agreement (AD-05) states which transportation is included in the base rate and which is charged separately and the rate. Any charge is explained to the resident before the first charge is made. Residents who receive SSI are not charged in a way that reduces the personal needs allowance.
The case manager documents each outside appointment and ride in the resident record, and staff record any problem or missed appointment and notify the physician or family as needed.
The Administrator reviews all optional programs, special services and transportation each quarter as part of GOV-02, and notifies DOH before any change that requires approval.

responsibilities.duty: Makes the Schedule 6 election, submits Schedule 7D and the §487.11(l)(1) waiver request, confirms DOH approvals before starting a program, approves vendors and reviews programs quarterly.
Screens respite guests under AD-01 and AD-02, arranges appointments and transportation and keeps records.
Runs social programming, plans outings and day care activities and supervises escorts.
Support residents and guests with transport and activities and report concerns.
Approves the optional services offered and confirms the facility has adequate staff and space.

Space verification showing bedroom, toilet, bath and call-system minimums are still met
Respite stay records, evaluations and agreements
Social day care participant files and attendance
[SPECIAL SERVICES LIST], vendor credentials, insurance and confidentiality statements
Transportation log and appointment records in the resident file
Quarterly program review notes

policies.title: Admission and Retention Standards and Resident Profile
policies.applies_to: Administrator, case manager, nursing or health care staff, direct care staff and all applicants and residents
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] admits and keeps only people whose needs the home may lawfully meet, to describe the residents the home serves, and to require active efforts to find another placement when a resident can no longer be retained.
policies.policy:
This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Schedule 6, item 7a (Admission Policies: admission and retention standards) and item 7b (Admission Policies: resident profile that includes a description of any target populations).

Item 7a, admission and retention standards. [AGENCY NAME] admits and retains only people whose needs it may lawfully meet. Under 18 NYCRR §487.4 (C1), the home will not accept or retain any person in the 13 excluded groups listed in the rule. These include a person who needs continual medical or nursing care, who is chronically bedfast, who has chronic unmanaged incontinence, or who is a danger to self or others. The full list of the 13 groups is reproduced on the admission screening checklist [ATTACHMENT: 487.4 SCREENING CHECKLIST], and staff screen every applicant and every resident against all 13 groups. [AGENCY NAME] is licensed as an Assisted Living Residence (ALR), which means 5 or more residents with 24-hour on-site monitoring (Public Health Law §4651, C22). The Assisted Living Program (ALP) is excluded from that definition and is addressed separately in ALP-01 and ALP-02. Certification level: [ALR / EALR / SNALR] as approved.

EALR aging in place. If [AGENCY NAME] is approved as an Enhanced Assisted Living Residence, a resident may remain as needs increase when a physician's report supports it, as provided in Public Health Law §4655 (C23) and 10 NYCRR §1001.10 (C18). Retention of a resident who needs 24-hour skilled nursing follows only the exception in §1001.10 and EALR-01.

SNALR. If approved as a Special Needs Assisted Living Residence, [AGENCY NAME] admits residents with special needs, such as dementia, under the approved plan only (see SNALR-01), and does not admit residents who are outside that plan.

Item 7b, resident profile and target populations. [AGENCY NAME] serves adults who need housing, food, supervision, personal care, case management and activities and whose needs can be met within the services and staffing approved for this home. Target population: [DESCRIBE, e.g., ADULTS AGE 65 AND OLDER; ADULTS WITH EARLY-STAGE DEMENTIA UNDER SNALR-01; OTHER]. Anticipated resident mix at opening: [NUMBER OF ADULTS 65+ / UNDER 65 / MEDICAID-SSI / PRIVATE PAY]. The profile is updated in Schedule 6 if the target population changes.

When a resident can no longer be retained, the home makes persistent efforts to find an alternative placement and follows AD-06.

definitions.definition: The 13 categories of people a home may not accept or retain, including people who need continual medical or nursing care, are chronically bedfast, have chronic unmanaged incontinence, or are a danger to self or others.
An assisted living residence: 5 or more residents with 24-hour on-site monitoring (Public Health Law §4651).
An Enhanced Assisted Living Residence, certified to allow residents to age in place with a physician's report (Public Health Law §4655).
A Special Needs Assisted Living Residence, approved to admit residents with special needs under an approved plan.
A defined group the home intends to serve, such as older adults or people with dementia, described in the resident profile.

procedures: The Administrator keeps the 487.4 screening checklist (all 13 excluded groups) in the admissions file and trains the case manager and nursing or health care staff on it during orientation (ORI-01).

When an inquiry or referral arrives, the case manager gathers basic information on diagnoses, mobility, continence, behavior, medications, cognition and supports needed, and records it on the inquiry form [FORM].

The case manager screens the inquiry against the 13 excluded groups. If the applicant falls into any group, the case manager notifies the Administrator, the applicant is not accepted, and the case manager helps the family find other options.
For applicants who pass the first screen, the case manager starts the pre-admission process in AD-02, including the medical evaluation (DSS-3122) and the written Administrator interview.

The Administrator makes the final admission decision after reviewing the medical evaluation, the case manager's evaluation and the interview. The decision and reasons are recorded in the admission file.
The Administrator confirms that the home's approved certification level and staffing can meet the applicant's needs. An applicant needing services outside the approved level or plan is not admitted.

For EALR, when a resident's needs increase, the case manager requests a physician's report on whether the resident can remain, and the Administrator decides about retention based on the report and EALR-01.
For SNALR, only applicants who fit the approved special-needs plan are admitted to the memory care unit, and the Administrator confirms fit before admission under SNALR-01.
The case manager rescreens every resident against the 13 excluded groups at each reassessment (AD-03), at each annual medical evaluation and whenever a change of condition occurs (RS-04).

If a resident appears to meet an excluded group or the home can no longer meet the resident's needs, staff notify the Administrator the same day. The Administrator reviews the resident's condition, supports available and possible changes to the ISP.

If retention is no longer lawful or safe, the Administrator and case manager begin persistent efforts to find alternative placement, with contact with the resident, representative, physician and potential placements. Each effort is dated and recorded in the resident record.
The Administrator issues any discharge or termination notice only under AD-06 and the resident protections rules, and does not shorten any notice period or process.

Once a year, the Administrator and the governing body review the resident profile, including the actual resident mix, against the profile in Schedule 6 and amend Schedule 6 if the population served has changed.
Admission decisions are made without discrimination under NDI-01. The reasons for any denial are based only on the screening standards in this policy.

responsibilities.duty: Makes final admission and retention decisions, keeps the 487.4 checklist current and approves the resident profile.
Screens applicants and residents against the 13 groups, coordinates evaluations and documents placement efforts.
Review health information, flag changes of condition and support physician reports for EALR aging in place.
Approves admission standards and reviews the resident profile annually.

documentation: 487.4 screening checklist for each applicant and each reassessment
Inquiry form and admission decision record with reasons
Physician's report for EALR retention
Records of alternative placement efforts with dates and contacts
Annual resident profile review

policies.title: Pre-Admission Evaluation and Admission Interview
policies.applies_to: Administrator, case manager, nursing or health care staff, applicants, resident representatives and the applicant's physician
policies.purpose: To make sure every applicant receives a complete medical, case management and Administrator evaluation before admission, is given all required information, and that the decision and any reasons for denial are documented.
policies.policy:
This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Schedule 6, item 7c (Admission Policies: pre-admission evaluation policy).

No person is admitted until the following are complete. (1) A medical evaluation on form DSS-3122 completed within 30 days before admission and repeated at least every 12 months (18 NYCRR §487.4, C1). (2) A written Administrator interview with the applicant before admission (§487.4). (3) For an Assisted Living Residence, a case manager evaluation before admission and at least every 12 months using the DOH personal data and resident evaluation form (10 NYCRR §1001.10, C18).

At or before the interview, the applicant receives the admission agreement, the resident rights statement, the facility rules and the Ombudsman/legal-services sheet, and is offered the opportunity to review the latest DOH inspection report (§487.4). The Administrator documents the admission decision, and the reasons for any denial.

definitions.definition: The medical evaluation form completed by the applicant's physician, which must be dated within 30 days before admission and renewed at least every 12 months.
A written interview of the applicant by the Administrator before admission to determine whether the home can meet the applicant's needs.

definitions.term: Personal data and resident evaluation form
definitions.definition: The DOH form the ALR case manager uses to evaluate the applicant before admission and at least every 12 months.
A person authorized by the resident, or by law, to act for the resident, such as a health care proxy agent.

procedures: The case manager opens a pre-admission file for each applicant on first serious inquiry and records the date, contact person and source of referral.

The case manager sends the applicant or representative the DSS-3122 and asks the applicant's physician to complete it. The case manager checks that the evaluation is dated no more than 30 days before the planned admission date.
If the DSS-3122 will be more than 30 days old on the admission date, the case manager requests a new one. Admission is delayed until a current evaluation is received.

The Administrator and case manager review the completed DSS-3122 for diagnoses, medications, mobility, continence, cognition, behaviors and any condition that falls under an excluded group in AD-01. Questions go back to the physician in writing.

The case manager completes the ALR evaluation using the DOH personal data and resident evaluation form, meeting with the applicant, and with the representative and family when the applicant agrees, and records the applicant's needs, preferences and supports.

At or before the interview, the case manager or Administrator gives the applicant or representative the admission agreement, the rights statement, the facility rules and the Ombudsman/legal-services sheet, and records the date given on the checklist [FORM].

The Administrator offers the applicant the chance to review the facility's latest DOH inspection report, which is kept available at [LOCATION], and records that the offer was made and whether it was accepted.

The Administrator conducts the interview in person, or by another way that suits an applicant who cannot attend, in plain language and with an interpreter if needed (NDI-01). The Administrator writes a summary of the interview covering the applicant's needs, expectations, understanding of services and charges, and ability to live in a group setting.

The Administrator answers questions about services, charges, house rules and the right to choose outside health care providers, and checks the applicant's understanding of how the personal needs allowance works for SSI recipients (AD-05).

The Administrator, with the case manager and nursing or health care staff as needed, decides whether the home can meet the applicant's needs under AD-01. The decision, the date and the reasons are written in the pre-admission file.

If admission is denied, the Administrator tells the applicant and representative promptly, gives the reasons in writing and suggests other options, and files a copy of the notice. The reason must not be a prohibited basis under NDI-01.

If admission is approved, the case manager schedules the admission date, confirms medications and physician orders are ready, confirms the signing of the admission agreement under AD-05, and prepares the initial ISP under AD-03.

The case manager repeats the medical evaluation (DSS-3122) and the case manager evaluation for each resident at least every 12 months. The due dates are on the tracking log and the case manager reviews the log monthly.
For respite guests (OPT-01), the same medical evaluation, interview and evaluation steps apply before the stay.
Completed forms are placed in the resident record under REC-01 on the day of admission, and the pre-admission file of any applicant not admitted is kept under REC-01 retention rules.

responsibilities.duty: Conducts and documents the written interview, offers the DOH inspection report and makes and records the admission decision.
Obtains the DSS-3122, completes the DOH evaluation form, distributes the required documents and tracks 12-month updates.
Review medical information with the Administrator and case manager.
Completes the DSS-3122 within the 30-day window and responds to questions.

documentation: DSS-3122 with date
DOH personal data and resident evaluation form (ALR case manager evaluation)
Written Administrator interview
Checklist showing date the agreement, rights statement, rules and Ombudsman/legal-services sheet were given
Record that the latest DOH inspection report was offered
Admission decision and reasons for any denial
12-month tracking log

policies.title: Individualized Service Plan (ISP) and Reassessment
policies.applies_to: Case manager, Administrator, nursing and direct care staff, residents, representatives and outside providers
policies.purpose: To ensure each resident has a written Individualized Service Plan that reflects the resident's needs and choices, is evaluated at least every 12 months, and is updated whenever the resident's condition changes.
policies.policy:
This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Schedule 6, item 7d (If you are applying for an Assisted Living Residence, also submit: ISP form, policy and process). The ISP form [ATTACHMENT: ISP FORM] and this process are submitted with Schedule 6, item 7d.

Every resident of the Assisted Living Residence has an Individualized Service Plan (ISP) (10 NYCRR §1001.10, C18). The case manager evaluates each resident before admission and at least every 12 months using the DOH personal data and resident evaluation form (§1001.10). The ISP is updated when the resident's condition changes and is shared with the resident, the representative and outside providers involved in care, with the resident's agreement. For adult home residents, case management duties follow 18 NYCRR §487.7 (C4), and the same ISP process is used for all residents so that service delivery is consistent.

definitions.definition: The Individualized Service Plan: a written plan for each resident stating needs, services, who provides them, how often, and the resident's goals and preferences.
A fresh evaluation of the resident's needs by the case manager, done at least every 12 months and after any significant change.
A new or worsening physical, cognitive, mood or behavior problem, or functional decline that may require a change in services (see RS-04).
A home care agency, hospice, therapist, physician or other professional who is not facility staff but provides services to the resident.

procedures: Before admission, the case manager completes the DOH personal data and resident evaluation form with the applicant (AD-02) and uses it as the basis of the initial ISP.

The case manager drafts the initial ISP on the ISP form before or on the day of admission, listing needs in personal care, medication assistance, supervision, mobility, nutrition and diet, continence, activities, mental health and social needs, and any services from outside providers.
The ISP states for each service who will provide it (facility staff or outside provider), how often, and any limits. Services that the home may not lawfully provide are not placed in the ISP (AD-01).

The case manager reviews the draft ISP with the resident, and with the representative when the resident agrees, records the resident's own goals and choices, and makes changes the resident requests where they are safe and feasible.
The resident, or representative, and the case manager sign and date the ISP. A copy is offered to the resident and the original is filed in the resident record.

The case manager shares the ISP with direct care and medication staff who need it to do their work, and with outside providers involved in the resident's care, with the resident's consent, within [3] business days of completion.
Direct care staff keep a care summary of ISP tasks in [LOCATION] and record completion of tasks on the daily record [FORM].

The case manager reassesses each resident at least every 12 months using the DOH personal data and resident evaluation form, together with the annual medical evaluation (AD-02), and updates the ISP. The due date is entered on the tracking log.
The case manager also reviews the ISP with the resident at least every [90] days and notes whether services are effective and whether the resident's preferences have changed.

When staff notice a change of condition, they report it to the case manager and the Administrator the same day (RS-04). The case manager meets the resident within [2] business days, reassesses and updates the ISP.

The case manager updates the ISP after any hospitalization, fall, new diagnosis, medication change, hospice start, behavior change or request from the resident or family, and records the reason for each update.

If reassessment shows the resident's needs may fall under an excluded group in AD-01 or exceed the home's approved level, the case manager informs the Administrator immediately and AD-01 and AD-06 procedures begin.
The case manager notifies the resident's physician and outside providers of ISP changes that affect their services, and records the notice.
The Administrator reviews a sample of ISPs each quarter for completeness, timeliness and consistency with care delivered, as part of GOV-02.

responsibilities.duty: Completes evaluations, writes and updates the ISP, reviews it with the resident and shares it with providers.
Approves the ISP form and process, reviews ISPs and responds to needs the home cannot meet.
Follow the ISP, document tasks and report changes in condition.
Take part in ISP development and review and say what they want.

documentation: ISP form for each resident, signed and dated
DOH personal data and resident evaluation form (initial and every 12 months)
Record of ISP updates and reasons
Record of sharing with outside providers
12-month and 90-day review tracking log
Quarterly ISP audit

policies.title: Palliative Care (EALR/SNALR) and Advance Directives
policies.applies_to: Administrator, case manager, nursing and direct care staff, residents, representatives, physicians and hospice providers
policies.purpose: To describe how [AGENCY NAME] supports residents with serious or life-limiting illness, honors residents' wishes about future care, and coordinates with hospice and the resident's physician.
policies.policy:
This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Schedule 6, item 7e (If you are applying for an Assisted Living Residence, also submit: Palliative Care Policy (EALR and SNALR)).

As an applicant for [EALR / SNALR / BOTH] certification under Public Health Law §4655 (C23) and 10 NYCRR §1001.10 (C18), [AGENCY NAME] provides this palliative care policy. Palliative care is care that aims to relieve pain and other symptoms and to support the resident's comfort, dignity and own goals, and it is not limited to the last days of life. Hospice is permitted when the conditions in 10 NYCRR §1001.10 are met, and the resident keeps the right to choose a hospice provider and physician.

The home asks every resident about advance directives at admission, records them in the chart and honors them. This includes a health care proxy, a living will and any Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment (MOLST) signed by the resident's physician. Goals of care are reviewed at each reassessment and on any change of condition. The home coordinates care with hospice and the resident's physician, and follows RS-06 for hospice and death of a resident. No resident is refused admission or retention solely because he or she has declined or chosen life-sustaining treatment, but retention remains subject to the standards in AD-01 and EALR-01.

definitions.definition: Care focused on comfort, symptom relief and quality of life for a resident with a serious illness, alongside other treatment.
A program of comfort-focused care for a resident near the end of life, provided by an outside licensed hospice agency.
A resident's written or recorded instructions or choice of decision-maker for future health care, such as a health care proxy or living will.
Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment: a physician's order form reflecting the resident's choices about resuscitation and other life-sustaining treatment.
What matters most to the resident about treatment and daily life, discussed and recorded to guide care decisions.

procedures: At the admission interview or on the day of admission, the case manager asks the resident whether the resident has a health care proxy, living will, MOLST or any other instruction about care at the end of life, and records the answer on the advance directive form [FORM].

If the resident has a document, the case manager asks for a copy, places it at the front of the chart in a marked section, and notes it on the face sheet so that staff and emergency responders can find it.

If the resident has no document, the case manager gives the resident information, offers to help the resident discuss options with a physician or other advisor, and records that information was offered. Signing a document is never a condition of admission or retention.

The case manager confirms with the physician whether a MOLST exists, files it in the chart, and tells the resident and representative where it is kept. A copy goes with the resident on any transfer to a hospital (RS-04).

The case manager discusses goals of care with the resident at each reassessment (AD-03), when a serious diagnosis is made, after a hospitalization and when the resident or family asks, and records the discussion and any changes.

Staff make sure every employee knows where advance directives are kept and honors them. In an emergency, staff follow the resident's documented wishes and emergency procedures in RS-04 and call 911 unless a valid order covers the situation.

When a resident has a serious or life-limiting illness, the case manager and Administrator meet with the resident, representative and physician to review the ISP and to arrange comfort measures, pain management orders, diet, positioning and emotional and spiritual support.
The ISP for a resident receiving palliative care states the comfort goals, who provides each service, symptom monitoring done by staff and the physician to be called for new symptoms.

When the physician recommends hospice or the resident requests it, the case manager helps the resident choose a licensed hospice agency, confirms the conditions in 10 NYCRR §1001.10 are met, and obtains a written coordination agreement or plan of care from the agency.

The case manager coordinates a plan with the hospice team that states who provides personal care, medication assistance and supervision, how hospice staff give orders to the home, and how the home reaches hospice 24 hours a day.

Staff report any new pain, symptom or decline to the nurse, case manager or hospice on call without delay, and record it. Medications for comfort follow MED-01 and MED-02, and only staff authorized and trained under those policies assist with them.

The Administrator checks that the home's staffing, space and services can support the resident's needs. If needs exceed what the home may lawfully provide, the Administrator follows AD-01, EALR-01 and AD-06 and keeps the resident's wishes central in any planning.

The home supports resident and family needs near the end of life, including visits at any hour, spiritual or cultural practices the resident chooses, and respect for privacy and dignity (RS-02, SOC-01).
After a death, staff follow RS-06, including notification of the representative and physician, and respect the resident's documented wishes.
The Administrator trains staff on this policy at orientation and in annual in-service (ORI-01, ORI-02), and reviews the policy each year with the governing body.

responsibilities.duty: Asks about and records advance directives, leads goals-of-care discussions, coordinates with hospice and the physician and updates the ISP.
Approves the palliative care approach, confirms the home can meet the resident's needs and ensures staff training.
Monitor symptoms, communicate with physician and hospice and guide comfort care.
Know where advance directives are, give comfort and personal care as planned and report changes.
Make their own choices about care and tell staff of changes.

documentation: Advance directive form completed at admission
Copies of health care proxy, living will and MOLST in the chart
Goals-of-care discussion notes at each reassessment and change of condition
Hospice election and coordination plan
Updated ISP for palliative care
Staff training records on this policy

policies.title: Admission Agreement, Fees, Deposits, Price Posting and Refunds
policies.applies_to: Administrator, business office staff, case manager, residents and representatives
policies.purpose: To ensure every resident signs a clear, DOH-approved admission agreement, that charges, deposits and refunds are fair and disclosed, and that required rate information is posted.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] uses the DOH model admission/residency agreement and the EALR, SNALR and ALP addenda that apply to its approved program. The agreements are reviewed and pre-approved as part of Part II of the application (18 NYCRR §485.6, C29), and the home does not change approved wording or use a different form without DOH approval.

The admission agreement contains the content required by 18 NYCRR §487.5(d) (C2), including the offer of the SSI/HR personal allowance and the refund terms. For residents who receive SSI, the 2026 SSI Congregate Care Level 3 rate is $1,688 per month. The resident keeps $262 per month for personal needs, and the facility's share is about $1,426. The home does not charge an SSI resident any amount that would reduce the resident's personal needs allowance below $262.

As an Assisted Living Residence, [AGENCY NAME] posts the starting monthly rate, the rent range, the approved agreement and the fee summary on its website and in the facility, and reports annual quality measures to DOH (Public Health Law §4656, C24). The agreement lists the services included in the base rate and any additional charges and how they are set. Operating an ALR without approval is a class A misdemeanor (Public Health Law §4656(5)), and the home does not admit residents or advertise ALR services before approval is in place.

definitions.definition: The written contract between the resident and the home that states services, charges, resident rights and the conditions for discharge, using the DOH approved form.
An approved attachment to the agreement for EALR, SNALR or ALP services.
The monthly amount, $262 for SSI Congregate Care Level 3 in 2026, that the resident keeps for personal use.
The required public display of the starting monthly rate, rent range, approved agreement and fee summary on the website and in the facility.
Fees for services not included in the base rate, listed in the agreement with the amount or how it is calculated.

procedures: The Administrator submits the DOH model admission/residency agreement and any EALR, SNALR and ALP addenda with Part II of the application and keeps the DOH-approved versions on file. Only approved versions are used.

Before any resident is admitted, the Administrator prepares a rate schedule that states the base rate, the services it includes and each additional charge, and checks that it matches the approved agreement and the posted price information.

At or before the admission interview, the case manager gives the applicant or representative the agreement to read (AD-02) with time to read it and ask questions. Staff offer to explain it and to give it in the applicant's language or in accessible format (NDI-01).

The Administrator reviews with the applicant the services included, additional charges, deposits if any, payment due date, the offer of the SSI/HR personal allowance, the refund terms and the discharge and termination terms (AD-06).

For applicants who receive or will apply for SSI, the Administrator explains that the resident keeps $262 per month for personal needs (2026 level) and that the total SSI Congregate Care Level 3 amount is $1,688, and records that this was explained.
The Administrator does not collect any amount from an SSI resident that would reduce the personal needs allowance below $262 per month, and any resident funds are handled under FUN-01.

The applicant or representative and the Administrator sign and date the agreement before or on the day of admission. The resident receives a complete copy and the original is filed in the resident record.
If a deposit or advance payment is collected, the business office issues a receipt and records the amount, date and purpose. The deposit is held and refunded only as the approved agreement provides.

Refunds: if a resident leaves, dies or is discharged, the business office calculates the amount owed on a pro-rated basis as the agreement states, prepares a written statement and issues the refund to the resident or the estate or representative within the period set in the agreement [DAYS]. The calculation is kept in the resident record.

The Administrator posts the starting monthly rate, rent range, approved agreement and fee summary on the website and in a public place in the facility [LOCATION], and checks the posting each month and after any rate change.

Before changing any rate or additional charge, the Administrator gives residents the written notice required by the approved agreement, files the notice and updates the price posting on the same date the change takes effect.
Staff do not change, add to or waive agreement terms orally. Any change goes through the Administrator in writing and an addendum is signed if DOH-approved wording allows it.
For EALR, SNALR and ALP residents, the case manager attaches the applicable approved addendum to the agreement and confirms the resident understands the added services and charges.
The Administrator submits the annual quality measures report and pays the ALR biennial fee as required by Public Health Law §4656, and keeps proof of filing.
The Administrator reviews agreements, billing practices and the price posting each year as part of GOV-02 and reports any problem to the governing body.

responsibilities.duty: Keeps only approved agreements in use, explains terms, signs agreements, ensures price posting and quality reporting and handles refunds.
Prepare billing, issue receipts, calculate refunds and protect the personal needs allowance.
Delivers the agreement at the interview, attaches addenda and answers resident questions.
Approves rates and charges and reviews compliance annually.

documentation: DOH-approved admission/residency agreement and addenda
Signed agreement and receipt of copy for each resident
Rate schedule and additional charge list
Deposit receipts and refund calculations
Price posting proof (website capture and facility posting log)
Notices of rate change
Annual quality measures report and biennial fee proof

policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Termination Notice
policies.applies_to: All residents of [AGENCY NAME] (adult home / enriched housing program with Assisted Living Residence licensure); Administrator, Case Manager, nursing and direct-care staff, business office
policies.purpose: To make sure that every discharge, transfer or termination of residency is lawful, is carried out with the required written notice and legal-services information, and is preceded by persistent efforts to find an appropriate alternative placement. The policy also explains how the retention standards for admission apply once a resident is in the home.
policies.policy:
This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Schedule 6, item 7a - Admission Policies (all applicants): admission and retention standards. Admission standards and the resident profile are in AD-01. This policy covers the retention side of those standards and the discharge process.

[AGENCY NAME] admits and retains only people whose needs the home may lawfully meet under 18 NYCRR 487.4. The home may not accept or retain a person in any of the 13 excluded categories in that section. These include a person who needs continual medical or nursing care, is chronically bedfast, has chronic unmanaged incontinence, or is a danger to self or others. A resident who no longer meets the retention standards may not simply remain in the home. A resident also may not be removed except through the process in this policy.

The home will not terminate a resident's residency except on 30 days' written notice given on the DOH-prescribed form (18 NYCRR 487.5(f)). The notice will be accompanied by a list of free legal and advocacy services. A copy will go to the DOH regional office within 5 days. If the resident objects to the termination, the home will not remove the resident without a court proceeding. Before and during the notice period, staff will make persistent efforts to find an alternative placement (18 NYCRR 487.4). The home will document each effort.

For an ALR resident whose needs require 24-hour skilled nursing care, termination follows the retention exception and the Social Services Law provision cross-referenced in 10 NYCRR 1001.10. The Administrator will confirm the exact text with the DOH regional office before applying that exception, and will document that confirmation. A resident discharged voluntarily is handled under steps 14 and 15. Medical emergencies and hospital transfers are handled under RS-04.

definitions.definition: The criteria in 18 NYCRR 487.4 that determine whether a resident's needs may still lawfully be met by the home, including the categories of persons who may not be retained.
A home-initiated end of residency, which requires 30 days' written notice on the DOH form and a court proceeding if the resident objects.
A setting that can lawfully and safely meet the resident's assessed needs, such as a nursing home, a higher level of care, a family home or another licensed setting.
The NYS DOH Regional Office (Capital District, Central NY, Western NY or Metropolitan Area) that oversees the home.
The physician's evaluation required within 30 days before admission and at least every 12 months, used to identify whether a resident still meets retention standards.

procedures: Identification: Any staff member who observes a change that may mean a resident no longer meets retention standards (for example, a need for continual nursing care, becoming chronically bedfast, unmanaged incontinence, or danger to self or others) reports it to the Case Manager the same day.
Same-day response: The Case Manager notifies the Administrator and the nurse or designated health professional. The resident's physician is notified under RS-04 if there is a clinical change.

Review: Within [3] business days the Administrator, Case Manager and nurse review the resident's current DSS-3122 medical evaluation and ISP. They also review any new physician information and determine whether the needs can lawfully be met with added services, such as outside home care or hospice under RS-06 and EALR-01.

Resident and representative involvement: The Case Manager meets with the resident and the resident's representative or family (with the resident's consent). They discuss the findings, the options and the resident's wishes, and offer Ombudsman and legal-services contact information.
Documentation: The Administrator records the determination, the evidence relied on and the options considered in the resident record, and signs it.

Alternative placement efforts: If the home cannot lawfully retain the resident, the Case Manager begins documented, persistent efforts at alternative placement. These include referrals to at least [3] appropriate providers, contact with the resident's physician and social services district where applicable, and involvement of family. Each contact is logged with date, person contacted and outcome.

Notice preparation: The Administrator completes the DOH-prescribed termination notice form, stating the reasons, the effective date (at least 30 days after notice) and the resident's right to object. The Administrator attaches the list of free legal and advocacy services.

Delivery: The Administrator personally delivers the notice and attachments to the resident and sends a copy to the resident's representative, if any. The delivery date and method are documented, and the resident acknowledges receipt where possible.
Regional office copy: Within 5 days of giving the notice, the Administrator sends a copy to the DOH regional office and keeps proof of transmission.

Resident objection: If the resident objects, the Administrator will not remove the resident or force the move before a court proceeding is held and decided. The Administrator consults [FACILITY COUNSEL] and the regional office on next steps. The home continues to provide services and to pursue alternative placement during the proceeding.

Ongoing placement work: The Case Manager continues to document placement efforts throughout the notice period, updates the resident and representative at least weekly, and informs the Administrator of any barrier.

24-hour skilled nursing need in an ALR: When the reason is a need for 24-hour skilled nursing, the Administrator first confirms the applicable statutory and regulatory requirements with the regional office, in line with 10 NYCRR 1001.10. The Administrator applies them in addition to steps 1 through 11, and records the confirmation in the resident record.

Transition planning: Before the move, the Case Manager coordinates transfer of the ISP summary, current medication list, physician orders and other clinical information with the receiving provider. The Case Manager arranges transportation with the resident and family, with a staff escort when appropriate.

Voluntary discharge: If a resident chooses to leave, the Case Manager documents the resident's request and the planned date and helps with transition. Refunds follow AD-05, and funds and property follow FUN-01.

Departure day: On the day of discharge, staff return all personal property, funds and medications belonging to the resident per FUN-01 and MED-01. The resident or representative signs a receipt, and the nurse or Case Manager completes a discharge note.

Closing the record: Within [5] business days after departure, the Administrator reviews the file for completeness, including notice copies, proof of regional office transmission, placement log and receipts. The file is then retained under REC-01.

Review: The Administrator reviews every termination and discharge quarterly with the quality assurance process in GOV-02 for patterns, such as preventable discharges, and updates admission screening in AD-02 if needed.

responsibilities.duty: Makes the final retention determination, signs and serves the termination notice, sends the copy to the regional office within 5 days, consults counsel, and ensures no removal occurs over a resident's objection without the required court proceeding.
Identifies retention concerns, leads alternative placement efforts, keeps the placement log, informs the resident and representative, and coordinates the transition.
Assesses clinical needs, advises on whether needs can be met, and prepares clinical transfer information.
Report changes in condition promptly, and support the resident during the transition.
Processes refunds and final accounting under AD-05 and FUN-01.

documentation: Retention determination and rationale in the resident record, signed by the Administrator
Copy of the DSS-3122 and the current ISP relied on
Copy of the DOH-prescribed termination notice and the free legal and advocacy services list, with proof of delivery
Proof of transmission of the notice to the regional office within 5 days
Alternative placement log (dates, providers, outcomes)
Record of any resident objection and any court proceeding
Record of confirmation with the regional office for any 24-hour skilled nursing termination
Discharge note, property and funds receipt, and medication transfer record

policies.title: Resident Fund Accounts, Funds and Personal Property
policies.applies_to: All residents; Administrator, business office staff, Case Manager, and any staff who handle resident money or valuables
policies.purpose: To protect resident money and personal property, to offer resident fund accounts to every SSI and SNA recipient, and to make sure that all handling of resident funds is voluntary, accurate and transparent.
policies.policy:
This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Schedule 6, item 8 - Resident Fund Accounts. [AGENCY NAME] will offer a resident fund account to every resident who receives SSI and/or SNA, even if the home does not accept SSI/SNA as payment in full.

The admission agreement states the offer of the personal allowance and the refund terms, as required by 18 NYCRR 487.5(d) (see AD-05). Resident funds and valuables will be handled in accordance with the resident funds requirements of 18 NYCRR Part 487 that apply to adult homes. The Administrator will confirm the applicable subdivisions with the DOH regional office before opening and will update this policy with any specific requirements.

For 2026, the SSI Congregate Care Level 3 benefit is $1,688 per month ($994 federal plus $694 state). The resident keeps a personal needs allowance of $262, and the home's share is approximately $1,426. The home will never require a resident to give up the personal needs allowance. The home will keep resident funds separate from operating funds of [AGENCY NAME]. It will provide the Resident Fund Account Statement to residents (Schedule 6 item 31). No resident is required to use the home to hold funds. Staff may not borrow from, accept gifts or loans from, or use resident funds or property.

definitions.definition: A separate account or ledger maintained by the home, at the resident's written request, to hold and track the resident's personal funds.
The portion of the SSI/SNA benefit reserved for the resident's personal use. In 2026 it is $262 per month under SSI Congregate Care Level 3.
Supplemental Security Income and Safety Net Assistance, public benefits that residents may receive.
The written statement of deposits, withdrawals and balance given to the resident (Schedule 6 item 31).
Cash, jewelry, documents and other items of value that a resident asks the home to safeguard.

procedures: Offer at admission: At or before admission, the Case Manager or Administrator asks whether the applicant receives SSI and/or SNA. If so, the person offers a resident fund account in writing and explains how it works. For other residents, the offer is made on request.

Explain choices: The offer is made in plain language, and the resident is told that using the account is voluntary and can be stopped at any time. The Case Manager gives the resident the Ombudsman and legal-services information (see RS-02).

Written authorization: If the resident accepts, the resident signs a written authorization naming who may deposit and withdraw. A refusal is also documented and signed, and the offer is repeated at each annual reassessment.

Separate account: The business office opens an individual ledger and maintains resident funds in an account separate from the operating funds of [AGENCY NAME] at [BANK NAME]. Resident funds are never commingled with operating funds.
Deposits: Each deposit is received by two staff where possible, counted in front of the resident or representative, and recorded with a dated, numbered receipt.

Withdrawals: The resident or the authorized representative may withdraw at any reasonable time. The business office issues the funds, records the amount, date and purpose, and obtains a signature or documented refusal to sign.

Personal allowance: The business office confirms that the personal needs allowance ($262 per month in 2026 for SSI Congregate Care Level 3) is made available to the resident each month, and verifies the figure each January 1.
Home charges: Charges are taken only as stated in the signed admission agreement and as permitted by 18 NYCRR 487.5(d). The Administrator reviews any deduction before it is made.

Statements: The business office gives each account holder the Resident Fund Account Statement (Schedule 6 item 31) at least quarterly, upon request and at discharge, and explains it to the resident when needed.
Monthly reconciliation: The business office manager reconciles each ledger to the bank balance monthly. The Administrator reviews and signs the reconciliation within [10] days of month end.

Valuables and property inventory: At admission the Case Manager lists the resident's personal property and any valuables handed to the home, with the resident or representative. The resident signs the list. Changes are added as they occur.
Safekeeping: Valuables the resident asks the home to hold are kept in a locked location accessible only to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and the business office manager, with an access log.

Loss, theft or discrepancy: Staff report any suspected loss, theft or discrepancy to the Administrator immediately. The Administrator investigates, notifies the resident and representative, reports under SAF-01 and SAF-02 when abuse, exploitation or an incident is suspected, and documents the outcome.

Prohibited acts: Staff and volunteers may not borrow, accept gifts or loans, act as a resident's representative payee or agent, or sell items to residents. The Administrator reviews this with staff at orientation (ORI-01) and annually under PER-01.

Death of a resident: Within [3] business days of a death, the Administrator secures the funds and property, makes a signed inventory with a second staff member, and releases them to the legally authorized person. RS-06 applies.

Discharge or transfer: On discharge, the business office provides a final accounting. It returns the remaining funds, along with any refund due under AD-05, and the resident or representative signs a receipt. The home keeps a copy.
Audit: Once a year the Administrator, or [ACCOUNTANT], reviews the resident fund procedures and records for accuracy and for compliance with this policy. Findings are reported through GOV-02.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures that resident accounts are offered and kept separate from operating funds, reviews reconciliations, investigates discrepancies, and confirms current regulatory requirements with the regional office.
Maintains ledgers and bank accounts, processes deposits and withdrawals, reconciles monthly and issues statements.
Makes and documents the offer, explains the account, completes the property inventory and helps residents with access.
Do not handle resident funds unless authorized, report discrepancies at once, and do not accept gifts, loans or money from residents.

documentation: Signed offer of resident fund account, acceptance or refusal
Written authorization for each account holder
Individual ledgers, dated numbered receipts and withdrawal records
Monthly bank reconciliations signed by the Administrator
Resident Fund Account Statements (Schedule 6 item 31) and proof of delivery
Personal property and valuables inventory, with access log
Investigation records for any loss or discrepancy
Final accounting and receipt at discharge or death

policies.title: Mental Health Services Agreement and Coordination
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Case Manager, nursing and direct-care staff; residents with identified mental health needs
policies.purpose: To make sure that residents with mental health needs are referred to, and followed by, qualified mental health providers under a written agreement, and that crisis steps are documented in the Individualized Service Plan (ISP).
policies.policy:
Schedule 6, section 9 of the application requires a mental health agreement, and Part II program review under 18 NYCRR 485.6 includes the service plans and policies of the home. [AGENCY NAME] will maintain a written agreement with [MENTAL HEALTH PROVIDER / CLINIC] to provide or arrange mental health evaluation, treatment and crisis support for residents who need it. The Administrator will confirm the exact form and content required for the agreement with the DOH regional office before submission and before opening.

The home is not a psychiatric treatment setting. Admission and retention exclusions for people who are a danger to self or others apply (see AD-01 and AD-06). A resident who becomes a danger to self or others is handled through emergency response under SAF-02, and discharge follows AD-06.

Staff will make referrals promptly, support attendance at appointments, help residents follow the treatment plan, and record contacts and crisis steps in the ISP (AD-03). Residents keep the right to choose their own providers (RS-02).

definitions.definition: The written agreement between [AGENCY NAME] and a mental health provider describing the referral, evaluation, treatment, crisis and communication arrangements for residents.
The steps recorded in the ISP for staff to follow if a resident has a mental health emergency, including contacts and who to call.
A condition that is an exclusion from admission and retention and requires an immediate emergency response.

procedures: Agreement: Before opening, the Administrator signs a written agreement with [MENTAL HEALTH PROVIDER] covering referral, evaluation, treatment, crisis response, after-hours contact and information sharing.
