policies.title: Employee Health and TB Screening
policies.applies_to: All employees before employment and every 12 months thereafter; direct-care staff of the EALR and SNALR for immunization and TB records; all staff with potential exposure to blood or body fluids.
policies.purpose: To make sure employees are physically able to do their jobs without risk to residents, are screened for tuberculosis, are protected from bloodborne pathogen exposure and are managed properly after any exposure.
policies.policy: Before beginning work, and every 12 months afterward, each employee must have a statement from a physician, physician assistant or registered nurse that the employee is free from communicable disease and able to perform job duties, along with a TB risk assessment and testing (18 NYCRR §487.9(a)(8)). For EALR and SNALR direct-care staff, [AGENCY NAME] also keeps immunization and TB records (10 NYCRR §1001.11). [AGENCY NAME] maintains a bloodborne pathogen exposure prevention program and a written post-exposure procedure (10 NYCRR §1001.11) consistent with the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens standard (29 CFR 1910.1030). Employee health records are kept separate from personnel files and are confidential.

definitions.definition: A signed statement by a physician, physician assistant or RN that the employee is able to perform assigned duties and is free from communicable disease.
A documented screening of TB risk factors and symptoms plus testing (skin test or blood test) as directed by the examining clinician.
A specific contact of eye, mouth, other mucous membrane, non-intact skin or a needlestick/sharps injury with blood or other potentially infectious material.
The written plan identifying jobs with exposure risk and the protections, training and procedures used to prevent and respond to exposure.

procedures: The HR designee informs each applicant in the offer letter that a health statement and TB screening are required before the first shift, and gives the facility's health form.

The examining physician, PA or RN completes and signs the health statement, and the TB risk assessment and testing results are attached. HR reviews for completeness before the first shift. Incomplete forms mean no start.

For EALR and SNALR direct-care staff, HR also collects immunization records (including hepatitis B status, influenza and other immunizations required by the Administrator and the facility's infection control program) and TB records, and files them in the employee health file.

HR creates a separate, locked employee health file for each employee. Health records are not placed in the personnel file, and are shared only with the Administrator and the clinician as needed for work-fitness or exposure follow-up, or as law requires.

HR keeps a tracking log of due dates. At 60 days before the 12-month anniversary, HR reminds the employee to renew the health statement and TB assessment. Renewals must be on file by the anniversary date.
An employee whose statement or TB assessment has expired is taken off the schedule until it is received, and the Administrator documents the date of removal and return.

An employee with a positive TB test or TB symptoms is referred to their clinician for evaluation (including chest x-ray as ordered). The employee does not work in resident areas until a clinician provides written clearance, and the Administrator notifies the local health department as required and follows SAF-04.

An employee who has a communicable illness (e.g., fever, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, influenza-like illness) must not work until the Administrator, with clinician input where needed, confirms it is safe. The Administrator applies the exclusion rules in SAF-04 and the paid sick leave rules in WC-01.

Exposure prevention: the Administrator keeps a written exposure control plan listing job categories with exposure risk, universal precautions, hand hygiene, personal protective equipment (gloves, gowns, masks, eye protection), sharps containers and spill cleanup steps. The plan is reviewed at least annually.
The facility provides PPE and the hepatitis B vaccine series at no cost to employees with occupational exposure risk, and records any declination in writing, consistent with 29 CFR 1910.1030.
Post-exposure step 1: the employee immediately washes the area with soap and water (or flushes eyes/mucous membranes with water), then reports the exposure to the supervisor at once.

Post-exposure step 2: the supervisor sends the employee for medical evaluation the same day, preferably within 2 hours, to [OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH PROVIDER / EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT], and notifies the Administrator.

Post-exposure step 3: the Administrator arranges source-person testing where permitted by law, provides the evaluating clinician with the incident details and the employee's vaccination status, and ensures post-exposure prophylaxis and follow-up are offered. The employee receives the clinician's written opinion within 15 days.
The Administrator completes an incident report (SAF-02), a sharps injury log entry and a corrective action review within 7 days of the exposure.
All employees complete bloodborne pathogen training at hire and annually (ORI-01, ORI-02) with sign-in sheets and a competency check.
The Administrator reviews the health file tracking log monthly and reports overdue items to the governing body quarterly.

responsibilities.duty: Approves exposure control plan, makes fitness-for-duty and exclusion decisions, ensures exposure follow-up.
Collects and tracks health statements, TB assessments and immunization records and maintains separate health files.
Send exposed employees for same-day evaluation and complete incident reports.
Obtain annual health statements and TB assessments, follow standard precautions and report illnesses and exposures immediately.
Reviews immunization records and advises on exclusion and prophylaxis.

policies.title: Personnel Records and Staffing Schedules
policies.applies_to: All employees; the Administrator, HR designee and shift supervisors who prepare and keep schedules; all programs (Adult Home/Enriched Housing, ALR, EALR, SNALR and ALP).
policies.purpose: To keep complete, organized, confidential personnel records and accurate staffing schedules so [AGENCY NAME] can prove qualifications, training and staffing to DOH surveyors at any time.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a personnel record for every employee as required by 18 NYCRR §487.9(a)(7), including documentation of the Justice Center Staff Exclusion List check, and meets the ALR personnel record content requirements for ALR staff. It keeps staffing schedules (planned and actual) for 12 months in accordance with 18 NYCRR §487.9(a)(6). It documents orientation, in-service training and competency for every employee (18 NYCRR §487.9(a)(3)-(5)). Personnel records are retained for at least seven years after separation, consistent with the 7-year retention period for program and business records in 18 NYCRR §487.10(h), or longer if another law applies. Staffing schedules are kept at least the required 12 months. Records are kept confidential, are stored on-site or are readily available, and are produced to DOH on request.

definitions.definition: The employee file containing hiring, credential, clearance, training, evaluation, discipline and separation documents.
The written schedule showing names, positions, dates and hours of staff on duty each shift, including the planned schedule and what was actually worked.
A documented demonstration that an employee can perform assigned tasks, including direct observation where required (e.g., annual resident aide performance assessment).
The staff member designated to be in charge of the facility when the Administrator is not present, as set out in STF-01.

procedures: HR opens a personnel record for each new hire before the first shift, using the Personnel File Checklist approved by the Administrator.

The personnel record contains: application and résumé; verification of identity and work eligibility; credential/license/certificate copies; signed job description (JD-01); signed Rules of Conduct acknowledgment (PER-01); English proficiency documentation; Background Clearance Checklist with criminal history and Justice Center Staff Exclusion List results (PER-02); training and orientation records; annual performance evaluations; discipline records; and the separation notice.
Health records (health statements, TB and immunization, exposure records) are kept in a separate locked health file (PER-03) and are not included in the personnel record.

HR records orientation topics, dates, trainers and employee signatures for general orientation (ORI-01) and for aide and medication staff initial training and in-service (ORI-02), in accordance with 18 NYCRR §487.9(a)(3)-(5).

HR tracks competency documentation, including direct observation for annual performance assessments of resident aides and medication staff authorization renewals, and files each completed assessment within 7 days.
Administrator-approved personnel record audits are done at least twice a year on a sample of files using the checklist, and findings are corrected within 14 days.

The Administrator or designee prepares the staffing schedule at least two weeks ahead, showing every position and shift, the employee in charge, first-aid-trained staff on each shift (STF-01) and nursing coverage for EALR/SNALR (EALR-01).
Supervisors correct the schedule in real time when changes occur (call-outs, swaps, coverage), recording the actual hours worked. Actual staff hours are reconciled to timesheets weekly.

The Administrator checks each month that weekly personal care, housekeeping and food service hours meet the per-resident weekly hours of 18 NYCRR §487.9 (3.75, 1.0 and 2.0 hours respectively) and that case manager and program coordinator hours are met, and documents the result.

Staffing schedules, planned and actual, are filed by month and kept for at least 12 months and longer where the retention rules for program records apply. They are available for DOH surveyors on request.

Personnel records are stored in a locked file cabinet or access-controlled electronic system. Only the Administrator, HR designee and others the Administrator authorizes may access them. Each access to electronic records is logged.
Employees may review their own personnel record on written request within 5 business days, in the presence of HR. Employees may add a written rebuttal to any disciplinary entry.
DOH surveyors are provided with requested personnel records and schedules the same day, and the Administrator records what was copied or shown.

After separation, HR completes the exit checklist, closes the file and marks the retention-until date at seven years after the separation date. Files are destroyed only after the retention period by shredding or secure deletion, and a destruction log is kept (REC-01).
The Administrator reports file or schedule deficiencies to the governing body in the quality assurance review (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures records and schedules are complete, accurate and available to DOH; approves destruction.
Builds and maintains personnel and health files, tracks training and renewals, and runs the file audits.
Maintain accurate actual schedules and sign off on hours worked.
Document orientation, in-service and competency with sign-in sheets and assessment forms.

documentation: Personnel File Checklist and completed personnel records.
Orientation, in-service and competency records and sign-in sheets.
Planned and actual staffing schedules for the past 12 months or more.
Monthly weekly-hours compliance check.
Semiannual personnel file audit results and corrective actions.

policies.title: Workers' Compensation, Wages and Paid Sick Leave
policies.applies_to: All employees of [AGENCY NAME]; Payroll/HR designee and the Administrator; ALP home care aides employed under the licensed home care services agency (LHCSA) for the ALP.
policies.purpose: To make sure all employees are covered by workers' compensation, disability and paid family leave insurance, are paid at or above the legal minimum wage, and receive paid sick leave under New York law.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] carries workers' compensation, disability benefits and paid family leave coverage for all employees as required by New York law and posts the required notices. It pays at least the New York minimum wage under Labor Law §652: from January 1, 2026, $17.00 per hour in New York City, Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester counties and $16.00 per hour elsewhere in the state; the general rates are unchanged on January 1, 2027. Home care aides employed by the ALP's LHCSA are paid at least the home care aide minimum: $19.65 (downstate) and $18.65 (rest of state) in 2026, and $20.00 and $19.00 from January 1, 2027. Employees receive paid sick leave under Labor Law §196-b: 40 hours per calendar year for employers of 5-99 employees and 56 hours for employers of 100 or more. Domestic and companionship-service wage and hour rules (29 CFR 552) are applied to any covered home care or live-in positions. No employee is retaliated against for using sick leave, reporting an injury, filing a claim or raising a wage concern.

definitions.definition: Insurance that pays medical care and wage replacement to employees injured or made ill by their work.
Paid time off, accrued by the employee, for the employee's own or a family member's illness, injury or health care, or other uses allowed by Labor Law §196-b.
The higher minimum hourly wage that applies to LHCSA home care aides: $19.65 downstate and $18.65 elsewhere in 2026, rising to $20.00 and $19.00 on January 1, 2027.
New York City, Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester counties (higher rate), or all other counties (lower rate), based on the county where the facility is located: [ADDRESS].

procedures: Before the first employee starts, the Administrator purchases workers' compensation, disability benefits and paid family leave coverage from an authorized carrier or the State Insurance Fund, and files the certificate of coverage in the business records.

The Administrator posts the workers' compensation, disability and paid family leave notices, the minimum wage and paid sick leave notices, and the injury reporting instructions in the employee area, and gives the paid sick leave policy in writing at hire.

At hire, HR gives each employee a written pay notice stating the hourly rate, overtime rate, pay day and employer information, and obtains a signed copy. The Administrator keeps it in the personnel record (PER-04).

Each January and on any legal change, the Administrator checks the minimum wage and home care aide minimum for the facility's county [ADDRESS] and adjusts pay rates effective the law's effective date. The check is documented.

Payroll calculates each pay period from actual hours worked, pays overtime at one and one-half times the regular rate for hours over 40 per workweek (or as otherwise required by law), and gives each employee a pay statement every pay day.

For ALP home care aides employed by the LHCSA, Payroll confirms the home care aide minimum applies, pays at or above it ($19.65/$18.65 in 2026; $20.00/$19.00 from 1/1/2027) and reconciles the rate against the schedule at each change.
HR counts employees per calendar year to decide whether 40 or 56 hours of sick leave applies (40 hours for 5-99 employees; 56 hours for 100 or more), and records the determination each January.

Employees accrue paid sick leave at the rate set in the written policy (at least one hour for every 30 hours worked), may use it as it accrues, and may carry over unused hours to the following year. Use up to the annual cap is permitted. Written notice is requested for foreseeable absences, and medical documentation is not demanded for short absences except as the law allows.
Payroll tracks accrued, used and remaining sick leave and shows the balance on each pay statement or on request.

Injured employees report any work injury or illness to the supervisor immediately and to the Administrator the same day. The supervisor arranges first aid or emergency care, and the Administrator completes an incident report (SAF-02).

Within 10 days of a lost-time or medical-treatment injury, the Administrator files the employer's report of injury with the workers' compensation carrier and the Workers' Compensation Board as required, and gives the employee the claim information and forms.
The Administrator coordinates return to work with the treating provider's restrictions and offers modified duty where possible.
Employees who take family leave file under paid family leave. The Administrator provides the required forms and maintains job protection and benefits as required by law.

The Administrator reviews payroll, sick leave and workers' compensation records at least quarterly and reports exceptions and corrections to the governing body (GOV-01). Underpayments are paid within the next pay period and documented.
Complaints about pay, sick leave or retaliation are handled under the employee grievance procedure in PER-01. Employees are told they may also contact the New York State Department of Labor.

responsibilities.duty: Purchases and maintains coverage, posts notices, approves pay rates and reviews quarterly payroll compliance.
Calculates pay, tracks sick leave accrual, issues pay notices and statements and updates wage rates on law changes.
Approve sick leave, report injuries and keep time records accurate.
Report hours accurately, report injuries immediately and give notice of foreseeable sick leave.

documentation: Certificates of workers' compensation, disability and paid family leave coverage.
Posted notices and sign-off log of the posting dates.
Signed pay notices and annual wage-rate check.
Timesheets, payroll registers and pay statements.
Sick leave policy, annual headcount determination and accrual and use ledger.
Injury reports, employer reports to carrier and return-to-work records.
Quarterly payroll compliance review.

policies.title: Job Descriptions for All Staff Positions
policies.applies_to: Every position at [AGENCY NAME], including administrator, case manager, program coordinator (enriched housing), activities director, resident aides/personal care aides, medication staff, EALR/SNALR nursing staff, home health aides and advanced home health aides, food service, housekeeping, laundry and maintenance, and each employee, supervisor and the Administrator.
policies.purpose: To define in writing what each position does, who it reports to, what qualifications it needs and what tasks it may and may not do, so employees work within their scope and residents receive safe, consistent care.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written job description for every staff position, as required for ALRs by 10 NYCRR §1001.11. This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Sched. 6, item 19 — Job Descriptions for all staff positions. For the EALR and, if licensed, the ALP, which employ Home Health Aides (HHAs), the HHA job description lists the tasks HHAs are authorized to perform, all within the HHA scope of tasks (Procedure 9 and the HHA task list in Procedure 10). Each job description includes the title, reporting line, qualifications, hours, essential duties, tasks the position may not perform, required training and licenses, and the weekly staffing standard the position supports (for example, personal care of at least 3.75 hours, housekeeping of at least 1.0 hour and food service of at least 2.0 hours per resident per week under 18 NYCRR §487.9; case manager 0.5 hour per resident per week and combined personal care, housekeeping and food staff of 6 hours per resident per week in the enriched housing program under 18 NYCRR §488.9). Each employee receives a copy at hire and has the description reviewed annually.

definitions.definition: A written statement of a position's title, supervisor, qualifications, duties, limits and training requirements.
A trained and certified aide who provides personal care and health-related tasks under the supervision of a registered nurse, within the HHA scope of tasks.
An HHA with additional training and certification who may perform specified advanced tasks only under RN delegation and supervision, as allowed by law and ALR rules.
The list of tasks a position may legally and safely perform; tasks outside it must be performed by or delegated by a licensed professional.

procedures: The Administrator prepares a written job description for every position before it is filled, using the agency template with the sections listed in the policy, and signs and dates it.
Each description names the position's supervisor and the line of reporting, including who covers in absence and who serves as employee in charge (STF-01).

Administrator: oversees daily operations; is responsible for compliance, staffing, resident safety and admissions; meets the approval, hours and qualifications requirements (QUAL-01); and is the contact for DOH.

Case manager (and program coordinator for enriched housing): case manager is on site at least 20 hours per week under 25 beds, scaled to 40 hours per week at 45 or more beds (10 NYCRR §1001.11); in enriched housing, 0.5 hour per resident per week (18 NYCRR §488.9). Duties include admission assessments, ISP development and reassessment, service coordination and resident advocacy (AD-02, AD-03). The program coordinator's hours are as set in QUAL-01.
Activities director: plans and runs activities (ACT-01), including the SNALR activities schedule (SNALR-02), maintains activity records and coordinates volunteers (VOL-01).

Resident aides / personal care aides: provide personal care, supervision and support within their training, including 40 hours of initial training, 12 hours of annual in-service and an annual performance assessment with direct observation (ORI-02). They may not perform tasks reserved for nurses or require delegation unless trained, certified and delegated.

Medication staff: assist residents with self-administered medications only after authorization and training (MED-02), within the limits of the ALR and facility policy. Medication staff may not make clinical judgments or change doses.

EALR/SNALR nurses: the RN is on site 8 hours per day, 5 days per week, and an LPN 8 hours per day on the other 2 days, with an RN on call 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, subject to any waiver at 40 or fewer beds (10 NYCRR §1001.11; EALR-01). The job description sets out assessment, care planning, delegation, supervision of HHAs and aides, and physician communication duties.

HHA job description (EALR and ALP): each HHA description lists the authorized tasks. They are to be performed only within the HHA scope of tasks and under RN supervision, and include: personal care (bathing, grooming, oral care, dressing, toileting, incontinence care and skin care); assistance with transfers, positioning, ambulation and range-of-motion exercises as ordered; assistance with eating and fluids; measuring and recording temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, weight and intake and output; assistance with self-administered medications only as allowed by law and facility policy; light housekeeping and meal preparation related to the resident's care; observing and promptly reporting changes in condition to the RN and recording them (RS-04); and following the ISP.

The HHA description also lists tasks HHAs may not perform: assessments, care planning, sterile procedures, medication administration, and any task outside the HHA scope unless the RN lawfully delegates it to a qualified advanced home health aide. Any advanced task requires the advanced HHA certification, written RN delegation and supervision (EALR-01).

Food service, housekeeping, laundry and maintenance descriptions state sanitation, safety and infection-control duties (FS-01 to FS-03, HK-01), the required training and the weekly staffing hours they support (food service at least 2.0 hours and housekeeping at least 1.0 hour per resident per week).

Every description states a general statement that the employee must speak, read and write English (18 NYCRR §487.9(a)(13)), must have a current health statement and TB assessment (PER-03), must be cleared under PER-02, must follow the Rules of Conduct (PER-01) and must report abuse and incidents (SAF-01, SAF-02).
At hire, HR gives the employee a copy of the job description and reviews it at orientation (ORI-01). The employee signs and dates an acknowledgment, which HR files in the personnel record (PER-04).

Supervisors review each employee's job description with the employee at the annual performance evaluation and update it as duties change. The Administrator re-signs and re-issues any revised description and gets a new acknowledgment within 14 days.

Before assigning a new or changed task, the Administrator or the nurse confirms in writing that the person is qualified and trained for the task and that it is within the position's scope. If it is not, the task is not assigned.
The Administrator keeps a master binder (or electronic file) of all current job descriptions available for DOH surveyor review, and reviews it with the governing body at least annually (GOV-01).

Distributes descriptions at hire and annually, obtains signed acknowledgments and maintains the master file.
Defines HHA and advanced HHA tasks, delegates and supervises within HHA scope.
Review descriptions at annual evaluations and report scope concerns.
Know and perform the duties in their job description and not perform tasks outside it.

policies.title: Activities and Social Programming
policies.applies_to: All residents of [AGENCY NAME]; all activities staff, aides and volunteers who plan, lead or support activities
policies.purpose: To ensure that [AGENCY NAME] provides a planned, varied and documented activities program as a required minimum service, and that a one-month activity schedule is available for the Department of Health (DOH) application and for residents and families.
policies.policy: Activities are a required minimum service for every resident (18 NYCRR 487.7(a)). [AGENCY NAME] provides a scheduled program that offers cultural, spiritual, physical, social and intellectual activities every week, with options for residents who prefer small-group or in-room activities. A one-month activity schedule is prepared and submitted with Schedule 6. This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Sched. 6, item 21, p.5 — Activity Schedule for One Month. The activities program is led by a qualified activities director. Under 18 NYCRR 487.9(c), the administrator may serve as activities director in a facility under 50 beds if the administrator meets the qualifications (see QUAL-01). Participation is voluntary. Attendance is recorded. The schedule is posted and offered in a form each resident can read or hear.

definitions.definition: The qualified staff member responsible for planning, scheduling, leading and documenting the activities program. In a facility under 50 beds this may be the administrator if qualified.
A calendar showing every activity offered during one month, with day, time, location, category and leader. It is Attachment ACT-01-A and is filed with Schedule 6.
Cultural, spiritual, physical, social and intellectual activities. Each category must appear on the schedule every week.

procedures: 1. The Activities Director completes the Activity Interest Survey with each resident within 14 days of admission, in coordination with the Case Manager's admission interview (see AD-02). The survey records interests, past hobbies, faith or cultural practices, mobility limits, hearing and vision needs, and preferred times of day.

2. By the 20th of each month, the Activities Director drafts the next month's calendar. Input comes from the interest surveys, the resident organization (see ORG-01), and staff and volunteer suggestions.

3. Each week of the calendar must include at least one activity in each category: cultural (music, films, crafts, trips, holiday and heritage events); spiritual (services, readings, reflection, visiting clergy as residents request); physical (chair exercise, walking group, balance or stretching, gardening); social (cards, bingo, birthday and coffee socials, intergenerational visits); and intellectual (trivia, current-events discussion, word games, book club, computer or tablet use).
4. The calendar lists activities on weekdays and on at least one weekend day, with at least one morning, one afternoon and one evening option each week.

5. The calendar includes an in-room or one-to-one visit option for residents who cannot or prefer not to join groups, including residents with limited mobility. Activities Staff record each in-room contact.

6. The Administrator reviews and approves the calendar by the 25th. The approved calendar is posted in the common area, given to each resident, and shared with family members on request. Large print is available.
7. The one-month calendar for the first full month of operation is attached to the Schedule 6 submission as Attachment ACT-01-A. A copy is kept in the survey-readiness binder.
8. Activities Staff lead each activity, check that the space is safe and accessible, and prepare supplies before it begins. Aides help residents get to and from activities.

9. Activities Staff record attendance for every activity on the Activity Attendance Log, noting each resident's name, activity, date and level of participation. Activities Staff also record residents who declined.

10. Any resident whose participation drops noticeably over two consecutive weeks is reported to the Case Manager. The Case Manager follows up for possible mood, health or change-of-condition concerns (see RS-04, MH-01).
11. Trips outside the facility follow transportation and supervision rules in OPT-01. Volunteers who help follow VOL-01.
12. For residents in the SNALR unit, activities follow the separate schedule in SNALR-02.

13. Each month the Activities Director reviews the attendance log, summarizes participation by category, and gathers resident feedback. The Administrator uses the summary in quality assurance review (see GOV-02).
14. Changes to the posted calendar are written on the posted copy and announced at least one day ahead whenever possible. Residents are never required to attend an activity.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the monthly calendar, ensures adequate activities staffing and supplies, and serves as activities director only if qualified and the facility is under 50 beds.
Surveys interests, drafts and posts the calendar, leads or arranges activities, keeps attendance logs and reports concerns.
Reviews low-participation reports and follows up on possible changes in condition or mood.
Remind and assist residents to attend and help them with mobility and toileting needs during activities.

documentation: Activity Interest Survey (each resident)
One-Month Activity Schedule (Attachment ACT-01-A), filed with Schedule 6
Monthly posted calendars
Activity Attendance Log
In-room visit log
Monthly participation summary and resident feedback notes

policies.title: Social Contact and Visitors
policies.applies_to: All residents, their families and friends, visitors, and all staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To describe how [AGENCY NAME] encourages contact between residents, relatives and friends, and to make sure visitor access is consistent with the resident rights statement.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] encourages residents to stay connected with relatives, friends and the community. This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Sched. 6, item 22, p.5 — Social Contact: a description of how the facility will encourage contact between residents, relatives and friends. Visitor access is consistent with the resident rights statement posted and given to each resident under 18 NYCRR 487.5(a). Visiting is open and welcoming. Any limit applies only for a documented health, safety or privacy reason, and is never used as a penalty. Residents are supported to use the telephone, mail, video calls and community outings, as part of the supervision and activities services required under 18 NYCRR 487.7(a) and (d). The visitor policy is explained at the admission interview.

definitions.definition: Any family member, friend, representative, clergy member, advocate or other person who comes to see a resident.
A person the resident names to be notified of changes in condition, events and incidents, as recorded in the resident's record.

procedures: 1. At the admission interview, the Administrator or Case Manager reviews the visitor policy with the applicant and any family member present. The applicant also receives the resident rights statement and facility rules (see AD-02, HR-01, RS-02). The review is documented on the admission checklist.

2. Visiting hours are [VISITING HOURS] daily and are posted at the front desk and in the resident handbook. Visits outside those hours are arranged on request. Visits for a resident who is seriously ill or at end of life are welcome at any hour.

3. At the first interview and at least annually, the Case Manager asks each resident whom they want to see, call and write, and records each person's name, contact details and relationship in the resident's record.
4. The Case Manager asks each resident whom to notify about changes in condition, events and incidents, and records the designated contacts.
5. Visitors sign in and out at the front desk for safety and emergency accounting. Sign-in is not a condition of visiting. Staff greet visitors courteously and help find the resident.
6. Residents may meet visitors in their rooms, in the [VISITING AREA] or outdoors. A private meeting space is available on request. A resident may refuse any visitor, and staff respect that refusal.

7. Staff may ask a visitor to leave only if the visitor is endangering residents or staff, is disruptive, or the resident asks for them to leave. The Administrator documents the reason and any follow-up. If abuse or neglect is suspected, SAF-01 applies.
8. Residents may use the facility telephone in a place that allows private conversation. Staff help residents place calls and answer calls without requiring a reason.
9. Staff deliver incoming mail unopened on the day it arrives and mail outgoing letters promptly. Postage and envelopes are provided on request for residents who cannot buy them.
10. The facility keeps a tablet or computer available for video calls. Activities Staff and aides help residents set up and join calls, with privacy where requested.

11. The Activities Director holds family-friendly events such as holiday gatherings, birthday socials and open houses at least quarterly. Invitations are sent to designated contacts. Events appear on the monthly calendar (see ACT-01).

12. Community outings, religious services, shopping trips and local events are scheduled and supervised under OPT-01 and ACT-01. Residents may also go out with family or friends. Residents sign out and in so the facility knows who is out, and staff note expected return times.

13. Residents who have few visitors are identified by the Case Manager, who arranges friendly-visitor volunteers (see VOL-01), the Ombudsman program or faith-community visitors if the resident wishes.
14. A resident's concern about restricted visiting is handled under RS-03 (grievances). Any restriction applied to a resident must be documented in the record with its reason and review date.

Records residents' preferred contacts, explains the visitor policy at admission and supports residents with few visitors.
Plans family-friendly events, outings and video-call support.
Welcomes visitors, keeps the sign-in log and reports safety concerns.
Help residents with calls, mail, getting ready for visits and outings.

policies.title: House Rules (Smoking, Pets, Quiet Hours)
policies.applies_to: All residents, visitors and staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To set out the facility's house rules, ensure applicants receive them at or before the admission interview, and ensure no rule conflicts with resident rights.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has written house rules covering smoking, pets, quiet hours, alcohol and guests. This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Sched. 6, item 23, p.5 — House Rules, if any; the house rules are submitted with Schedule 6. Under 18 NYCRR 487.4, the house rules are given to each applicant at or before the admission interview, together with the admission agreement, rights statement and Ombudsman/legal-services sheet. House rules must not conflict with the resident rights statement under 18 NYCRR 487.5(a). Rules are used to protect safety, health and the comfortable enjoyment of the home by all residents. They are not used to limit rights or as punishment. A rule that cannot be reconciled with a resident right is not enforced and is revised.

definitions.definition: The written rules of daily life at the facility. They are listed in Attachment HR-01-A and are reviewed at least annually.
Daily hours when noise is kept low so residents can sleep and rest.
A trained animal that does work or performs tasks for a person with a disability. Service animals are handled under NDI-01 and are not treated as pets.

procedures: 1. The Administrator drafts the house rules with input from the resident organization (see ORG-01). The Administrator checks each rule against the resident rights statement (see RS-02) and records the check on the House Rules Review Form before issuing them.

2. Smoking: smoking, vaping and open flames are not permitted inside the building. Smoking is allowed only in the designated outdoor area at [LOCATION], a safe distance from entrances, and in line with applicable state and local law. Residents who smoke are screened for safe smoking at admission and when their ability changes. Staff do not store or handle lighters or tobacco for residents with unsafe habits without a documented plan with the resident. Oxygen use and smoking follow EM-02.

3. Pets: resident-owned pets may be allowed only with prior written approval from the Administrator. Approval depends on the animal's health records, vaccinations, temperament and size, and on room space, and on the resident's ability to feed and clean up after the pet or arrange this independently. The facility's decision is made in writing within 10 business days. Service animals are accommodated under NDI-01. Facility pets and visiting therapy animals are screened for health and temperament.

4. Quiet hours: quiet hours are [QUIET HOURS] daily. Residents may stay up and use their rooms at any hour. Televisions and radios are kept at a level that does not disturb others, and headphones are offered. Staff keep noise low in the evening and overnight.

5. Alcohol: residents may have alcohol in moderation if their physician has not restricted it and it does not conflict with their medications. Alcohol is kept in the resident's own room and not in common areas. Staff do not serve alcohol except at approved events. Alcohol and medication concerns are referred to the Case Manager.
6. Guests: guests are welcome under SOC-01. Overnight guests need the Administrator's approval in advance. Guests must follow house rules and may be asked to leave under SOC-01 procedure 7.

7. Personal items: residents may furnish rooms with their own belongings within fire-safety and space limits in EM-02. Space heaters, extension cords and candles are not allowed. Details on personal property are in FUN-01.
8. The final rules are issued as Attachment HR-01-A and submitted with Schedule 6. The facility keeps one copy in the resident handbook and one in the survey-readiness binder.

9. At or before the admission interview, the Administrator gives each applicant a copy of the house rules with the admission agreement, rights statement and Ombudsman/legal-services sheet. The Administrator goes over the rules and answers questions. The applicant signs the Admission Interview Checklist to acknowledge receipt. (See AD-02.)

10. House rules are posted in the common area. Changed rules are given in writing to every resident at least 30 days before taking effect, except when needed immediately for safety, and are discussed at the resident organization meeting.

11. When a resident breaks a house rule, staff first speak with the resident respectfully and privately. The Case Manager explores any health, cognitive or mental-health cause and updates the Individualized Service Plan if needed (see AD-03). Repeated or serious violations are reviewed by the Administrator. Rule violations alone do not result in discharge. Any discharge follows AD-06 and the notice rights in RS-02.
12. Residents may raise concerns about any rule through RS-03 (grievances) or through the resident organization.
13. The Administrator reviews the house rules at least once a year with the resident organization and updates them when laws or the facility's practices change.

Reviews rules with applicants and residents, screens for safe smoking, and follows up when rule problems reflect health or care needs.
Applies the rules respectfully and consistently, and reports unsafe situations to the Administrator.

policies.title: Resident Organization and SNALR Family Organization
policies.applies_to: All residents; families and representatives of SNALR residents; administrator and staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To support residents' right to form an organization, and for the SNALR unit a family organization, and to ensure the administrator provides space and responds to their input.
policies.policy: Residents may form an organization under 18 NYCRR 487.5(b). This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Sched. 6, item 24, p.5 — Resident Organizations and, if SNALR, Family Organization Policies. The Administrator provides meeting space and responds to the organization's input. Staff do not control the organization, choose its officers or attend meetings unless invited. For SNALR residents, [AGENCY NAME] supports a family organization for family members and representatives, who may speak on behalf of residents who cannot. No resident or family member is penalized or treated differently for taking part or raising concerns.

definitions.definition: A group formed by and for residents to discuss concerns and suggest improvements. Its governance is set by its members.
For SNALR, a group of family members, friends and representatives of residents who meet to share information and give input on the program.
A response from the Administrator to the organization's input, given within 14 days and recorded.

procedures: 1. At the admission interview and again in the admission packet, the Case Manager tells each resident (and each SNALR family member) about the organization and gives the meeting schedule and contact person.

2. The Administrator posts a notice inviting residents to form a resident organization on opening day and again every year. The notice gives the meeting space and a contact person. The Case Manager helps residents who want help organizing.
3. The Administrator provides a private, accessible meeting space [LOCATION], supplies such as paper and pens, and help with notices and large-print agendas. The facility asks for no fee.

4. The organization chooses its own officers, meeting schedule and rules. Staff may support logistics if asked, such as setting up the room and helping residents attend. Staff attend only when invited and do not direct discussions.
5. The organization may meet without staff present. Staff do not monitor, question or retaliate for what is said.

6. The Administrator or designee meets with the organization at least once each quarter if invited, to share facility news and to listen. These meetings may be combined with the organization's regular meeting.

7. Concerns, requests and suggestions from the organization are given to the Administrator in writing or through the organization's officer or the Case Manager, and logged on the Resident Organization Input Log.

8. The Administrator responds in writing or in person at the next meeting, and in any case within 14 days. The response states what will be done, by when, or why a request cannot be met. The response is recorded on the log.
9. Matters raised that involve a grievance are also handled under RS-03. Matters that suggest abuse or neglect are handled under SAF-01 immediately.
10. Menu, activity, house-rule and outing suggestions from the organization are passed to the dietitian, Activities Director and Administrator, who respond (see FS-01, ACT-01, HR-01).
11. SNALR family organization: the SNALR program staff invite family members, friends and representatives of SNALR residents to form a family organization at admission and annually afterward.

12. The Administrator hosts at least one family organization meeting every quarter, with notice of at least 14 days sent to each designated contact. SNALR program staff attend to give program updates, such as staffing, activities (SNALR-02), safety (SNALR-01) and policy changes, and to answer questions. Families may also meet without staff present.
13. The family organization may give input on SNALR care, activities, environment and communication. Input is logged and answered under steps 7 and 8.
14. Meeting minutes are kept by the organization or, if asked, by a staff member. Copies are kept in the facility with the log, and posted when the organization agrees.

responsibilities.duty: Provides space and support, receives input, responds within 14 days and prevents retaliation.
Informs residents and families, assists with organizing and passes concerns to the Administrator.
Supports the family organization and attends meetings to share program information.
Helps with notices, setup and accessibility, and uses suggestions in planning.

documentation: Posted invitation notice and dates
Meeting schedule and minutes
Resident Organization Input Log with Administrator responses and dates
Family organization notices and attendance (SNALR)
Admission checklist showing organization information given

policies.title: Menus, Therapeutic and Modified Diets, and Diet Information for Kitchen Staff
policies.applies_to: All residents; food service staff, dietitian or dietetic technician, aides and nurses of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To ensure residents receive nutritious, appealing meals and snacks on a set schedule, that modified diets are defined and offered as ordered, and that kitchen staff always have current and accurate information on each resident's diet, allergies and preferences.
policies.policy: Daily food service is a minimum service of the ALR (10 NYCRR 1001.10) and food service is a required resident service under 18 NYCRR 487.7(a). This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Sched. 6, item 26(a) — Food Services: three weeks of menus for meals and snacks, including special modified diets such as finger foods and consistency modifications, a definition of each diet offered, and the time of each meal and snack service. It also meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Sched. 6, item 26(e) — policy and procedure for kitchen staff to have current and accurate information on each resident's prescribed diet, allergies, food preferences and any changes. Food service staffing meets 18 NYCRR 487.9: at least 2.0 hours per resident per week, and never fewer than 35 hours per week. Food service is supervised by a qualified dietitian or dietetic technician under a written agreement stating duties and time (18 NYCRR 487.9(j)(3)-(4)). Therapeutic and modified diets are served only on a written order from the resident's physician or other authorized practitioner. Meals are served at regular times, and the three-week menu cycle is attached as Attachment FS-01-A.

definitions.definition: A nutritionally balanced diet with no restriction other than food allergies and personal preferences.

definitions.term: No Added Salt / Low Sodium Diet
definitions.definition: A diet prepared without added salt, with high-sodium items limited, as ordered.
A diet with carbohydrate portions spread evenly across meals and snacks, with concentrated sweets limited, as ordered.
Foods that are soft, moist and chopped or ground to ease chewing.
Foods blended to a smooth, pudding-like texture requiring no chewing.
Meals and snacks cut into bite-sized pieces that can be picked up and eaten by hand, for residents who cannot use utensils or who do better with hand-feeding, including residents with dementia.
Liquids thickened to a texture ordered by the practitioner, used only on written order following a swallowing evaluation.
A written order from the resident's practitioner stating the diet, texture and any restrictions.
A current card or list kept in the kitchen showing each resident's diet, texture, allergies, dislikes and preferences.

procedures: 1. Meal and snack times: breakfast [7:30 AM–8:30 AM]; mid-morning snack [10:00 AM]; lunch [12:00 PM–1:00 PM]; afternoon snack [3:00 PM]; dinner [5:00 PM–6:00 PM]; evening snack [8:00 PM]. Water, juice and a light snack are available at all hours. Times are posted in the dining room and on the monthly calendar. Residents may eat in their rooms on request or when ill.

2. Three-week menu cycle: the dietitian or dietetic technician writes a three-week cycle of menus for all meals and snacks. Each menu lists the regular diet and every modified diet offered, including finger foods and consistency modifications. The menu is Attachment FS-01-A and is filed with Schedule 6. The cycle includes culturally varied choices, fruit and vegetable servings, and a choice of at least two entrées at lunch and dinner.

3. Modified diets offered: regular; no added salt; consistent carbohydrate; mechanical soft; pureed; finger foods; and thickened liquids on order. Other diets are provided on written order when the dietitian can plan and prepare them safely. Each diet is defined in this policy and in the menu attachment.

4. Dietitian agreement: the Administrator keeps a written agreement with a qualified dietitian or dietetic technician stating duties and hours (18 NYCRR 487.9(j)(3)-(4)). Duties include approving menus, writing diet instructions and diet cards, training kitchen staff, and visiting at least [MONTHLY]. The Administrator keeps the agreement on file.
5. Menus are posted at least one week ahead. Menus change only for supply problems, with a substitute of equal nutrition. Substitutes are written on the posted menu, and the as-served menu is kept.

6. Admission diet information: at admission, the Case Manager (RN or LPN-supervised as applicable) records the diet order from the medical evaluation (DSS-3122), allergies, food intolerances, swallowing or chewing problems, cultural and religious food practices and preferences, and likes and dislikes. This is recorded on the Diet Information Form, and the form is given to the kitchen the same day, before the resident's first meal. If an order is unclear, the Case Manager calls the practitioner before the first meal to clarify it.

7. Diet cards and diet list: the Food Service Supervisor keeps a current Diet Card for each resident and a master Diet List in the kitchen. Allergies are marked clearly in red on both. The list is dated and signed by the Food Service Supervisor each time it is updated. Out-of-date lists are removed and filed.

8. Changes: when a practitioner changes a diet order, a resident's allergy or preference changes, a resident returns from a hospital or rehab stay, or a resident has a swallowing problem, the staff member who learns of it tells the Case Manager at once. The Case Manager sends a signed Diet Change Notice to the kitchen within 2 hours, or before the next meal, whichever comes first, and also tells the Employee in Charge. The Food Service Supervisor updates the diet card and diet list immediately and confirms in writing.

9. Weekly check: the Food Service Supervisor and Case Manager compare the Diet List against resident records every week and when the census changes. Differences are corrected the same day. The check is dated and signed in the Diet Verification Log.

10. Every cook and aide who serves meals checks the diet card or tray ticket for every resident at every meal. Residents who need pureed, mechanical-soft or finger foods or thickened liquids are served the right texture. If a staff member is unsure, they ask the Food Service Supervisor before serving.

11. Allergy safety: allergens are kept and prepared separately where feasible. Staff wash hands and clean surfaces and utensils before preparing an allergen-free meal. Residents with allergies are told the ingredients of any substitute. Anyone with a suspected allergic reaction receives first aid and emergency care under RS-04.

12. Preferences: staff ask residents about food preferences at admission, at monthly food comment times, and through the resident organization (see ORG-01). The dietitian reviews comments and adjusts menus. Personal and cultural foods brought in by family are allowed if safe and consistent with the resident's diet, and are labeled and dated.

13. Weight and intake: aides weigh residents monthly (18 NYCRR 487.7(e)) and report an unplanned weight change of 5 percent or more in 30 days, or poor intake for 3 consecutive days, to the Case Manager, who informs the practitioner and the dietitian and updates the Individualized Service Plan (AD-03).

14. Staffing: the Administrator schedules food service staff so hours total at least 2.0 hours per resident per week, and never fewer than 35 hours per week. Schedules and hours calculations are kept under PER-04. Food service training is in FS-03.
15. Food service staff do not change a diet on their own. They refer questions about diet orders to the Case Manager or dietitian.

policies.title: Food Purchasing, Storage, Temperature Control and Food Protection
policies.applies_to: Food service staff, aides who serve food, the dietitian and the administrator of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To ensure that food is bought from safe sources, stored properly, kept at safe temperatures and protected from contamination from delivery to service.
policies.policy: All food purchasing, storage, preparation and service at [AGENCY NAME] complies with 10 NYCRR Part 14 and local health codes. This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Sched. 6, item 26(g) — Food Services: policy and procedure for food purchase and storage. It also meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Sched. 6, item 26(h) — policy and procedure to ensure meals and snacks are handled properly to ensure proper temperatures and other food protections. Temperatures of refrigerators, freezers and hot-holding units are logged. Meals and snacks are protected from contamination. Stored food is labeled and dated. The Administrator confirms the current text of 10 NYCRR Part 14 and local code before opening and at each annual review of this policy.

definitions.definition: The range between 41°F and 135°F, in which bacteria grow quickly. Potentially hazardous food is not kept in this range.
Food that needs temperature control for safety, such as meat, poultry, fish, dairy, cooked rice, cut melons and cooked vegetables.
First in, first out: older stock is used before newer stock.
The transfer of germs or allergens from one food, surface, hand or utensil to another.

procedures: 1. Purchasing: the Food Service Supervisor orders food only from approved, licensed or inspected suppliers. No home-canned or home-processed foods and no uninspected game are served. Approved suppliers are listed and reviewed yearly by the Administrator.
2. Ordering: orders are based on the three-week menu cycle (FS-01) and current diets and census. The Food Service Supervisor keeps a par-level list and orders so stock is rotated and not excessive.

3. Receiving: a trained staff member checks each delivery against the order. The staff member checks for damaged or leaking packages, past-date items and signs of pests, and takes the temperature of refrigerated and frozen items. Cold food is received at 41°F or below and frozen food is solidly frozen. Unsafe items are refused and the refusal is recorded on the Receiving Log.
4. Put-away: refrigerated and frozen food is put away within 30 minutes of delivery. Shelf-stable food is put away at once.

5. Dry storage: dry goods are kept off the floor on shelves, in a clean, dry, ventilated room, at least [6 inches] off the floor and away from walls. Chemicals, cleaners and medications are never stored with food or above it. Dented cans and swollen, leaking or damaged packages are removed.

6. Labeling and dating: opened, prepared and leftover foods are put in covered, labeled containers with the item name and the date opened or prepared. Leftovers are used within 3 days or discarded. Staff use FIFO rotation and check dates every day. Resident and family food brought in is labeled with the resident's name and date.

7. Refrigeration: refrigerators are kept at 41°F or below and freezers at 0°F or below. Each unit has a working thermometer. Staff record temperatures on the Temperature Log twice daily, at opening and at close, with initials. Raw meat, poultry and fish are stored below and away from ready-to-eat foods.

8. Out-of-range temperatures: if a unit is out of range, staff tell the Food Service Supervisor at once. The Supervisor checks the food, discards food held above 41°F for over 4 hours, calls for repair and records the action on the log. The Administrator is told the same day.

9. Cooking: cooked food reaches safe internal temperatures, checked with a clean, calibrated probe thermometer: poultry 165°F; ground meat 155°F; pork, fish and eggs held for service 145°F; reheated leftovers 165°F. Final temperatures are recorded on the Production Record for each meal.

10. Hot holding and cold holding: hot food is held at 135°F or higher and cold food at 41°F or lower from preparation until service. Hot-holding and cold units are not used to cook or reheat food. Temperatures are checked and recorded before service begins and every [2 hours] during service. Food outside the safe range is reheated once to 165°F within 2 hours or discarded.
11. Cooling: cooked food to be stored is cooled quickly in shallow pans or ice baths, from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours and to 41°F within a further 4 hours. Cooling temperatures are recorded.
12. Thawing: frozen food is thawed in the refrigerator, under cold running water or in a microwave as part of immediate cooking. It is never thawed at room temperature. Thawed food is not refrozen.

13. Protection from contamination: staff wash hands for at least 20 seconds before handling food, after using the restroom, after touching raw foods, face or hair, and after handling trash. Staff with vomiting, diarrhea, fever, sore throat with fever, jaundice or infected cuts are excused from food handling (see PER-03 and SAF-04). Staff wear clean uniforms, hair restraints and gloves for ready-to-eat foods. Separate cutting boards and utensils are used for raw and ready-to-eat foods.

14. Serving meals and snacks: food is served with clean utensils and covered when transported to rooms or the SNALR unit. Meals taken to rooms are delivered promptly, at proper temperatures, and picked up within 1 hour, or discarded if left. Snacks and beverages left out for residents are kept sanitary and temperature-safe. Items needing refrigeration are kept cold until served.

15. Cleaning: food-contact surfaces, equipment and utensils are washed, rinsed and sanitized after each use and on the cleaning schedule. The dishwasher temperature or sanitizer concentration is tested and recorded each meal. Floors, walls and storage are cleaned on the HK-01 schedule.
16. Pest control: the Administrator keeps a pest-control contract and has the kitchen serviced regularly. Staff report signs of pests immediately.

17. Water and power failure: if water or power is lost, the Food Service Supervisor follows the emergency food and water plan in EM-01. Food from a failed refrigerator is evaluated for safety before use.

18. Inspections and records: the Food Service Supervisor reviews logs weekly and signs them. The Administrator reviews them monthly and keeps them for at least [1 year], or longer if required by REC-01. Findings from health inspections are corrected at once and recorded.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures compliance with 10 NYCRR Part 14 and local code, approves suppliers and reviews logs monthly.
Orders, receives and stores food, supervises temperatures and sanitation, reviews logs and corrects problems.
Reviews food safety practices during visits and trains staff on safe handling.
Follow temperature, labeling, handwashing and cleaning rules and record required checks.
