Receiving Log
Refrigerator/Freezer Temperature Log (twice daily)
Production Record with cooking, hot-holding and cooling temperatures
Dishwasher temperature or sanitizer log
Cleaning schedule and sign-offs
Pest-control contract and service reports
Corrective-action notes
Health inspection reports

policies.title: Food Service Staff Training
policies.applies_to: All dietary and food service staff, including cooks, helpers, dietary aides and any other employee who prepares, serves or handles food or food-contact surfaces, and their supervisors.
policies.purpose: To make sure everyone who prepares or serves food at [AGENCY NAME] is trained before working independently and is retrained on a regular schedule, so that residents receive safe food that matches their diet orders and allergy needs.
policies.policy: This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Sched. 6, item 26(i) — Food Services: policy on food service staff training. [AGENCY NAME] provides orientation and in-service training to all food service staff and documents it, as required by 18 NYCRR §487.9(a)(3)-(5) (C6). Food service staff complete orientation before they work unsupervised. They then complete in-service training on a scheduled basis throughout the year. Training covers: sanitation under Part 14; resident diets, including therapeutic and modified diets; food allergies; and safe food temperatures. Training records are kept for each employee. Food service staffing hours are set in the staffing plan (GOV-01 and STF-01), and the agency provides at least 2.0 hours of food service per resident per week (C6). Training does not substitute for those hours.

definitions.definition: Any employee, whether full-time, part-time or temporary, who prepares, portions, serves or delivers food, or cleans food-contact equipment and areas.
Training given at hire, before the employee works independently in the kitchen or dining area.
Scheduled, recurring training after orientation, covering required topics and any problems found in QA reviews or inspections.
The state sanitary code for food service establishments, which sets sanitation requirements for how food is handled and stored.

procedures: The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] designates a Food Service Supervisor who is responsible for dietary staff training and for the training records.
On or before the first day of work, the Food Service Supervisor gives each new food service employee a written orientation checklist covering the topics in steps 3 through 8.
Orientation covers personal hygiene: handwashing, glove use, clean uniforms, hair restraints, and reporting illness to the supervisor before starting a shift.
Orientation covers sanitation under Part 14: cleaning and sanitizing surfaces, dishes and equipment, cross-contamination prevention and pest control.
Orientation covers safe temperatures: cold holding, hot holding, cooking, cooling and reheating. Staff are shown how to use and clean thermometers and how to complete the temperature logs (FS-02).

Orientation covers resident diets: reading the diet order, the diet card and the diet list; therapeutic and modified diets (including texture-modified and liquid-consistency diets); and substitutions (FS-01).

Orientation covers food allergies and intolerances: identifying allergens on the resident's diet information, preventing cross-contact, and the emergency response to a suspected allergic reaction (call 911 and notify the nurse or Employee in Charge).

Orientation covers resident rights and dignity in dining, confidentiality of diet and health information, reporting resident changes (poor intake, choking, swallowing problems) and abuse reporting duties (SAF-01).
New employees work alongside a trained employee until the Food Service Supervisor has watched them perform each core task correctly. The supervisor signs the competency checklist.

The Food Service Supervisor builds an annual in-service calendar. It includes sanitation, safe temperatures, diets, allergies, emergency procedures and infection control, and is reviewed against QA findings (GOV-02).
In-service sessions are held on the calendar dates. The trainer records the date, topic, length, trainer and attendee signatures on the training attendance sheet.
An employee who misses a session completes a make-up session within 30 days. The supervisor records it.
The Food Service Supervisor retrains any employee immediately when an inspection, temperature log review, resident complaint, allergen error or diet error shows a gap. The retraining is documented.
Food service staff attend the facility-wide fire, evacuation and emergency training given under EM-01 and EM-02.

Each month the Food Service Supervisor checks that every dietary employee's file contains the orientation checklist, competency sign-off and in-service records, and reports gaps to the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME].
Training records are filed in the personnel file (PER-04) and held for the period required by REC-01. They are available for surveyor review at any time.

responsibilities.duty: Provides time and resources for training, verifies that the annual calendar is completed, and acts on compliance gaps.
Delivers or arranges orientation and in-service training, signs competency checklists, keeps training records and retrains staff when problems are found.
Complete orientation and in-service training, sign attendance sheets, follow the training in daily work and ask when unsure.
Support training on diets, allergies, choking risk and swallowing changes when asked.

documentation: Orientation checklist and competency sign-off for each employee
Annual in-service calendar and attendance sheets
Make-up and retraining records
Monthly training compliance check
Temperature and sanitation logs reviewed in training (FS-02)

policies.title: Volunteers
policies.applies_to: All volunteers (community, family, student, faith-based and resident volunteers) and the staff who recruit, orient and supervise them.
policies.purpose: To allow volunteers to enrich resident life while protecting residents' rights, safety, privacy and health, and to make sure volunteers are oriented, supervised and never used to meet required staffing.
policies.policy: This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Sched. 6, item 27 — Volunteer Policy and Orientation, if volunteers are to be used in the facility. [AGENCY NAME] uses volunteers to supplement, never replace, paid staff. Every volunteer receives orientation before beginning, covering resident rights, confidentiality (including HIV-related information) and emergency procedures. Volunteers are supervised by a designated staff member. As facility policy, volunteer time does not count toward the required staffing hours or the 24-hour supervision, personal care, housekeeping or food service hours in 18 NYCRR §487.9 (C6). Resident volunteers follow 18 NYCRR §487.9(b) (C6): a resident's volunteer activity is voluntary, and the resident is not required to work in place of paid staff.

definitions.definition: A person who gives time to the facility without pay and is not counted as staff.
A resident who chooses to help with a facility activity or task, subject to §487.9(b).
The staff member designated by the Administrator to approve, orient and supervise volunteers.

procedures: The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] names a Volunteer Coordinator, usually the Activities Director, in the job description (JD-01).

A person who wants to volunteer completes a volunteer application and an interview with the Volunteer Coordinator. Volunteers must be at least the minimum age set by [AGENCY NAME] and may not work unsupervised if they are minors.

The Volunteer Coordinator verifies identity and asks about any health condition that could affect residents, such as a contagious illness. Volunteers with symptoms of a contagious illness must not volunteer until cleared. Volunteers are screened in line with PER-03 and SAF-04, and any background check required by [AGENCY NAME] is done under PER-02.
Before the first shift, each volunteer attends orientation covering the resident rights statement (RS-02), including dignity and privacy.

Orientation covers confidentiality: not discussing residents outside the facility, not sharing or photographing resident information, and the special protection of HIV-related and other health information (RS-07).
Orientation covers emergency procedures: fire alarm response, evacuation routes, who to notify and how to call for help (EM-01, EM-02).
Orientation covers abuse, neglect and exploitation: what to look for and that the volunteer must tell staff immediately (SAF-01).
Orientation covers infection prevention (handwashing, staying home when ill), a list of what volunteers may not do, and who supervises them.
The volunteer signs an acknowledgment of orientation and confidentiality. The coordinator files it in the volunteer file.
Volunteers do not give personal care, administer or handle medications, handle resident funds, transport residents, or take responsibility for supervision of residents.
A named employee is on duty and responsible for supervising volunteers during each volunteer shift. Volunteers sign in and out on the volunteer log.
Volunteer hours are never counted as staffing. Staffing schedules (PER-04, STF-01) list only paid employees.

Resident volunteers take part only by choice. The Activities Director and the resident's service plan document the activity, and the resident may stop at any time. Residents are not required to perform duties of paid staff and are not used to meet staffing, in line with §487.9(b).
The Volunteer Coordinator reviews each volunteer's performance. The Administrator may end a volunteer's service for breach of rules, confidentiality or resident rights.
The Volunteer Coordinator refreshes orientation topics yearly for long-term volunteers and reports to the Administrator on volunteer use during QA (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the volunteer program, designates the coordinator and ensures volunteers are not used to meet staffing requirements.
Screens, orients, schedules, supervises and records volunteers; ensures a staff supervisor is assigned each shift.
Directs and watches the volunteer's work and removes the volunteer from any task that is outside the allowed scope.
Follow orientation, keep resident information confidential, report concerns immediately and sign in and out.

documentation: Volunteer application and interview notes
Signed orientation and confidentiality acknowledgment
Volunteer sign-in/out log
Resident volunteer participation notes (voluntary, by choice)
Annual QA review of volunteer use

policies.title: Resident and Facility Records and Retention
policies.applies_to: All staff who create, use, store or release resident or facility records, including medical, administrative, financial, program and personnel records, in paper or electronic form.
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] keeps complete, accurate, secure and retrievable resident and facility records for the periods required by law, and can produce them to the Department of Health on request.
policies.policy: This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Sched. 6, item 28 — Record Keeping policy for maintaining records and reports (records component; reports are covered in REC-02). [AGENCY NAME] keeps resident and facility records as required by 18 NYCRR §487.10(c)-(d) (C7). Individual resident records are kept for 3 years after the resident's death or discharge. Program, business and renewal records are kept for 7 years (§487.10(h)). The home uses forms mandated by the Department and keeps required postings (§487.10(f)-(g)). Records for Assisted Living Residence residents also contain the content required by 10 NYCRR §1001.10(i)(8) and §1001.12. Resident records are confidential and protected under HIPAA (45 CFR 164) and RS-07. Records are available to DOH staff when requested, and are kept secure, legible and accurate. The Quality Assurance plan is updated at least every two years, and the quality improvement committee meets at least every six months (§487.10(d)(5)(ix)) (C7).

definitions.definition: All documents about an individual resident, including the DSS-3122 medical evaluation, admission interview, admission agreement, rights acknowledgment, individualized service plan, progress and incident notes, medication records, advance directive information, discharge or death records and ALR-required content.
Records about operation of the home, including program, business, financial, staffing, drill, inspection, QA, license/renewal and maintenance records.
Minimum time a record must be kept before authorized destruction.
A form the Department requires the facility to use, such as DSS-3122 or DSS-2963.

procedures: The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] designates a Records Custodian who is responsible for record organization, access, storage and retention, and for this policy.

A resident record is opened at admission. It contains the items required by §487.10(c), including the DSS-3122 medical evaluation (completed within 30 days before admission and at least every 12 months), the written administrator interview, the signed admission agreement and rights statement, and the ISP (AD-02, AD-03, AD-05).
For ALR residents, the Records Custodian makes sure each record also contains the content required by 10 NYCRR §1001.10(i)(8) and §1001.12 and checks this at admission and during each reassessment.

Staff enter notes in ink or in the approved electronic system, dated, timed and signed with name and title. Late entries are marked as late. Errors are corrected by a single line and initialed, never erased or whited out.
Mandated forms are used in the current Department version. The Records Custodian checks the DOH website each quarter for form updates and replaces old versions.
Facility records are kept in the categories required by §487.10(d): program, business, financial, staffing schedules and personnel, drills, inspections, maintenance, QA and renewal records.
Paper records are kept in locked cabinets in a restricted area. Electronic records require unique user IDs and passwords, have role-based access, are backed up and are never shared by staff.

Staff access resident records only as needed for their duties. Releases of information outside the facility require the resident's (or legal representative's) written authorization, except where the law allows or requires disclosure (RS-07).

The required postings (§487.10(g)), such as the operating certificate, the Department of Health inspection report availability, resident rights, Ombudsman and complaint information, and price posting under REC-02, are displayed where residents can see them. The Administrator checks them monthly.

Individual resident records are retained at least 3 years after the resident's death or discharge. Program, business and renewal records are retained at least 7 years (§487.10(h)). If another law, a pending survey, investigation or litigation requires longer, the longer period applies.

When a resident is discharged, transferred or dies, the Records Custodian closes the record within 30 days, adds the discharge or death documentation and moves it to closed storage with the retention end date shown.
Staffing schedules are kept 12 months and personnel records are kept as required by PER-04.

The Records Custodian keeps a destruction log. Records past the retention period may be destroyed only with the Administrator's written approval and by shredding or secure deletion. Nothing is destroyed while a hold is in place.

The Records Custodian audits a sample of resident records quarterly for completeness and timeliness and reports findings to the quality improvement committee (GOV-02). The QA plan is updated at least every two years and the committee meets at least every six months.
If the facility closes or changes ownership, the Administrator follows Department requirements to keep records accessible for the full retention period.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures records are complete, secure and retained; authorizes destruction and approves release of records.
Maintains the filing system, retention schedule, destruction log and form updates; runs audits.
Keep resident records accurate and current, including the medical evaluation, ISP and reassessments.
Document accurately and timely, protect confidentiality and report lost or misused records immediately.

documentation: Records index and retention schedule
Record audit results (quarterly)
Records destruction log with approvals
Release-of-information authorizations
Posting checklist (monthly)
QA plan and committee minutes

policies.title: Required Reports to the State
policies.applies_to: The Administrator, designated report preparers, the Case Manager, the Employee in Charge and all mandated reporters.
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] submits every required report, notification and posting to the Department of Health, the Justice Center and other authorities accurately and on time.
policies.policy: This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Sched. 6, item 28 — Record Keeping policy for maintaining records and reports (reports component). [AGENCY NAME] submits: the annual financial statement DSS-2963, the quarterly statistical report and the quarterly resident roster (18 NYCRR §487.10(e), C7); the Incident Report under §487.7(d); next-business-day DOH notifications under 18 NYCRR §487.12 (C9) for a work stoppage, fire, loss of a fire system, no hot water or loss of essential services; Justice Center reportable incidents immediately on reasonable cause under 18 NYCRR §487.14 (C10); annual quality measures and price posting for ALRs under Public Health Law §4656 (C24); and notice to the DOH regional office within 3 business days of a key vacancy. Justice Center and other reporting duties are in addition to each other. Reporting to one agency does not replace reporting to another. The agency maintains a current Health Provider Network (HPN) account with 24/7 contacts, updated monthly (§487.12).

definitions.definition: The annual financial statement filed with the Department.
Reports on census and resident data submitted each quarter.
An event that must be reported to the Justice Center by mandated reporters on reasonable cause (SAF-01).
A vacancy in a position for which the regulations require notice to the regional office, including the Administrator (QUAL-01).
The Department's Health Provider Network, used for emergency contacts and communications.

procedures: The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] assigns a Reports Coordinator and a back-up, and keeps a reporting calendar listing each report, due date, responsible person and submission method.

Annual financial statement: the Reports Coordinator and the accountant prepare DSS-2963 and the Administrator reviews and signs it. It is filed by the due date set by the Department on the form. A copy is kept as a business record (REC-01).

Quarterly statistical report and quarterly resident roster: the Reports Coordinator compiles them from the resident census within the first days after each quarter closes, and the Administrator reviews them for accuracy before submission by the Department's due date.

Incident Report under §487.7(d): any staff member who witnesses or learns of an incident or accident completes the facility incident report form before the end of the shift and gives it to the Employee in Charge, who notifies the Administrator the same day (SAF-02).

Next-business-day DOH notifications: when there is a work stoppage, fire, loss of a fire system, no hot water or loss of any essential service, the Employee in Charge notifies the Administrator immediately, and the Administrator (or designee) notifies DOH by the next business day by the Department's method. The notification is recorded on the DOH notification log (EM-01).

Justice Center: a mandated reporter who has reasonable cause to suspect a reportable incident reports it to the Justice Center immediately. Reporting is not delayed for supervisor approval. The Administrator starts the facility investigation (§487.14) and protects residents from further harm (SAF-01).

Staff also make any other required reports, such as those to law enforcement, the Ombudsman or the Department, as set out in SAF-01, SAF-02 and RS-04. A report to one agency never replaces a required report to another.
Key vacancies: when a key position becomes vacant, the Administrator notifies the DOH regional office within 3 business days and records the date, position and interim coverage (QUAL-01, STF-01).

HPN: the Reports Coordinator confirms on the first business day of each month that the HPN account is current and that 24/7 emergency contacts are correct. Changes are made at once and the review is logged.

ALR annual quality measures: the Administrator collects the measures required by the Department, reviews them with the quality improvement committee and files them annually as required by Public Health Law §4656 (C24).

ALR price posting: the Administrator posts the starting monthly rate, the rent range, the approved admission agreement and the fee summary on the facility website and in the facility, as §4656 requires. Postings are verified monthly and updated within 5 business days of a change (AD-05).
Any change of the facility's approved information that must be filed with the Department (such as ownership, administrator or capacity changes) is reported under GOV-01.
A report is not considered done until the Reports Coordinator has saved proof of submission (confirmation, receipt or copy), recorded the date and initialed the calendar.
Each quarter the Administrator reviews the calendar for late or missed reports, investigates the cause and records corrective action (GOV-02).
All reports and supporting records are retained under REC-01 (7 years for business and program records, 3 years after death or discharge for individual records).

responsibilities.duty: Signs and submits reports, makes DOH and Justice Center notifications or confirms them, and verifies postings.
Maintains the reporting calendar, prepares reports, checks HPN monthly and files proof of submission.
Reports emergencies and incidents to the Administrator immediately, and makes the first call to the Justice Center, 911 or others if needed.
Report reportable incidents to the Justice Center immediately on reasonable cause.

documentation: Reporting calendar with proof of submission
DSS-2963, quarterly statistical reports and rosters
Incident reports
DOH notification log and Justice Center report numbers
Key vacancy notice records
HPN monthly check log
ALR quality measure filings and price-posting verification

policies.title: Housekeeping, Laundry and Maintenance Plans
policies.applies_to: Housekeeping, laundry and maintenance staff, supervisors, the Administrator and any contractor who cleans or maintains the building and equipment.
policies.purpose: To keep the building clean, safe, sanitary and in good repair, and to prevent infection and hazards, by setting out clear housekeeping, laundry and preventive maintenance plans.
policies.policy: This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Sched. 6, item 29 — Housekeeping Plan, and item 30 — Maintenance Plan. Housekeeping: [AGENCY NAME] provides at least 1.0 hour of housekeeping per resident per week (18 NYCRR §487.9(h), C6). Laundry service is part of the housekeeping plan. Maintenance: the building meets the environmental standards of 18 NYCRR §487.11 (C8): bedrooms of at least 100 square feet (single) and 160 square feet (double), at least 1 toilet per 6 residents and 1 bath or shower per 10 residents, a working call system, and sprinklers throughout buildings of 25 or more beds. Assisted Living Residence structural standards in 10 NYCRR §1001.13 also apply (C21), including the fixed area for SNALR beds. A written preventive maintenance schedule covers fire systems, water temperature, the call system and HVAC. Written logs are kept for inspections and repairs.

definitions.definition: Paid staff hours spent on cleaning, laundry and related tasks, in addition to required personal care and food service hours.
Scheduled inspection, testing and servicing of equipment and building systems done before failure.
The resident emergency call system that lets residents summon staff from bedrooms and bathrooms.
A service needed for resident health and safety, such as heat, hot water, electricity, water, or a working fire alarm or sprinkler system.

procedures: The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] appoints a Housekeeping Supervisor and a Maintenance Supervisor, who may be the same person in a small home, and posts their names in the staff directory.

The Housekeeping Supervisor calculates the weekly housekeeping hours from the census (at least 1.0 hour per resident per week) and builds the schedule. The hours are recorded in the staffing schedule (PER-04, STF-01).

Resident rooms are cleaned on a set schedule, at least weekly, and as needed for spills or soiling. Bathrooms, dining areas, lounges, corridors, stairwells and entrances are cleaned on a daily schedule posted in the housekeeping office.

Staff use Department-approved or EPA-registered disinfectants according to the label, with the correct contact time, and follow SAF-04 for blood and body-fluid cleanup, isolation rooms, and outbreak cleaning. Chemicals are stored in locked areas away from food and medication.
Safety data sheets are kept in the housekeeping area and staff are trained on them at orientation (ORI-01).

Laundry plan: resident clothing, linens and towels are washed on a set schedule, at least weekly for bed linens and towels and sooner when soiled. Soiled and clean laundry are kept apart. Soiled linens are bagged at the point of use and washed at the temperatures and with the products given in the laundry procedure.

Residents' personal laundry is labeled, returned to the right resident, and not mixed with that of others. Residents who wish to do their own laundry may do so, with help if needed, in line with their service plan (RS-05).

The Maintenance Supervisor keeps a preventive maintenance schedule listing each system, the task, how often it is done and who does it. It covers the fire alarm, sprinklers and extinguishers, emergency lighting, hot water temperature, the resident call system, heating/ventilation/air conditioning, elevators or lifts, and exits.

Fire systems are tested and serviced by qualified personnel according to the schedule and code. Staff follow EM-02 and check exits and extinguishers weekly. The call system is tested at least weekly in sample rooms and fully at least monthly, and any defect is repaired immediately or an interim safeguard is put in place.

Water temperatures at resident-use taps are checked weekly and recorded on the water temperature log. Any out-of-range reading is reported at once and corrected, and residents are protected from scalds or no hot water.

Staff report a hazard or repair need on a written work request. The Maintenance Supervisor ranks it (emergency, urgent or routine), repairs emergencies immediately and records the date and action taken. Resident-safety hazards are fixed or made safe the same day.

If a loss of heat, hot water, electricity, water or a fire system occurs, the Maintenance Supervisor notifies the Administrator immediately, who notifies DOH by the next business day and protects residents (EM-01, REC-02).

Maintenance checks that bedroom sizes, toilet and bath ratios, call-system coverage and sprinkler coverage still meet §487.11 and, for ALR, §1001.13 standards after any renovation or room use change. The Administrator submits plans to the Department before structural changes.
For SNALR, the Maintenance Supervisor confirms that SNALR beds remain in the fixed area as approved, and that the area's safeguards work (SNALR-01).

The Administrator and Maintenance Supervisor walk the building monthly with a checklist (including resident rooms, common areas, kitchen, grounds, odors, pests and safety hazards). Findings go on the work-request list with a due date.
Pest control is done by a licensed contractor on a regular schedule, with service reports filed. Trash and biohazard waste are removed on schedule.
All inspection, test, repair and contractor service records are kept in written logs and retained per REC-01. Results are reported to the quality improvement committee (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the plans and budget, ensures required hours and standards are met and makes required notifications.
Schedules and supervises cleaning and laundry, trains staff and keeps cleaning logs.
Runs the preventive maintenance schedule, prioritizes repairs and keeps inspection and repair logs.
Report hazards, spills, broken equipment and call-system problems immediately.

documentation: Housekeeping and laundry schedules
Weekly housekeeping hour calculation (1.0 hr/resident/week)
Preventive maintenance schedule
Water temperature, call system, fire system and HVAC logs
Work request and repair log
Monthly building walk-through checklists
Pest control and contractor service reports

policies.title: Non-Discrimination, Reasonable Accommodation and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers and contractors involved in marketing, admission, service delivery, discharge and complaints, and all applicants and residents.
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] admits, serves and retains people fairly, provides reasonable accommodations for disabilities, and gives language help to residents with limited English, in a way consistent with DAL DACF 23-15 and the Part II requirements for admission policies.
policies.policy: This policy meets DOH-5098 (1/26) Sched. 6, item 32 — admission procedures and policies, including a non-discrimination statement and reasonable accommodation policy, consistent with ACF DAL# DACF 23-15. It is part of the admission policies submitted in Part II (18 NYCRR §485.6, C29). Non-discrimination statement: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate in admission, retention, services, discharge or treatment on the basis of race, color, national origin or limited English proficiency, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, age, disability, source of payment, marital or familial status, military status or any other characteristic protected by federal or New York law, consistent with 42 USC 2000d and 42 USC 12101. Admission and retention decisions are based only on the criteria in 18 NYCRR §487.4 (C1): whether the home may lawfully meet the person's needs, and none of the listed conditions that prevent admission or retention apply. A disability alone is never a reason to refuse admission. The home provides reasonable accommodations and interpreter and translation help to residents and applicants with limited English.

definitions.definition: A change in rules, policies, practices, services or the physical setting that gives a person with a disability an equal chance to use and enjoy the home, unless it would cause undue hardship or a fundamental change in the program, or would conflict with §487.4 limits on whom the home may lawfully serve.
A person who does not speak English as a primary language and has a limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English.

A person who is fluent in English and the other language and trained to interpret accurately and impartially. Family or other residents are not used unless the resident chooses it and a qualified interpreter is also offered.
The Department's Dear Administrator Letter on admission procedures, non-discrimination and reasonable accommodation for adult care facilities.

procedures: The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] is the Non-Discrimination and Accommodation Coordinator. The name and phone number [PHONE] are included in the admission packet and on the posted notice.
The non-discrimination statement is posted in the lobby, included in the admission packet and on the website, and read or explained to each applicant at the admission interview (AD-02).

Staff who market the home or take inquiries use the same screening questions with every caller. Staff are trained to avoid questions about protected characteristics and to answer inquiries about accessibility, services and cost fairly.

Admission decisions are made by the Administrator, with the nurse or Case Manager as needed, using only the §487.4 criteria, the DSS-3122 medical evaluation and the written administrator interview (AD-01, AD-02). The decision is recorded with the specific criterion relied on.

Source of payment (private pay, SSI or Medicaid ALP) is never used to refuse a person who otherwise meets criteria, unless the home has no bed available or has been approved for a different program. Waitlist order is applied evenly and recorded.

An applicant or resident may ask for a reasonable accommodation orally or in writing at any time. Staff accept any request and give it to the Coordinator within one business day. No one is asked to use a particular form.

The Coordinator meets with the person within 5 business days, or sooner for urgent needs. They discuss the disability-related need, the options, and any information needed from a health care provider, asking for only what is necessary.

The Coordinator decides promptly, in writing, and tells the person the decision, the reasons and the way to appeal or complain. If a request cannot be granted as made, the Coordinator offers a different effective accommodation.

Approved accommodations (such as a room near the dining room, grab bars, large-print materials, extra time, assistance with forms or a service animal) are added to the ISP (AD-03), shared with the staff who need them and rechecked at each reassessment.

A request is denied only if it would cause undue financial or administrative burden, fundamentally change the program, pose a direct threat that cannot be reduced, or require care the home may not lawfully provide under §487.4. The Administrator reviews every denial and records the reasons.

Language access: at the first contact the staff ask the applicant or resident what language they prefer. The preference is entered in the resident record. The home uses qualified interpreters (in person, by phone or by video) and a language line contract at no cost to the resident.

Key documents (the admission agreement, rights statement, house rules, grievance procedure, Ombudsman information, emergency instructions and consent forms) are translated or explained orally in the resident's language. Staff record the date and the interpreter used (AD-05, RS-02).
Staff do not require residents to bring their own interpreter, and do not use another resident or a minor to interpret, except in a real emergency until a qualified interpreter is reached.

All staff are trained on this policy at orientation and yearly (ORI-01). Staff who discriminate, harass or retaliate against any person for asking for an accommodation or complaining are disciplined under PER-01.

Complaints about discrimination or denial of accommodation are handled under RS-03. The person is told that they may also contact the Ombudsman, the DOH regional office or other civil-rights agencies, and no one is retaliated against.

The Coordinator keeps a log of admission denials, accommodation requests and decisions, and language services. The Administrator reviews the log quarterly with the quality improvement committee to look for patterns (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Serves as Coordinator, makes admission and accommodation decisions, and reviews denials and logs.
Identify accommodation and language needs at the interview and put them in the ISP.
Treat everyone equally, accept accommodation requests and use interpreters, and report discrimination.

documentation: Posted and distributed non-discrimination statement
Admission decision record showing §487.4 criteria used
Accommodation request, decision and ISP update records
Language preference and interpreter use records
Translated or explained documents log
Quarterly review of denials, accommodations and complaints

policies.title: Quality Assurance, Survey Readiness and Posting
policies.applies_to: Administrator, quality improvement committee, all department heads and all staff of [AGENCY NAME], including ALR, EALR, SNALR and ALP programs where licensed
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] runs a written quality assurance (QA) program, is ready for Department of Health (DOH) surveys at all times, corrects cited violations on time, reports quality measures, and posts the notices and information that New York requires.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written QA plan that the Administrator and the quality improvement committee review and update at least every two years, as required by 18 NYCRR §487.10(d)(5)(ix). The quality improvement committee meets at least every six months, and [AGENCY NAME] will meet more often when data show a need. The facility is surveyed for recertification every 12 or 18 months under Social Services Law §461-a. It stays survey-ready year-round. Any violation cited by DOH is corrected within 30 days and the correction is documented. As an Assisted Living Residence, [AGENCY NAME] reports annual quality measures to DOH and posts its starting monthly rate, rent range, approved admission agreement and fee summary on its website and in the facility, as required by Public Health Law §4656. The DOH adult care facility complaint line, 1-866-893-6772, and resident rights materials are posted where residents and visitors can see them, in line with Social Services Law §460-d. Postings and records follow 18 NYCRR §487.10(g)-(h). This policy applies the quality assurance requirement of 18 NYCRR §487.10(d)(5)(ix). No staff member may retaliate against anyone who raises a quality or safety concern.

definitions.definition: The written plan that sets out how [AGENCY NAME] measures, reviews and improves resident care, safety and services.
The standing committee that reviews QA data and recommends corrective action. It meets at least every six months.
A DOH on-site survey that takes place every 12 or 18 months to determine continued compliance.

definitions.term: Statement of Deficiencies / Plan of Correction
definitions.definition: The DOH list of cited violations and the facility's written plan and evidence showing how and when each violation was corrected.
The annual data set that an Assisted Living Residence reports to DOH under Public Health Law §4656.

procedures: The Administrator appoints the quality improvement committee in writing. Members include the Administrator, Case Manager, a direct-care or medication staff representative, food service lead, housekeeping/maintenance lead, the supervising nurse where EALR/SNALR is operated, and a resident or Resident Council representative.

The Administrator writes the QA plan. The plan lists the indicators to be tracked: incidents and accidents, falls, elopements, medication errors, grievances, resident satisfaction, infection events, staff training completion, drill completion, and timeliness of reassessments.
The Administrator reviews and updates the QA plan at least every two years, and sooner after a change in license, program or services. The review date and approval signature are recorded on the plan.

The committee meets at least every six months and records minutes: attendees, data reviewed, findings, corrective actions, person responsible and due date. The Administrator sets the calendar for the year in January.

Before each meeting, the Case Manager and department heads compile data from incident reports (see SAF-02), grievance logs (see RS-03), medication error records (see MED-02), infection logs (see SAF-04), training records and drill records.
The committee tracks each action item to completion and reports its status at the next meeting. Items still open after two meetings are escalated to the governing body (see GOV-01).

The Administrator keeps a survey-readiness binder, in paper or electronic form, containing the operating certificate and ALR license, current census, staffing schedules, drill records, training records, personnel files index, resident roster, QA minutes, and prior survey results.

Each month the Administrator or designee walks the building using a self-inspection checklist covering postings, medication storage, kitchen and food storage, exits and fire equipment, hot water, resident rooms, and cleanliness. Findings are corrected promptly and logged.

When DOH announces or begins a survey, the Administrator or the highest-ranking person on duty notifies the Administrator, greets the surveyors, gives them the requested records and a workspace, and assigns a staff escort. Staff answer questions truthfully and no one may coach residents or alter records.
At the exit conference, the Administrator records each finding, asks for clarification of any citation that is unclear, and writes down the DOH contact for questions.

On receipt of the Statement of Deficiencies, the Administrator assigns each cited item to a responsible person, writes a plan of correction, and corrects each cited violation within 30 days. The Administrator keeps dated proof of correction (photos, revised policies, training sign-in sheets, work orders) and submits the plan and evidence to the DOH regional office as directed.
The Administrator reviews the root cause of each citation with the committee, and the committee decides whether the QA plan or any policy needs to change.

Each year the Administrator, with the Case Manager and nursing staff where applicable, compiles the ALR annual quality measures and submits them to DOH in the form and by the date DOH specifies. A copy of the submission is retained.

The Administrator keeps the ALR starting monthly rate, rent range, approved admission agreement and fee summary current on the facility website and on the posting board, and updates both within [NUMBER OF DAYS, e.g., 5] business days of any approved change (see AD-05).

The Administrator posts the DOH adult care facility complaint line, 1-866-893-6772, the Ombudsman contact, the resident rights materials, the operating certificate and other required notices in a common area accessible to residents and visitors (see RS-02). The Administrator checks the postings weekly and replaces any that are missing or illegible.

The Administrator keeps QA plans and committee minutes as program records for seven years. Individual resident records are kept three years after death or discharge, as required by 18 NYCRR §487.10(h) (see REC-01).
The Administrator reports QA activity and survey results to the governing body at least [FREQUENCY, e.g., quarterly].

responsibilities.duty: Approves the QA plan, reviews survey results and QA reports, and provides resources for correction.
Leads QA, chairs the quality improvement committee, maintains survey readiness, submits plans of correction, files annual quality measures and keeps required postings.
Supplies resident-related data, helps with satisfaction surveys and follows up on resident-related actions.
Complete self-inspections for their areas and carry out corrective actions on time.
Cooperate with surveyors, report concerns and take part in corrective training.

documentation: Written QA plan with dated revisions and approval signatures
Quality improvement committee roster, agendas, minutes and action-item tracker
Monthly self-inspection checklists
DOH survey reports, Statements of Deficiencies, plans of correction and proof of correction within 30 days
Annual ALR quality measures submission and confirmation
Dated posting checklist with copies of posted notices, including the 1-866-893-6772 complaint line
Website and posting records of ALR rate, rent range, agreement and fee summary

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers, contractors and agency-affiliated staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To prevent abuse, neglect and exploitation of residents, to require immediate reporting of suspected mistreatment, to make sure every report is investigated, and to protect residents and reporters from harm or retaliation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect, mistreatment and exploitation of residents. Where [AGENCY NAME] is a facility subject to the Justice Center, it and its mandated reporters report every reportable incident to the Justice Center immediately upon reasonable cause, as required by 18 NYCRR §487.14. The facility starts an investigation of every reported or suspected incident. These duties are in addition to the other reporting duties under Part 487, including the incident, death and felony reporting in 18 NYCRR §487.7(d). The Administrator confirms with the DOH regional office whether, and for which programs, [AGENCY NAME] is subject to the Justice Center. Whether or not it is, staff must report suspected abuse immediately to the Administrator, protect the resident, and follow the incident-reporting steps in SAF-02. Staff exclusion list and State Central Register checks are described in PER-02. Residents may use the DOH complaint line (1-866-893-6772) or the Long-Term Care Ombudsman at any time, and staff must never discourage or block them. Retaliation against any reporter, resident or witness is prohibited and is grounds for discipline up to and including termination.

definitions.definition: An incident of abuse, neglect or other mistreatment that must be reported to the Justice Center when the facility is subject to its jurisdiction. Examples include physical abuse, sexual abuse, psychological abuse, deliberate inappropriate use of restraints, neglect and exploitation (such as misuse of a resident's funds or property).
A staff member or other person who by law must report a reportable incident on reasonable cause. At [AGENCY NAME], all employees are treated as mandated reporters.
Facts that would lead a reasonable person to suspect that abuse, neglect or exploitation has occurred. Proof is not required before reporting.
Improper use of a resident's money, property or resources for someone else's benefit.
Discipline, threats, harassment, schedule changes, discharge or other adverse action taken because someone made a report in good faith or took part in an investigation.

procedures: Before starting work, each new employee, volunteer and contractor reads this policy and signs an acknowledgment. Abuse recognition and reporting is part of general orientation (see ORI-01) and annual in-service training (see ORI-02).

The Administrator checks the Staff Exclusion List and State Central Register for each candidate before hire and follows the screening schedule in PER-02. No one with a disqualifying finding works with residents.

The Administrator posts this policy summary, the DOH complaint line (1-866-893-6772), the Ombudsman contact information, and the Justice Center hotline where applicable. These postings go in a common area and in the staff break area.

Any staff member who sees, hears or suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately protects the resident by separating the resident from the alleged abuser, getting medical care if needed, and calling 911 if anyone is in danger.

The staff member reports immediately, by phone, to the Administrator or the on-call administrator at [PHONE]. If the alleged abuser is the Administrator, or the Administrator cannot be reached, the staff member reports directly to the governing body representative at [PHONE] and to DOH.

If the facility is subject to the Justice Center, the staff member or the Administrator makes the report to the Justice Center hotline (1-855-373-2122) immediately on reasonable cause, without waiting for approval or for investigation results. Telling a supervisor does not replace a personal report by the mandated reporter. The staff member records the date, time and report or confirmation number.

The Administrator or the senior person on duty also follows the reporting steps in 18 NYCRR §487.7(d) and SAF-02. This includes completing an Incident Report, notifying the resident's physician, emergency contact or representative, and DOH as required, and notifying law enforcement when a crime is suspected.

The accused employee or volunteer is removed from resident contact immediately and stays off duty or on non-resident duties until the investigation is complete or the Administrator decides otherwise in writing.

The Administrator starts the facility investigation without delay and in all cases before the end of the next business day. The investigation includes securing the scene, interviewing the resident, witnesses and the accused separately, reviewing schedules, records and any video, and taking written or recorded statements. The Administrator cooperates with the Justice Center, DOH, law enforcement and the Ombudsman.
Evidence is preserved. Staff must not alter, discard or rewrite records, and no one may question the resident in a way that leads or pressures them.

The Administrator or Case Manager meets with the affected resident and any witnessing residents to offer support and to arrange medical, mental health or counseling services (see MH-01). The Case Manager updates the resident's Individualized Service Plan if safety needs have changed (see AD-03).

The Administrator informs the resident and the resident's representative of the outcome of the investigation, within the limits of confidentiality, and informs staff of any facility-wide changes needed.

When an allegation is substantiated, the Administrator takes corrective action. This includes discipline up to termination, and filing the reports required by law, including notifying any licensing authority or registry when applicable (see PER-01 and PER-02).

Any person who retaliates against a reporter, resident or witness is subject to discipline. The Administrator reviews the reporter's schedule, assignment and treatment for 90 days after a report to ensure no retaliation occurs, and records the review.

Residents may call the DOH complaint line (1-866-893-6772) and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman at any time without permission. Staff provide a private phone and help dialing when asked (see RS-02 and RS-03).

The Administrator logs every allegation, whether or not it was substantiated, and summarizes the log for the quality improvement committee (see GOV-02). The summary is checked for patterns by staff member, shift, location and type.
The Administrator reviews this policy at least once a year and after any substantiated case, and updates training as needed.

responsibilities.duty: Receives reports, ensures immediate reporting to the Justice Center when applicable, DOH and law enforcement, starts and directs the investigation, protects reporters, and imposes corrective action.
Prevent mistreatment, report immediately on reasonable cause, protect the resident, and cooperate with investigations.
Supports the affected resident, arranges counseling and updates the service plan.
Receives reports on allegations, ensures independent review where the Administrator is implicated, and enforces the no-retaliation rule.
Completes exclusion list and State Central Register checks and maintains training records.

documentation: Signed staff acknowledgments of this policy
Justice Center report confirmation numbers (where applicable) and DOH notification records
Incident Reports and investigation file (statements, interview notes, evidence log, findings, corrective actions)
Resident and representative notification records
Allegation log and QA summaries
Anti-retaliation follow-up review records
Training sign-in sheets for abuse prevention and reporting
Exclusion list and State Central Register check records (see PER-02)

policies.title: Incident and Accident Reporting, Elopement and Missing Resident
policies.applies_to: All employees; Administrator; Case Manager; supervising nurse (EALR/SNALR); SNALR staff
policies.purpose: To make sure incidents and accidents are handled, documented and reported on time, that a missing resident is found quickly, and that required notifications are made to DOH, families, physicians and police.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] follows 18 NYCRR §487.7(d) for resident supervision, evacuation, missing-resident steps, emergency and illness response, reporting of death, suicide attempt and felony, and the events that require an Incident Report. Staff complete an Incident Report for every event that meets a trigger in §487.7(d) and for every other event that affects resident health or safety. The facility notifies DOH by the next business day of the events listed in 18 NYCRR §487.12: a work stoppage, a fire, loss of a fire system, no hot water, or loss of essential services. Missing-resident procedures start immediately when a resident cannot be found. Residents with dementia, cognitive impairment or a history of wandering are assessed for elopement risk and given individualized safeguards. Incidents are reviewed in the quality assurance program (see GOV-02). Abuse and neglect allegations are also handled under SAF-01. Suspected restraint use is handled under SAF-03.

definitions.definition: Any event that harms or could have harmed a resident, visitor or employee, or that disrupts operations. Examples are falls, injuries, medication errors, fire, loss of power, deaths, suicide attempts, alleged crimes and missing residents.
The written report of an incident that is completed on the facility's form, or any DOH-required form, containing who, what, when, where, injuries, actions taken, and notifications made.
A resident who cannot be located, whose whereabouts are unknown, who has left without notice or sign-out, or who has not returned when expected.
A resident who is cognitively impaired or at risk leaves the building or grounds without staff knowledge or supervision.
A documented assessment of a resident's risk of leaving the facility unsafely, which leads to safeguards in the Individualized Service Plan.

procedures: Any employee who witnesses or learns of an incident or accident first protects residents, calls 911 for an emergency, provides first aid by trained staff (see STF-01), and notifies the employee in charge.

The employee in charge notifies the Administrator by phone immediately for deaths, suicide attempts, fires, alleged crimes, missing residents, serious injuries and abuse concerns, and by the start of the next business day for all others.

The staff member who saw or found the event completes an Incident Report before the end of the shift. The report records the date, time, location, persons involved, witnesses, description, injuries, treatment, actions, and who was notified. It is factual and does not speculate about fault.

The employee in charge notifies the resident's physician or nurse practitioner of any injury, illness or change in condition, and notifies the resident's emergency contact or representative. The notice and time are recorded in the Incident Report and resident record (see RS-04).
The Administrator reviews each Incident Report within one business day, confirms that the required notifications were made, and decides on follow-up or investigation.

Death, suicide attempt, felony: staff call 911 when appropriate and notify the Administrator immediately. The Administrator makes the reports required by 18 NYCRR §487.7(d), notifies DOH and law enforcement as required, informs the representative and physician, and preserves the scene (see RS-06). Suspected abuse is also reported under SAF-01.

DOH notification: the Administrator notifies the DOH regional office and enters the information required in the Health Commerce System by the next business day for a work stoppage, fire, loss of a fire system, no hot water, or loss of essential services, as described in 18 NYCRR §487.12 and EM-01. Notices are logged with date, time, contact and any reference number.

Missing resident, steps 1-3: As soon as a resident is thought to be missing, the staff member alerts the employee in charge, who announces a code to all staff and starts a coordinated search. Staff check the resident's room, bathrooms, common areas, the sign-out log, the grounds, parking areas and nearby streets, and check for transportation or visitor information.

Missing resident, steps 4-6: The employee in charge assigns staff to search specific areas without leaving the building uncovered, checks recent photographs and a description of clothing, phones the resident's family or representative, and calls the places the resident often goes. For a resident with dementia, cognitive impairment, a wander-risk flag, medical vulnerability or when the weather is dangerous, the employee in charge calls 911 immediately, without waiting. For any other resident, the employee in charge calls 911 or local police if the resident is not found within [30] minutes of the search starting, or sooner if there is concern for safety.

The employee in charge gives police the resident's name, description, photo, medical conditions, medications, and last known location, and keeps a log of the search times and people contacted. The Administrator is notified at the start of the search.

When the resident is found, staff provide care and a medical check, notify police, the physician and family, and end the search. A missing-resident Incident Report is completed, and the resident's ISP is updated.

Wander-risk assessment: during pre-admission and admission (see AD-02), and again at each reassessment and after any change in condition, the Case Manager or nurse screens each resident for wandering. The assessment is documented, and the Individualized Service Plan sets safeguards (see AD-03).

Safeguards for residents at risk include a current photo on file, supervision and check frequency, door alarms or approved secured exits where permitted, a sign-out and return process, a plan for outings, and staff awareness at shift change. Locked or secured units are used only in an approved SNALR/fixed area (see SNALR-01 and SAF-03).

The Administrator or Case Manager meets with the resident and the family after any elopement or missing-resident event to review the risk and any changes to safeguards or the level of care (see AD-01 and AD-06).

Falls and accidents: after any fall, staff do not move a resident with a suspected injury, call for help, and provide first aid. The nurse or Case Manager reviews the fall within one business day, looks for causes, and updates the ISP (see RS-05).

The Administrator keeps a monthly incident log with the type, date, location, shift and outcome of each incident, and presents trends to the quality improvement committee at each meeting (see GOV-02).

The Administrator retains Incident Reports in the facility's records, kept apart from the resident record where policy requires it. The reports are kept for the retention period in REC-01 and are available to DOH on request.

responsibilities.duty: Directs immediate response, calls 911, starts missing-resident searches, makes initial notifications and ensures reports are written.
Reviews every report, makes DOH, police and other required notifications, investigates, and presents trends to QA.
Conducts wander-risk assessments, updates ISPs, follows up with residents and families, and reviews falls.
Report incidents immediately, complete Incident Reports and take part in searches.

documentation: Incident Reports with supervisor review signature
Missing-resident search log and police report reference numbers
Notification log: physician, family or representative, DOH, police and the time of each
DOH next-business-day notification records and Health Commerce System entries
Wander-risk assessments and ISP safeguards
Monthly incident log and QA trend reports
Staff training records on emergency and missing-resident response

policies.title: Restraints and Restrictive Practices
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers and contractors; Administrator; Case Manager; nursing staff; SNALR staff
policies.purpose: To ensure that no resident is physically restrained, that least-restrictive alternatives and positive behavior supports are used, and that any use or suspected use of a restrictive practice is reported and corrected.
policies.policy: Physical restraints are prohibited at [AGENCY NAME], as required by 18 NYCRR §487.7(e). No employee, volunteer or contractor may restrain a resident for discipline, convenience, staffing reasons or to control behavior. This includes tying, binding or holding a resident down, using belts or vests, geriatric chairs with trays or tables that a resident cannot remove, bed rails used to prevent a resident from getting out of bed, or any device that prevents free movement. Staff use the least restrictive alternative and approaches that prevent or reduce distress and risk, and they document those approaches in the Individualized Service Plan. Doors are locked only in an approved SNALR or other fixed area and never to confine a resident in a non-approved area (see SNALR-01). Any actual or suspected restraint is stopped immediately and reported as an incident (see SAF-02). When it may amount to abuse or mistreatment, it is also reported under SAF-01.

definitions.definition: Any manual method, physical or mechanical device, material or equipment attached to or near a resident's body that the resident cannot easily remove and that limits free movement or normal access to the body.
Any practice that limits a resident's freedom of movement, choice or access, including seclusion, confinement to a room, withholding of food or activities as punishment, and locked doors.
A safe approach that meets the resident's needs with the smallest limit on freedom, such as environmental change, supervision, toileting schedules, or activities.
A documented, individualized, non-physical strategy to prevent or respond to distress or challenging behaviors, based on the resident's history and triggers.

procedures: The Administrator includes the restraint prohibition and alternatives in general orientation (see ORI-01) and in annual in-service training for all direct-care staff (see ORI-02). Each employee signs an acknowledgment that restraints are prohibited.

During pre-admission evaluation and admission interview (see AD-02), the Case Manager or nurse identifies behaviors, fall risks or wandering that might lead staff to consider restraint, and plans alternatives before admission.

The Case Manager develops individualized, non-physical approaches with the resident, the family or representative and, where applicable, the physician and mental health provider. Examples include adjusting routines, identifying triggers, offering activities, adding supervision, toileting schedules, a lower bed, a bed or chair alarm that does not restrict movement, hip protectors, non-slip footwear, and an evaluation of pain, medications and infections. These are written into the ISP (see AD-03).
Staff use verbal redirection, calm communication, and offers of choice first when a resident is agitated. They do not use force, holds or devices to control behavior.

Staff may use physical contact only for protection in an emergency when a resident or another person is in immediate danger and only for the shortest time necessary. The staff member calls the employee in charge and 911 or the mental health crisis line, and an Incident Report is completed on the same shift.

Bed rails, chairs and devices are assessed individually. A device that a resident cannot remove or that prevents getting up is not used. Any device a resident requests for comfort or mobility, such as a grab bar, is assessed by the nurse or Case Manager, and the resident's ability to remove it is recorded.

Doors and exits: Resident rooms and common areas are not locked from the outside. Secured exits are used only in the approved SNALR unit or other approved fixed area, with a written plan and with safeguards that keep residents safe and give access to outdoor space and activities (see SNALR-01).
No staff member may withhold food, fluids, medication, personal care or activities, or confine a resident, as punishment or to gain compliance.

Any staff member who sees or suspects a restraint or restrictive practice removes the restraint safely if possible, ensures the resident is safe and comfortable, and reports to the employee in charge immediately.

The employee in charge notifies the Administrator immediately, and the staff member completes an Incident Report before the end of the shift. The Administrator decides whether the matter must also be reported under SAF-01 as abuse, neglect or mistreatment, and makes those reports.
The Administrator investigates, interviews staff and the resident, retrains or disciplines as needed (see PER-01), and tells the resident's representative.
The nurse or Case Manager reviews the resident's needs after any restraint event, and revises the ISP and the behavior-management approach.

The Case Manager reviews the behavior-management approaches at each reassessment, and at least after any change in condition. A resident whose needs cannot be met without restraint, or whose safety cannot be assured, is referred for evaluation and may need discharge planning under AD-06.
The Administrator reports restraint events and the effectiveness of alternatives to the quality improvement committee (see GOV-02). The facility's goal is zero restraint events.

responsibilities.duty: Enforces the prohibition, investigates reports, retrains or disciplines staff and reports events to QA.
Assesses behaviors and fall risks, designs and documents least-restrictive alternatives and reviews them at each reassessment.
Use only non-physical approaches, never restrain, and report suspected restraint immediately.
Responds to behavioral emergencies, calls 911 or crisis services, and ensures an Incident Report is done.

documentation: Staff acknowledgments of the restraint prohibition and training sign-in sheets
ISP entries showing behavior-management approaches and alternatives
Fall-risk and device assessments
Incident Reports and investigation files for any actual or suspected restraint
SNALR secured-area approval and plan (where applicable)
QA reports on restrictive-practice events

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers and contractors; Administrator; supervising nurse (EALR/SNALR); housekeeping, laundry, food service and direct-care staff
policies.purpose: To prevent and control infection among residents and staff, to protect employees from bloodborne pathogens, to screen staff for tuberculosis, and to report outbreaks on time.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains an infection prevention and control program that includes a bloodborne pathogen exposure program and a post-exposure procedure, as required by 10 NYCRR §1001.11(h) and the federal Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030. Employees receive an annual physician, physician assistant or registered nurse statement and a tuberculosis (TB) assessment under 18 NYCRR §487.9(a)(8), and EALR/SNALR direct-care staff also keep immunization and TB records under 10 NYCRR §1001.11. A significant-risk exposure is determined using the standards of 10 NYCRR Part 63 and the guidance of the physician or local health department. Outbreaks and reportable diseases are reported to the local health department as required by law. All staff follow standard precautions, hand hygiene, cleaning, disinfecting and laundry procedures in this policy. Infection events are reviewed in the quality assurance program (see GOV-02).

definitions.definition: Infection-control practices applied to all residents at all times, including hand hygiene, gloves and other protective equipment, safe handling of sharps, respiratory hygiene and safe cleaning of surfaces and linens.
Contact of eyes, mouth, mucous membranes or non-intact skin with blood or other potentially infectious material, or a needlestick or cut with a contaminated sharp.
An exposure that carries a significant risk of transmitting a bloodborne pathogen, as determined by a clinician under 10 NYCRR Part 63 and current public health guidance.
A TB risk assessment and screening, as required by 18 NYCRR §487.9(a)(8), with testing or evaluation as directed by the physician or health department.
An increase above the usual number of cases of an infectious illness, such as gastrointestinal or respiratory illness, in a defined group of residents or staff.

procedures: The Administrator designates an infection control coordinator (the supervising nurse where EALR/SNALR is operated, or another trained staff member, named in writing as [INFECTION CONTROL COORDINATOR NAME]). The coordinator reviews this program at least annually.

General orientation covers standard precautions, hand hygiene, bloodborne pathogens, the exposure procedure, and respiratory etiquette (see ORI-01). Direct-care staff receive refresher training annually (see ORI-02). Training is documented with date, content and signatures.

Staff wash hands with soap and water or use an alcohol-based rub before and after contact with each resident, before preparing or serving food or giving medications, after using the toilet, after removing gloves and when visibly soiled. Soap and water is used when hands are visibly soiled and when residents have diarrheal illness.

The Administrator supplies gloves, gowns, masks, eye protection, hand-hygiene products, sharps containers and disinfectants at the points of use. Staff wear gloves for contact with blood, body fluids, secretions, non-intact skin and contaminated surfaces, and remove them and wash hands afterward.

Pre-employment and annual health: Each employee provides an annual physician, PA or RN statement of health and a TB assessment, as required by 18 NYCRR §487.9(a)(8) (see PER-03). The Administrator keeps these in the personnel file. EALR/SNALR direct-care staff also have immunization and TB records on file under 10 NYCRR §1001.11. Staff with a positive TB screen or symptoms are referred for evaluation and may not work with residents until cleared.

Staff with fever, vomiting, diarrhea, undiagnosed rash, or other contagious conditions notify the employee in charge before the shift and do not work with residents or handle food until they are symptom-free for the period set by the facility's physician or health department guidance, which is ordinarily at least 48 hours after symptoms end for gastrointestinal illness. Employees with sick leave rights are reminded of them (see WC-01).

Bloodborne pathogen exposure control plan: the coordinator writes and maintains the plan, which identifies job tasks with exposure risk, available protective equipment, hepatitis B vaccination offered to at-risk employees at no cost, the sharps handling rules, and the post-exposure procedure. The plan is reviewed each year and when tasks or equipment change.

Post-exposure procedure, steps 1-3: After a needlestick, cut, splash or other exposure, the employee immediately washes the wound with soap and water, flushes splashed eyes or mucous membranes with water, and reports to the employee in charge without delay. The employee in charge notifies the Administrator the same day.

Post-exposure procedure, steps 4-6: The employee is sent right away, preferably within two hours, to the clinician or emergency department listed in the exposure plan, [CLINIC OR EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT NAME AND PHONE], for evaluation, counseling, testing and any recommended post-exposure prophylaxis. The clinician determines whether the event is a significant risk exposure under 10 NYCRR Part 63. The source resident's information is handled confidentially and in line with applicable law (see RS-07).

The Administrator records the exposure on an Incident Report and exposure incident record that includes the circumstances and device involved, and reviews whether a safer device or practice is needed. Medical records related to exposures are confidential and kept separate from the general personnel file.

Cleaning and disinfecting: Housekeeping staff clean and disinfect high-touch surfaces, such as doorknobs, rails, light switches, call devices, dining tables, and bathrooms, at least daily and as needed, with an EPA-registered disinfectant used according to its label. Blood and body-fluid spills are cleaned immediately with gloves and an approved disinfectant (see HK-01).

Laundry: Staff handle soiled linen and clothing with gloves, do not shake it, and bag it at the point of use. Soiled laundry is kept apart from clean laundry, and is washed in hot water with detergent and dried completely. Clean linen is stored covered and away from soiled items. Contaminated sharps and items go in puncture-resistant containers, and regulated waste is disposed of in a lawful way.
Food and kitchen: Food handlers follow hand-washing, glove and illness-exclusion rules in FS-02 and FS-03.

Residents: The nurse or Case Manager asks about infection symptoms during daily care and at each change-of-condition review, and asks the resident's physician about care and isolation precautions when a communicable disease is suspected or diagnosed (see RS-04). Resident immunization for influenza, pneumococcal disease and other vaccines is offered as recommended by the physician and recorded in the resident record (see MED-02).

Outbreaks and reportable diseases: When two or more residents or staff develop the same infectious illness in a short period, or a reportable communicable disease is diagnosed, the employee in charge notifies the Administrator immediately. The Administrator reports to the local health department, [LOCAL HEALTH DEPARTMENT NAME AND PHONE], as required by law, and follows its direction. The Administrator also contacts the DOH regional office when required and enters any required report (see REC-02).

During an outbreak, the Administrator may order cohorting, room meals, visitor limits, increased cleaning, and exclusion of ill staff. The Administrator tells residents, representatives and staff what is needed, keeps a line list of cases, and does not end precautions until the health department says it is safe.

The coordinator keeps an infection log of resident and staff infections, the type, onset date, unit, and actions taken, and presents trends to the quality improvement committee (see GOV-02). The Administrator updates procedures when trends show a need.

documents.how_used: This is the official Part II program-review checklist. It applies to new adult homes and enriched housing programs, changes of operator, and new ALR, EALR, SNALR and ALP applications. The ALR and ALP applicant instructions say to submit only changed or new materials and to check 'No Change' where applicable. The 'required_items' list below uses the form's own item numbers. I left out paperwork that is not policy content: item 1 (application type check-boxes), item 2 (administrator/coordinator qualifications on DSS-3233, diplomas and transcripts), item 9 (Mental Health Agreement), item 12 (list of forms), item 15d–15f (support letters, nursing-facility transfer agreement, DSS contract), item 16 (waiver and equivalency list), item 18 (workers' compensation certificate), item 26(b)–(d) (dietary consultant agreement, resume and licenses), item 26(f) (kitchen and dining room diagram), and item 31 (resident fund account statement).
